Preface: The Question Behind the Question

The car park, twenty past eight in the evening. Father Anselm is holding his keys and wishing he were holding a cigarette, and a young woman is standing between him and the exit in the way that people stand when they have been building up to something for a month.

She is twenty-four. She works in marketing. She has a notebook in her bag with a cover the colour of a good decision, and she has been writing in it every day since her mother was diagnosed, three times in the morning and six in the afternoon and nine at night, because a video told her that the number was the method. Her mother is in remission. She is not sure, at night, whether that is a thing to be grateful for or a thing to be afraid of.

She says, quickly, and with a small apologetic laugh: Father, is it okay if I manifest?

I will call her Nadia. She is a composite of a dozen conversations, in the manner described at the end of this preface, but the notebook is not invented and neither is the question.

He has four minutes. He is tired. He knows exactly what the Church teaches about divination and superstition and the sin of tempting God, and he knows that none of it is quite the answer to the question she is actually asking, which is not a question about metaphysics at all. It is a question about whether anything is listening, and whether her mind is a power or a wound.

· · ·

This is not an unusual conversation. The question gets asked in Catholic parishes at the moment, usually by someone in their twenties, usually quietly, and usually with a slight apology attached.

The priest who is asked it has, as a rule, three options and no good one. He can say no, in which case he has given a correct answer to a badly understood question and has probably lost the person. He can say yes, in which case he has implicitly baptized a metaphysics that denies creation. Or he can say something true and complicated, in which case he has four minutes in a car park and a woman with a notebook waiting to hear whether her hope is a sin.

This book exists because none of those three answers is adequate, and because the Church has been here before — not with this exact phenomenon, but with this exact shape of problem. In the thirteenth century, a complete and self-consistent account of reality arrived in Western Europe from outside the faith, written by a pagan, mediated by Muslim commentators, taught in the universities to Christians who found it more intellectually satisfying than the theology they had inherited. Some wanted it banned. Some wanted it compartmentalized: true in philosophy, true in faith, never the two in the same sentence. One man, a Dominican of awkward manners and enormous patience, wanted to take it apart and rebuild it.

That man is the reason this book is possible. Thomas Aquinas is often described as having “baptized Aristotle,” which is a pretty phrase and a false one. He did not baptize Aristotle. He broke Aristotle and rebuilt him, and in the process he rejected a great deal: that the world is eternal, that the soul dies with the body, that everything happens by necessity, that God does not know or care about particulars. What he kept, he kept on new terms. What he rejected, he rejected by name and by argument. And the whole operation took fifty years and got him condemned.

The manifest space — the loose, networked world of the Law of Attraction, of Neville Goddard and The Secret, of scripting and the 369 method and SATS and revision, of the current and constantly mutating ecosystem of short videos in which a young woman explains that your thoughts create your reality — is not Aristotle. It is not a philosophy; it is a praxis with a theology attached, sold in a market, distributed by algorithm, and practiced by millions of people who would not recognize the word “metaphysics” if it were printed on their vision board. It is not a pagan science. It is a Christian heresy with excellent aesthetics.

That difference matters, and Part Three of this book argues that it changes the method. But the shape of the problem is the same. A system arrives that explains something true about human experience — that attention shapes action, that expectation shapes perception, that desire is a form of knowledge, that words are not neutral, that the interior life is not private — and then explains it wrongly, in a way that makes the creature into the creator and the creature’s suffering into the creature’s fault. The Church’s task is neither to deny the experience nor to accept the explanation. It is to give a better explanation and a better practice, and then to spend a generation teaching it.

That is the argument of this book, stated plainly: the manifest space can be harmonized with Catholic faith, but only by conversion and not by addition. The rest of the book does three things with that sentence. It shows what is true in the phenomenon, at the level of detail that a person who has done it would recognize. It says precisely what is false, claim by claim, with reasons rather than adjectives. And it proposes a practice — not a prohibition, a practice — that a woman with a notebook could actually keep on a Tuesday, and that her priest could hand her in four minutes. You cannot pour Catholic devotion into the Law of Attraction and stir. The metaphysics will curdle. What you can do — what the Church has done before, with Aristotle and with the Stoics and with the festivals of the peoples she evangelized — is to take the real goods, refuse the false framework, rebuild the practices inside a different causal architecture, and let the result be judged by its fruits over a long enough time to know.

· · ·

This is a research project, not a revelation. It has four sources, and it is worth naming them at the start, because the book’s credibility depends on keeping them distinct.

The first is Scripture, read in the Church’s tradition — above all Romans 8, 1 Corinthians 12, Colossians 3 and 1 John 3, which between them contain the whole theology of manifestation that this book will try to recover.

The second is the Thomistic corpus and the magisterial tradition that received it: the Summa, the disputed questions, Leo XIII’s Aeterni Patris, Fides et Ratio, Spe Salvi, Gaudete et Exsultate, the Catechism, and the 2003 Pontifical Council reflection on the New Age, Jesus Christ, Bearer of the Water of Life, which remains the most precise official description of the phenomenon in question and which has been largely forgotten.

The third is direct description of the manifest space: its primary texts, its practices, its vocabulary, and its people. I have tried throughout to describe it in its own terms before judging it, because a refutation of a straw man is not a refutation; it is a performance.

The fourth is the Church’s own procedure for discernment — the norms for judging private revelation, issued in 1978 and revised in 2024 — which turns out to be a ready-made instrument for classifying manifestation practices, and which supplies something this project badly needs: a way of saying “not now,” “with caution,” “under supervision,” and “no” without collapsing everything into a single verdict.

· · ·

Three warnings before we begin, because each of them is a way this book could be misused.

It is not a permission slip. Nothing here says that a Catholic may adopt the Law of Attraction with a holy water upgrade. Several of the claims at the heart of the manifest space are incompatible with the Creed, and Part Two identifies them by name. Anyone who reads this book as a licence has read it against its argument.

It is not a condemnation of persons. The people in the manifest space are not fools and they are not, as a rule, dabbling in anything they understand to be occult. They are mostly people who were handed a technique when they asked for hope, by a culture that had stopped offering them anything else. The blame for that lies considerably closer to the institution than to them.

It is not authoritative. I have no mandate to write any of this, and the Church has not asked me to. Everything here is submitted to correction. Where the book proposes practices, it proposes them for testing under pastoral supervision, not for adoption on my word. A book about discernment that asks to be believed on its own authority would have failed at the first page.

· · ·

What the reader is entitled to expect, then, is this: a description of the phenomenon that its adherents would recognize; a method derived from the most successful integration in the Church’s history; an audit of the claims, claim by claim, with verdicts; a positive theology of manifestation built from Scripture and the tradition; a set of concrete practices that could actually be tried; and a plan for the institutions that would have to carry it, over the decades it would take.

That is a large programme. It is not larger than the one Thomas took on, and he had worse handwriting and no search engine.

The question behind the question — the one the young woman in the parish is really asking — is not is manifestation allowed. It is: is reality responsive to me at all, and if it is, who is listening? She has been told by her culture that the answer is an impersonal law she can operate. She has been told by her religion, too often, that the answer is a distant decree she must accept. The Catholic answer is neither. It is that reality is responsive because it is created, that it is created by someone who listens, that her desire is a real participation in a real good, that her action is a real cause inside a providence that does not need to be manipulated because it has already gone to the Cross for her — and that what she is actually waiting for, whether she knows it or not, is not the thing she wrote in the journal. It is the manifestation of the children of God.

Everything else in this book is an unpacking of that sentence.

The Argument on One Page

If you read only one page of this book, read this one. Everything that follows is the working-out.

The manifest space is not primarily a set of false beliefs. It is a set of true observations attached to a false engine.

That sentence is the whole book. The observations are real: attention shapes perception, expectation shapes action, habit hardens into character, words do things, the interior life is not private. The engine is not: a universe that answers to the intensity of your feeling, that has no one at the centre of it, and that bills you for your own suffering.

· · ·

The argument in eight steps.

1. This is not a fringe. It is a grammar that a generation learned before it learned the Creed — a vocabulary, a set of procedures, and a mood, distributed by feed and group chat. It is the first spiritual system most of its adherents ever met that told them their inner life mattered — and it is not ancient wisdom but a datable American product, whose every rule has an author (chapters 1–2).

2. It works, partly, because it is partly true. Four of its observations are secure, and the Church has taught all four for longer than the movement has existed. What fails is the causal architecture — and the failure is not cosmetic, because it makes the creature into the creator and the sufferer into the author of her own suffering (chapters 3–4).

3. The Church has done this before. In the thirteenth century, Thomas Aquinas took a complete rival account of reality apart and rebuilt it inside the faith. He did it in six moves, he rejected about a third of what he received by name, it got him condemned, and the comparison has four limits that the book states rather than hides (chapters 5–7).

4. Four tests sort any spiritual claim: who is creator and who is creature; what is nature and what is grace; what is the cross and what is glory; who is this for — the self, or the Church (chapters 8–12).

5. Fourteen central claims, fourteen verdicts: four to integrate, three to correct, seven to reject. The verdicts are stated one by one, with reasons, so that a reader who disagrees knows exactly where to disagree (chapters 13–15).

6. The word is already ours. Manifestation is a divine act before it is a human technique. What the manifest space offers is a parody of a structure the Church owns — glory, provision, desire, hiddenness, sacrament, communion (chapters 16–24).

7. So keep the technique and change the addressee. Six marks distinguish a Catholic practice from a Christian-looking technique; four sets of transpositions convert the actual methods; one worked rite, the Novena of Desire, can be prayed as written; and two questions do most of the work at the bedside (chapters 25–32).

8. Then build, measure, and wait. Listen before you refute, publish the disputed questions, build the institutions, judge by fruit rather than testimonial, and give it fifty years. Answer the objections from both sides honestly — and where an objection cannot be answered, say so (chapters 33–40).

· · ·

If the argument is right, then the question is not whether the Church can survive the manifest space. It is whether the Church will do, with a generation formed by it, what she once did with Aristotle: describe it honestly, refuse what is false, keep what is true, and build something better that outlasts the argument.

What This Book Promises

Most books promise more than they deliver, and the blurbs are written by people who are not the author. Here is a promise written by the author, in advance, in the plainest terms available — so that you can hold the book to it, and so that you can put it down if it is not the book you need.

If you are a pastor, teacher, catechist, or spiritual director, this book promises you the ability to answer the question — is it okay if I manifest? — in about ninety seconds, without contempt and without lying, and then to hand the person something to do on Monday. The ninety seconds are in chapter 32. The something is in chapters 25 to 32, and one of them is a rite you can give away.

If you practice manifestation, or have tried to, this book promises not to tell you that you were stupid. It promises to take the thing you noticed seriously, to locate exactly where the mechanism you were handed goes wrong, and to argue that what you were reaching for is real, older, larger, and stranger than the technique — and that it can survive the thing the technique cannot survive, which is a refusal.

If you are a theologian, a scholar, or a sceptic, this book promises the strongest version of the argument, the sources for its claims, a stated method with four acknowledged limits, and the criteria by which it should be judged a failure. Chapter 36 is written to make the book falsifiable. Appendix A contains the forty questions where the real argument belongs.

If you are none of these — if you picked this up because someone sent you a chapter, or because the word in the title caught at something — this book promises that no chapter depends on a technical term introduced three hundred pages earlier, and that you can begin almost anywhere.

· · ·

What it does not promise. It does not promise that manifestation works, in the sense in which its teachers claim it works. It does not promise that the Church has a ready-made answer gathering dust in a curial drawer. It does not claim authority: no bishop asked for this book, no imprimatur attaches to it, and a reader who finds an error should assume the error is the author’s rather than the Church’s. It claims the help of the Holy Spirit, which is not a mandate from an office, and it would be a misuse of the first to pretend that it were the second. And it does not promise a resolution to the hardest question in the book, which is the question of why some prayers are answered and others are not; it promises only to state that question honestly and to refuse the two answers that are comfortable and false — that God is a mechanism, and that nothing is asked of us. It claims the help of the Holy Spirit, which is not the same thing as a mandate from an office, and it would be a misuse of the first to pretend that it were the second.

· · ·

What it costs you. Forty chapters. At ten minutes a chapter, the main argument is about seven hours — a long evening a week for two months, or a weekend and a half if you are the kind of person who reads a book the way other people take a course. The short path is three hours: chapters 1, 2, 3, 13, 16, 22, 26, 31, and 32, then the conclusion. The triage-only path is forty minutes: chapter 32 and Appendix B.

What it asks of you. Only what any argument asks: that you hold your objection in mind while the case is being made, and that you let it be answered before you decide it has not been.

· · ·

One more thing, and it is the reason for writing a book rather than a pamphlet. The claim being made here is not that a set of propositions is true — although that is part of it. The claim is that a practice is true, and practices cannot be argued into existence. They have to be described, taught, tested, and handed on by people who have done them. That is a work of years, and it is the work this book is trying to start. If you finish it and do nothing, the argument will have failed in the only way that matters.

A Note on Method, Sources, and Authority

On the object. “The manifestation space” is not a term of art and there is no magisterial document that uses it. I use it to name a field rather than a school: the loose network of books, videos, coaching programmes, journals, apps, hashtags and private practices gathered around a single proposition — that interior states (thoughts, feelings, assumptions, words, “vibrations”) causally produce exterior circumstances, and that the resemblance between the state and the circumstance is the mechanism. The field includes theistic versions (Word of Faith), mentalist versions (Neville Goddard and his many revivals), energetic versions (the Abraham-Hicks material), and thoroughly secularized versions (the self-help wing that speaks of “limiting beliefs” and “self-concept” and leaves the metaphysics vague). It includes practices from The Secret to “lucky girl syndrome,” from vision boards to “reality shifting,” from the 369 method to AI-generated affirmation audio.

On the term itself. There is a second, older, Catholic sense of manifestatio — the manifestation of conscience to a spiritual director, the epiphany of Christ, the discernment of claimed private revelations. I have not confused the two, but I have made the second do serious work in Part Three, because it turns out to be the strongest available answer to the first. The convergence is not a pun. It is the argument.

On description before judgment. Chapter by chapter, I have tried to state the manifest space’s positions in the strongest form I could find, from its own texts, before evaluating them. Where I quote Neville Goddard, I quote what he actually wrote. Where I characterize the practice of ordinary adherents, I am relying on the composite portraits described below, on the published sociological and journalistic literature, and on the pastoral experience reported to me by priests and campus ministers. Where I am uncertain, I say so.

On composite portraits. The people in this book are composites. Their details have been changed, combined, and in some cases invented, in the manner of reportage; no composite corresponds to a single identifiable person, and no quotation attributed to an anonymous person is a verbatim record. Direct quotations from published authors are real and are cited. I have not invented statistics. Where a number appears, it is drawn from published sources; where I am reasoning from impressions, I say “in my reading” or “the pattern I have seen.”

On citations. This is a work of synthesis rather than of archival scholarship, and the notes are correspondingly modest: citations appear in the text, in parentheses, in a short form that a reader can follow without a glossary. Primary sources are given by book, question, and article (for Aquinas by part, question, article: ST I, q. 1, a. 8). Magisterial documents are given by paragraph number. Appendix D lists the works I have relied on and indicates which are essential.

On the use of Thomas. I am not a medievalist and this is not a work of historical theology. The account of Aquinas in Part One is deliberately compressed and is aimed at extracting a method rather than settling disputed questions of interpretation. Readers who know the period will find omissions; I hope they will not find falsehoods. The claim I need from the history is narrow and, I think, secure: that the integration of Aristotle was achieved by describing the rival system accurately, separating its instruments from its metaphysics, subordinating its conclusions to revealed principles, rejecting specific theses by name, and institutionalizing the result over decades — and that this process was contested, slow, and at one point formally condemned.

On authority. This book has none. It is not a magisterial act, it is not approved by any bishop, and it does not ask the reader to accept anything on its own say-so. Where it proposes practices, it proposes them for supervised experiment. Where it makes doctrinal judgments, it tries to show its work from Scripture, the Catechism, and the recognized doctors, so that a competent authority can correct it quickly. A reader who finds an error should assume the error is mine and not the Church’s, and should say so.

On disagreement. The book argues against positions, not against people. If you practice manifestation and you are reading this, the book is not about how stupid you are. It is about how much of what you have already noticed is true, and what would happen if it were placed where it belongs.

Technical note. The manuscript is written in Markdown and built into a single-file HTML edition, a print edition (5.5 × 8.5 inches, for PDF), and an EPUB 3 edition by a small script in the same repository. Word counts and page counts are generated by the build, not asserted by the author: a 5.5 × 8.5 page at this type size carries about 243 words, and the finished book runs to about 75,803 words and 314 printed pages. The build report in the repository records the exact figures for every edition, and the same source produces the web, EPUB, and print versions, so a correction made once appears in all three.

Start Here — Three Ways Through This Book

Forty chapters, six parts, eight appendices. You do not have to read it in order, and most people will not. Here is the map, and here are the three routes through it.

· · ·

The map.

PartChaptersWhat it does
One — The Crisis and the Precedent1–7Describes the manifest space from the inside, then recovers the method by which Aquinas took Aristotle apart and rebuilt him — including what it cost him
Two — The Audit8–15Four tests, fourteen verdicts, a lexicon of thirty words, and an argument for why refutation alone never works
Three — The Reclamation16–24The positive theology: manifestation as a divine act, as gift, as glory, as hiddenness, as sacrament; providence, desire, and habitus
Four — The Practice25–32Six marks, four sets of transpositions, the Novena of Desire, and the triage sheet
Five — The Programme33–37What would have to be built: listening, the disputed questions, institutions, measurement, and a fifty-year horizon
Six — Contested Questions38–39The strongest objections from the tradition and from the manifest space, answered as far as they can be
Conclusion40The girl at 11:11, and the thing the whole world is waiting for
· · ·

Route one: straight through. Seven hours or so. The parts are built to be read in sequence, and the argument accumulates: Part Two assumes the method established in Part One, and Part Four assumes the theology established in Part Three. If you have the time, this is the route the book was written for.

Route two: the short path. Three hours, nine chapters and then the conclusion: 1 (the phenomenon), 2 (the grammar and where it came from), 3 (why it works), 13 (the fourteen claims and their verdicts), 16 (the word), 22 (providence), 26 (the six marks), 31 (the novena), 32 (the triage), then 40. Each stands on its own feet. This is the route for a reader who wants the argument without the scholarship.

Route three: triage only. Forty minutes: chapter 32 and Appendix B. That is the sheet you photocopy and keep in your breviary or your glove compartment. Come back for the rest when someone asks you a second question — because they will, and the second question is always harder than the first.

· · ·

For the pastor, catechist, teacher, or spiritual director, who needs something usable by Friday: read Part Two (chapters 8–15) and Part Four (chapters 25–32), then Appendix B. Come back for Part One when you want to know why this is not simply a matter of telling people to stop.

For the reader who is yourself drawn to manifestation — if you have a journal, if you have tried the methods, if some of it has worked and some of it has frightened you — begin with Part Three. It is written most directly to you, and it argues that the thing you have been reaching for is real, and larger and stranger and better than the mechanism you were given. Then read Part Two, which will be uncomfortable in places, and which is meant to be.

For the theologian, scholar, or sceptic, the argument is in Part One and Part Five. Part One establishes the method by analogy with the thirteenth century and states the four asymmetries that limit the analogy. Part Five sets out the programme, its governance, and the criteria by which it should be judged a failure. Appendix A contains forty disputed questions in outline, which is where I would expect the real argument to happen.

· · ·

For a study group, eight sessions of ninety minutes will cover the book without rushing it. The pattern that works is: everyone reads the two or three chapters beforehand; the session opens with one question from that week’s list; the group argues for fifty minutes; the last twenty are spent on the practice, which is to say on the exercise at the end of the relevant chapter, done rather than discussed.

SessionReadQuestion to open with
1chs. 1–2Why do people who have left the Church still believe that their thoughts create reality?
2chs. 3–7What did Aquinas actually refuse, and what did it cost him?
3chs. 8–12Apply the four tests to an ordinary piece of spiritual advice you have been given.
4chs. 13–15Which of the fourteen verdicts do you most want to argue with, and why?
5chs. 16–21What does the Church already have that the manifest space has counterfeited?
6chs. 22–24If God is provident, what is left for us to do?
7chs. 25–32Pray the Novena of Desire as a group, or take the triage and use it on a real case.
8chs. 33–40What would this parish have to build, and who would pay for it?
· · ·

A note on order. Each chapter opens with a promise — the line under its title tells you what the chapter will settle — and closes with three short blocks: the point (what it has established), do this (something to do, usually in ten minutes), and what this sets up (the next question). If you are reading for argument rather than practice, the three blocks will let you skip the exercises without losing the thread; if you are reading for practice, they are the part to keep.

A note on repetition. Because most readers arrive through a single chapter that someone sent them, the load-bearing distinctions are repeated where they are needed. This is deliberate. A book that assumes you read page one becomes unusable at page forty, and the person who needs chapter 32 is often the person who will never read chapters 1 to 31.

A note on tone. The book is written in the confidence that the reader is intelligent, has a life, and does not need to be scolded. Where it is sharp, it is sharp about ideas and institutions. Where it is gentle, it is gentle about the people who have been hurt by both.

· · ·

The appendices are not an afterthought; three of them are meant to be used.

A — The Forty Questions. The disputed questions in outline, with the state of the argument on each.

B — The Triage Card. One page. Photocopy it.

C — The Thirty-Day Pilot. A parish or campus programme, with a control group and a written protocol.

D — The Reader’s Guide and Bibliography. What to read next, in what order, and which ten works are essential.

E — A Glossary of Thirty Words. The vocabulary, including the words the manifest space has quietly redefined.

F — A Note on the Text. Sources, conventions, and the limits of the author’s competence.

G — Index of Citations. Every scriptural and catechetical reference, by book and paragraph.

H — Index of Names and Terms. Where each figure and idea is treated.

Part One

The Crisis and the Precedent

All men by nature desire to know.

Aristotle, Metaphysics I.1

Before anything can be harmonized, two things must be understood: the thing that is to be harmonized, and the operation by which the Church has harmonized anything like it before. This part supplies both. It describes the manifest space from the inside — its grammar, its implicit theology, and the real human needs it serves — and then returns to Paris in the thirteenth century to recover, in some detail, the method by which Thomas Aquinas took a rival account of reality apart and rebuilt it inside the faith. It ends with the cost of that method, which was considerable, and which anyone attempting the same thing should expect to pay.

Chapter 1

A Girl, a Journal, and a Universe

The phenomenon is not a fringe. It is a grammar that a generation learned before it learned the Creed — and the first task is to see it clearly enough to describe it without contempt.

She writes it three times in the morning, six in the afternoon, nine at night. Three, six, nine. The number of the method is in the method’s name, which tells you something about the kind of thing it is: not a doctrine to be believed but a procedure to be performed, and procedures are easier to love than doctrines.

The sentence she writes is in the present tense, because the present tense is the whole trick. Not I want a job that does not make me sick with dread. Not I hope I meet someone. But: I am grateful for my new job. I am grateful for my new job. I am grateful for my new job. Nine times, in a notebook with a cover the colour of a good decision, at 11:11, because the clock said 11:11 and the clock saying 11:11 is a sign, or it is not a sign, and either way it costs nothing to write it down.

She is twenty-four. She was baptized, confirmed, and made her first communion at a parish with a car park and a noticeboard. She can recite the Our Father and could not, if you asked her, tell you what the Church teaches about providence, because nobody ever told her, and because the question never came up in a way that made it urgent. What did come up, urgently, at 2 a.m., in the months after her mother’s diagnosis, was the question of whether anything at all was listening.

She has not left the Church. She goes at Christmas and sometimes at Easter, and she has a rosary in a drawer, and she has prayed it twice. She would describe herself, if pressed, as spiritual but not especially religious, which is a sentence she learned from the internet and which describes, accurately, a person who has a practice and no theology to hold it. She is not confused about whether God exists. She is confused about whether he is in the room.

And so: the notebook. The 11:11. The gratitude that is also a claim. She is not doing anything wicked. She is doing something that works, in the way that a placebo works and in the way that a habit works and in the way that a person who has been told she is powerless will seize on any lever, even a lever that does not exist, because a lever in the hand is better than a void.

· · ·

The manifest space is hard to see because it has no building. It is not a religion by any of the measures we use to count religions: no membership, no clergy, no creed, no census category. It is a vocabulary, a set of practices, and a mood, distributed through books and feeds and group chats, and it has become so ordinary among people under thirty-five that it functions the way “karma” functions: a word you use without committing to a cosmology.

The books are not marginal, though. The Secret has sold, by its publisher’s count, more than thirty million copies since 2006, and its central claim — that like attracts like, that thought is a form of transmission, that the universe is a catalogue from which you order by feeling — entered the general culture so completely that it is now difficult to parody. The earlier layer, the New Thought writers of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and above all Neville Goddard, whose shelf of short books and several hundred recorded lectures have been digitized, clipped, remixed, and set to ambient music by a revival that began around 2015 and has not yet crested — supplies the metaphysics. The newest layer supplies the liturgy: short video, first person, soft-spoken, direct address. You are going to script it. You are going to feel it as if it has already happened. You are not going to tell anyone.

None of this shows up in parish statistics. It shows up in confession.

“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It has been — a while. I think I’ve been manifesting, and I don’t know if that’s a sin.”

· · ·

Nadia is a composite, made of a dozen conversations, and I give her a name only so that the argument has somewhere to live. She works in marketing. She has a spreadsheet of her manifestations, colour-coded, and she is faintly embarrassed by it, which is itself interesting: she is embarrassed not by the practice but by the hope in it. She manifests a promotion, a specific number on a scale, and a man she has never met, whose initials she has written in the back of the notebook because a video told her that writing the initials is the step that makes it real.

Her mother is in remission. Nadia believes — and this is the sentence that should stop any pastor in his tracks — that she caused the remission. Not that her prayers were heard. That her frequency changed the outcome. She is not boasting. She says it the way a person says something they are afraid to say out loud, because if the thought created the remission, then the thought could have created the cancer, and she is not sure, at night, which one she was thinking in the year before the diagnosis.

Daniel is thirty-two and left the Church at nineteen, over a homily about Hell, and found manifestation through a business mentor. He is now, by any ordinary measure, a success: a coaching practice, an apartment, a body that suggests discipline. He is also the most honest person in this book. “It works,” he told me. “That’s the thing nobody wants to deal with. It works. And then you get the thing, and you discover that the reason you wanted it was that you thought it would make you feel like a person. And it doesn’t. So you manifest the next thing.” He has begun, in the last two years, to pray again, in secret, in a way he cannot explain and would not defend.

Father Anselm is fifty-eight and has been a pastor for twenty-one years. He is not a fool and he is not a liberal and he is not a reactionary; he is tired. He hears the question about manifestation perhaps twice a month. He has tried three answers. He has told a young woman that manifestation is superstition, and watched her face close. He has told another that it is “just a way of setting intentions,” and felt the sentence curdle in his mouth as he said it, because he knew it was not. He has said, “bring it to prayer,” and she did, and it did not stop, and she stopped mentioning it.

His problem is not that he does not know the doctrine. His problem is that the doctrine he knows is true and abstract and slow, and the thing he is competing with is false and concrete and available at eleven at night, and he has four minutes in a car park.

· · ·

Here is the thesis of this book in a form that a pastor can use in the car park.

The manifest space is not primarily a set of false beliefs. It is a set of true observations attached to a false engine.

The observations are real. Attention does shape perception and action. Habit does harden into character. Desire is not neutral and is not arbitrary. Words do things. The interior life is not private. Expectation is a form of causality. Nobody who has actually prayed, or actually loved, or actually grieved, will deny that the inside of a person is connected to the outside of the world. The manifest space noticed this, said it loudly, and built a practice around it, at a moment when large parts of Christian catechesis had stopped noticing it at all.

The engine is false. The claim that the connection runs by resemblance — that the thought of a thing causes the thing, by a law, because thought is a kind of energy and like attracts like — is not an exaggeration of Christian teaching. It is a replacement of it. It makes the creature the creator, the will the efficient cause, and the outcome the product of a technique. It has more in common with the cosmology of the Corpus Hermeticum than with the Gospel, and it produces, inevitably, a moral order in which the sick are the authors of their illness.

So the question for the Church is not: is this true or false? It is partly true and structurally false, which is the hardest combination, because a thing that is partly true can survive refutation indefinitely. The question is: what would it take to separate the observation from the engine, and give people the observation back with a better engine?

That is, more or less, the question Thomas Aquinas faced in the 1260s, with different material.

· · ·

Three costs make this urgent. They are not the costs usually named.

The first is the blame of the sufferer. A system in which interior states cause exterior circumstances has no way to account for innocent suffering, and so it must deny that suffering is innocent. The logic is not optional; it is internal. If you attracted the good, you attracted the bad. The manifest space tries to soften this with talk of “lessons” and “growth,” but the softness is cosmetic. Somewhere in the system’s basement there is a room in which a woman is told that she attracted her child’s leukemia, and the room is not empty.

The second is the evacuation of prayer. When a practice becomes a technique, the other person disappears. A technique addresses a mechanism; a prayer addresses a Father. The manifest space trains people, with great efficiency, to relate to the universe as a mechanism — and then those same people come to Mass and relate to God the same way, and find that it does not work, and conclude either that God is not there or that they are doing it wrong. This is the most pastorally destructive effect, and the least discussed, because it is invisible: nobody leaves the Church over manifestation. They just stop expecting anything from prayer.

The third is a rival soteriology with better user experience. The manifest space offers salvation — from powerlessness, from shame, from the sense of being a passenger in one’s own life — and it offers it in a form that is immediate, free at the point of use, aesthetically beautiful, and designed for a phone. The Church offers salvation too, and it is better, and it is slower, and it is administered by people who are tired and in a car park. This is not a fair fight, and pretending otherwise is not piety; it is wishful thinking.

· · ·

The rest of this book is the long answer. But the first move has to be the one that any honest encounter requires, and it is the move the Church has made badly for sixty years: describe the thing.

Not the thing you are afraid of. Not the thing the newspaper says. Not the thing that is easy to refute. The actual thing: what it claims, in what order, with what internal logic, with what implicit theology, and with what real human need at its centre.

That is the subject of the next two chapters. And the reason to do it carefully — the reason not to skip ahead to the verdict — is that the verdict you reach without a description is always the same verdict, which is no, and the Church has already tried no as a strategy, in 1277 and in 1959, and it did not work either time.

The point

The manifest space is not a set of false beliefs. It is a set of true observations attached to a false engine — which is why it survives refutation.

Do this

Name which of the four needs it meets in you, or in someone you love: agency, method, desire, beauty.

What this sets up

A system held together by a grammar cannot be answered one sentence at a time. So we need the grammar.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 2

The Grammar of Manifestation

It is not a doctrine but a grammar — seven rules that generate an indefinite number of teachings. That is why refuting one version leaves the others untouched.

A grammar is not a set of sentences. It is the small set of rules that generates an indefinite number of sentences, most of which have never been spoken. You cannot refute a grammar by refuting a sentence; the speaker will simply produce another sentence.

This is the first thing to understand about the manifest space, and the reason so much Catholic argument against it fails. A catechist who has demolished The Secret on a Tuesday will find on Wednesday that his student has moved on to Neville Goddard, who agrees with the demolition and offers a more sophisticated version. He will demolish Neville, and she will produce a “shadow work” coach, or a “nervous system regulation” account, or a Catholic influencer who has synthesized all of it with the Rosary. The sentences change. The grammar does not.

So let us state the grammar. Seven rules, in the order in which they do their work.

· · ·

1. Interior states cause exterior circumstances.

This is the engine, and it is non-negotiable. Thought, feeling, assumption, word, and expectation are causally efficacious beyond the body — not merely by shaping the agent’s actions (which is true and unremarkable) but by acting directly on the world.

Notice how the claim is usually softened in polite conversation (“it’s about mindset, really”) and how quickly it hardens again when someone is in pain (“you need to change your frequency”). The soft version is compatible with Christianity. The hard version is the one that does the work, and it is the one that must be addressed.

2. The mechanism is resemblance.

Like attracts like. Thought of a thing resembles the thing; therefore thought of the thing attracts it. This is the rule that distinguishes the manifest space from a generic optimism, and it is the rule that makes the whole system cohere. It is also the rule that is most obviously a fragment of an older cosmology — the sympathetic magic that the ancient world took for granted and that the Church spent four centuries instructing converts to abandon.

3. There is an agency on the other side, and it is ambiguous.

Usually called “the universe.” Formally impersonal — a law, a frequency, a field — but in practice addressed as a person: asked, thanked, negotiated with, occasionally scolded. Esther Hicks’s “Abraham” is explicit; Neville’s “imagination” is the human subject deified; the secular coaches avoid the question by speaking of “the field” or “quantum.” The ambiguity is functional. It allows the practitioner to feel the intimacy of prayer without the inconvenience of a God who might say no.

4. Desire is authoritative.

In the manifest space, desire is the compass and the credential. What you want is the signal of what is yours; the work is to clarify it, feel it, and remove the resistance to it. There is no doctrine of disordered desire, because there is no standard by which desire could be disordered. This is the rule that makes the system feel liberating, and it is the rule that makes it, in Christian terms, a moral catastrophe.

5. Resistance is the only obstacle.

Doubt, negativity, “limiting beliefs,” low vibration, “blocked energy” — these are the enemies. Their presence explains failure. Their absence guarantees success. The consequence, which the system cannot avoid, is that suffering becomes evidence of a personal failure of interiority. The dying person who is afraid is not dying; she is “resisting.” The poor man is not poor; he is “in scarcity.”

6. Technique is learnable and repeatable.

The system is a technology, and this is its great strength. There are methods with names. There are steps, timings, positions, scripts, journals, and 3 a.m. protocols. Anyone can do it. It does not require seminary, lineage, baptism, or worthiness. Compare this to the average parish’s offerings for a young adult in crisis, which are: the Rosary, Adoration, and a pamphlet.

The names rotate faster than any bibliography can track: the 369 method, scripting, the whisper method, the pillow method, SATS, revision, “lucky girl syndrome,” “reality shifting,” “assuming the state.” A book that refutes the names will be obsolete in two years. A book that describes the grammar will still be useful after they have been replaced — as they will be, and as they already have been twice since The Secret.

7. Verification is private and unfalsifiable.

Success is confirmed by “signs” (11:11, a song, a bird), by “the bridge of incidents” (the means by which the thing arrived), and by selective memory. Failure is never a disconfirmation; it is evidence of insufficient alignment. The system therefore cannot be refuted by experience, which is why it survives experience so well.

· · ·

Put the seven together and you can generate the whole field. Take rule 1 and drop rule 3, and you have secular psychology-of-abundance. Take rule 3 and make the agency personal and Christian, and you have Word of Faith: God is the mechanism’s enforcer, and faith is the lever. Take rule 2 and give it a physics vocabulary, and you have the “energy” wing. Take rule 4 seriously and drop rule 6’s discipline, and you have the aesthetic wing: candles, journals, and the ritual of self-care.

The variants matter for pastoral care. The theistic version is closer to Christianity and therefore harder to disentangle; the energetic version is further away and easier to name as foreign; the psychologized version is the most common among educated young Catholics and the hardest to object to, because it has learned to describe itself in the language of mental health. But the grammar is one grammar, and it is the grammar that has to be answered.

· · ·

Before going further, it is worth being precise about what the grammar is not, because three common Catholic characterizations are unjust and one is dangerously complacent. Let us clear them.

It is not simply greed. The prosperity-gospel caricature — name it and claim it, buy the jet — describes one wing of one variant, and it is not the centre of gravity of the present phenomenon. Most practitioners are not trying to get rich. They are trying to get unstuck: a job that does not destroy them, a body that works, a relationship, a reason to get up. A generation raised on precarity does not need a theology of abundance; it needs a reason to believe that effort is not futile, and it will take that reason wherever it finds it.

It is not simply the occult. Some of it is, and Part Two will draw that line carefully. But most of it has no interest in spirits and would be baffled by the accusation. The practitioners are not signing anything. They are journaling.

It is not simply stupidity. The people in this space include physicians, engineers, and at least one Carmelite I know of who reads Neville “for the psychology.” The system is internally coherent, psychologically sophisticated in places, and supported by real observations. Condescension is not an argument, and it is not even an accurate description.

The complacent view is the most dangerous: that it is harmless. It is not harmless. It is a theodicy, and it has victims, and they are usually sick, poor, or grieving. This is the point at which the Church’s response stops being an intellectual exercise and becomes a work of mercy.

· · ·

There is one more feature of the grammar that must be named, because it explains why the phenomenon spreads the way it does and why it will not be argued away: it is designed for the medium it lives in.

A creed needs a community to transmit it. A grammar needs only a sentence, and sentences are cheap. The manifest space is perfectly adapted to a world of short video, algorithmic recommendation, and parasocial intimacy: every element is a thirty-second unit, every unit is self-contained, every unit ends with an invitation to a practice, and the practice requires nothing but the viewer and her phone. It is the first spirituality in history that is optimized for distribution.

That is not a small advantage. It means the Church is not competing with a set of ideas; it is competing with a delivery system. And the delivery system has already learned something the Church keeps forgetting: that people do not adopt a metaphysics. They adopt a practice, and the metaphysics comes along quietly in the packaging.

Where the grammar came from

Seven rules, and every one of them has an author and a date.

That is the fact the manifest space most needs to conceal and the Church most needs to say. The system is not ancient wisdom recovered; it is not the perennial philosophy, and it is certainly not the faith of the martyrs in a new vocabulary. It is a datable product of the American nineteenth century, assembled out of clinical observation, hermetism, business optimism and therapeutic technique, and then repackaged three times. Kate Bowler, Beryl Satter, Tara Isabella Burton and Eva Illouz have told this history properly, and anyone who wants to argue with the manifest space should read them before arguing with it. But the argument of this book needs only the outline, because the outline is the point: what has a date can be judged, and a system with a history is a system that can be converted.

The engine came from a healer. Phineas Parkhurst Quimby (1802–1866) was a Maine clockmaker who became a mesmerist and then abandoned mesmerism for something he thought better: the claim that disease originates in the patient’s belief. He treated the sick by argument — by persuading them out of the belief he held to be the cause — and the cures were frequent enough to be noticed far outside New England. Quimby published almost nothing. His students published everything. Warren Felt Evans, a Swedenborgian minister, put the teaching into books — The Mental Cure (1869), Mental Medicine (1875) — and in doing so supplied the movement with the thing Quimby never had: a metaphysics.

The movement was named in the 1890s. By the end of the century “New Thought” was a network of teachers, journals, and correspondence courses, with Emma Curtis Hopkins — the movement’s teacher of teachers — training a generation of founders, and with Charles and Myrtle Fillmore’s Unity, Divine Science, and later Ernest Holmes’s Religious Science (The Science of Mind, 1926) institutionalizing it. Mary Baker Eddy’s Christian Science (1875) ran beside it and often against it; Satter’s Each Mind a Kingdom shows why the quarrel is instructive. Both were mind cure. They differed over matter, over gender, and above all over desire — and it is the branch that won that settled the rule that desire is authoritative.

The business wing added the promise. Wallace Wattles’s The Science of Getting Rich (1910), Charles Haanel’s The Master Key System (1912), Napoleon Hill’s Think and Grow Rich (1937), Joseph Murphy’s The Power of Your Subconscious Mind (1963), and — the decisive one for respectability — Norman Vincent Peale’s The Power of Positive Thinking (1952), which carried the method out of the sects and into mainline Protestant pews. Peale is the reason a Catholic pastor is now more likely to meet this material in a parishioner’s business reading than in her astrology app.

Neville Goddard gave it a theology. Born in Barbados in 1905, dead in Los Angeles in 1972, Goddard did what none of his predecessors could: he made the system metaphysically explicit, and he made it beautiful. His lectures are the reason this book quotes him rather than The Secret. He also made a distinction his popularizers drop, and the distinction matters for everything that follows: the law — imagination creates reality — is not the promise, which is Christ formed in the one who imagines. Chapter 16 takes that distinction seriously and shows what it costs him.

Then the algorithm finished the job. Rhonda Byrne’s film and book of 2006 repackaged the 1910 material for a new century; the short-video feed repackaged it again, in units of thirty seconds, with a practice attached to every one. Byrne’s own sources are the business wing and the channeled “Abraham” material of Esther Hicks, which is to say that The Secret is not a new revelation but a second-hand compilation — a fact that would embarrass the movement if the movement were embarrassed by anything.

The genealogy does three things for the argument. First, it shows that the seven rules are sediment, not revelation: rule 2, resemblance, is far older than Quimby — it reaches back through the Renaissance magic that the Church condemned in the sixteenth century as it condemned divination in the twentieth; rule 1 is a clinic; rule 3 is a law with the lawgiver removed; rule 4 is the twentieth century’s addition; rules 5 to 7 are packaging. Second, it dates the Church’s silence. Mind cure consolidated in the 1890s, in the same decade in which the Church’s own answer to the same question — how does a small and ordinary life become large? — was being written by a twenty-four-year-old Carmelite in Lisieux and published, after her death, as Story of a Soul. The Church had the better answer and did not distribute it, and the field was left to the sects. Third, and most usefully: a system with a history can be converted, because conversion is what the Church does with histories. Aristotle had a history too, and the men who gave him one in the thirteenth century were not refuting him. They were baptizing what could be baptized and burying the rest.

Which leaves the layer that has no author at all.

The newest layer is a machine

There is one further development that the description has to include, because it changes the economics of the whole field and because most writing about manifestation has not caught up with it.

The practice used to require a book, a course, or a coach — that is, an author, a price, and a person who could be asked a question. It now requires none of these. Affirmation audio is synthesized to order, in the practitioner’s own voice or in a voice she has chosen, and looped under a track that a program composed for her. Subliminal recordings are personalized with her name and her intention. Apps write the script, set the count, and remind her at the hour she is most suggestible. Chatbots will play the coach, the confidant, and — this is the part that should concern a confessor — the spiritual director, at three in the morning, in a tone that has been optimized never to disappoint.

Three consequences follow, and only the first is obvious.

The friction has gone to zero. A book can be argued with, and its author can be held to account. A generated track has no author, no community, no doctrine to state, and nobody to complain to. The movement is losing the last structures that made it describable — which is why this book has to describe a grammar rather than a list of teachings, and why a response organized around refuting particular books will be obsolete before it is printed.

The competitive advantage has become absolute. The manifest space’s god was always a god who could not refuse. The machine has now given that god a customer-service voice: infinitely patient, never tired, never disappointed, and constitutionally incapable of saying no. No parish, no director, and no confessor can compete with that on availability. The Church cannot win an availability contest and should stop trying to. What she has is presence, and presence does not scale — which is precisely why it is the thing the machine cannot counterfeit, and why the answer to an always-available technique is a person who is actually there on Thursday.

The mutation rate has outrun the magisterium. A curial document takes years; the idiom changes every eighteen months. This is the strongest argument for the method of this book over a list of prohibitions: the Church cannot rule on each new technique, and does not need to. Four tests and six marks will still work when the platform, the format, and the vocabulary have all been replaced, because they test the shape of a practice rather than its packaging.

There is a temptation here for the Church as well, and it should be named while we are being honest. The same tools will be offered to her, and some are good: a parish that can produce a decent audio examen for its own people is not doing anything wrong. But a chatbot cannot hear a confession, and a generated director is the perfect anti-director, because the one thing a director must be able to do is refuse. A machine trained to be affirming is a machine trained to be useless at exactly the point where the cure begins.

Which is why the answer to a grammar cannot be a refutation. It has to be another grammar — one that is true, and that generates practices, and that is at least as available at eleven at night.

The point

Manifestation is a grammar of seven rules, not a doctrine of one claim — and every rule has an author and a date. Refute a sentence and the grammar produces another; date the grammar and it becomes convertible.

Do this

Listen for the seven rules in the next piece of manifestation content you meet — and count how many are actually present.

What this sets up

A grammar implies a theology. Read the manifest space as a system, and it has every part but one.

Chapter 3

A Counter-Summa

Read the manifest space as a theological system rather than a set of tips, and it turns out to have every part — a God, a creation, an anthropology, a sin, a salvation, a revelation, a church, and an eschatology. The parts are wrong in a consistent way.

Nobody in the manifest space has written a Summa. They have, collectively, written one anyway.

The system has a doctrine of God, a doctrine of creation, an anthropology, a hamartiology (a doctrine of sin), a soteriology, a revelation, an ecclesiology, a sacramental theology, and an eschatology. None of these is stated as such; each is implied by the grammar described in the last chapter, and each can be extracted by asking the questions the tradition asks. Doing so is not pedantry. It is the only way to see that the manifest space is not a set of tips that happen to be attached to some odd ideas. It is a rival account of everything, with a hole where the creator should be.

Here is the extraction.

· · ·

On God. The manifest space’s God is either the universe or the self, and usually both at once. Neville Goddard is the most explicit, though the sentence he repeats most often is not his: “Man is all imagination. God is man and exists in us and we in him” — William Blake’s annotation to Berkeley, which Neville quoted in lecture after lecture until it became the load-bearing wall of his system. What Neville adds to Blake is not a metaphysics but a method for using it. The identification is not a metaphor in his system; it is the system’s foundation. In the energetic wing, the divine is an impersonal field of vibration, addressed in the second person out of courtesy. In the psychologized wing, the question is avoided, which is itself a theological position: a God so vague that nothing can be asked of him and nothing can be owed to him.

What is never present, in any variant, is a God who is other: free, personal, creator, able to say no, able to give what was not asked for, able to be loved rather than operated. The 2003 Pontifical Council document put the matter with unusual precision: the God of the New Age “is neither personal nor transcendent. Nor is it the Creator and sustainer of the universe, but an ’impersonal energy’ immanent in the world, with which it forms a ’cosmic unity’: ’All is one’” (Jesus Christ, Bearer of the Water of Life, §2.3.4.2).

On creation. If God is the self, creation is projection. The world is a mirror, an outpicturing, a “hardening into fact” of assumptions. Neville: “The world is yourself pushed out.” This is not a poetic gloss on the doctrine of creation; it is its exact inversion. In Genesis, God creates and the creature receives; the world is given, prior, and independent of my mood. In the manifest space, the world is a secretion of the psyche, and its intractability — the fact that it so often refuses to comply — becomes a scandal to be explained away rather than a signature of its givenness.

On the human person. The anthropology is exalted and, at the same moment, impoverished. Exalted, because the person is divine in seed: unlimited, creative, “the operant power.” Impoverished, because a being whose only real faculty is assumption, and whose only real problem is resistance, has no depth, no wound that is not a mistake, no capacity for tragedy, and no need of a saviour. The 2003 document again: “We are co-creators, and we create our own reality. Many New Age authors maintain that we choose the circumstances of our lives (even our own illness and health), in a vision where every individual is considered the creative source of the universe” (§2.3.4.1).

On sin. There isn’t any. There is only “imperfect knowledge,” “low vibration,” “limiting belief,” “misalignment.” The document says it in five words: “There is no sin; there is only imperfect knowledge.” This is the load-bearing error of the entire system, and everything cruel in it follows from this one point. If there is no sin, there is no forgiveness — only correction. If there is no forgiveness, there is no way to be relieved of the past except by denying it. And if there is no way to be relieved of the past except by denying it, then the practice of “revision” is not a quirk; it is a necessity, and it is a necessity that cannot work.

On salvation. Salvation is self-realization: the alignment of the interior with the desired exterior. It is achieved by technique, and it is verified by circumstance. This is Pelagianism with a user manual — indeed it is worse than Pelagianism, because Pelagius at least thought the human will was ordered to a good it had not invented. Gaudete et Exsultate names the modern form with precision: “justification by their own efforts, the worship of the human will and their own abilities… an excessive concern with programmes of self-help and personal fulfilment” (§57). That sentence was written about Catholics. It applies, with the polarity reversed, to the manifest space as well.

On revelation. “The universe is always speaking.” Signs, synchronicities, numbers, songs, dreams. The claim is not that God has spoken and we must listen; it is that everything is always speaking and we must decode. The effect is a permanent, low-grade interpretive anxiety: every event is a message, every message is about me, and no message is ever finished. This is the exact opposite of the peace that the tradition associates with obedience to a revelation that has actually been given.

On church. There is no church, and this is not an oversight. The manifest space is constitutively solitary: one person, one notebook, one phone. Where community appears, it is a market — a coach, a course, a membership, a retreat — and its logic is the logic of the customer relationship, which is to say, the logic of someone who cannot tell you no. The 2003 document’s phrase for the result is “spiritual narcissism,” and it asked the question that ought to be asked of every spiritual movement: “is it a form of self-worship?” (§3.2).

On sacraments. The methods. Scripting, the 369, SATS, revision, the whisper method, the pillow method, subliminals. They are rites in the strict sense: prescribed actions, performed at prescribed times, with prescribed words, believed to produce an effect ex opere operato — by the performance. The resemblance to Catholic sacramental practice is not accidental, and it is not innocent. It is the parody that the whole book is about.

On last things. The eschatology is realized and material: the job, the body, the partner, the money, now. There is no death, or rather there is a death that is treated as one more thing to be reframed. This is why the system cannot survive a funeral. It has no category for the irreversible, and the irreversible is where every human life ends up.

· · ·

Put like this, the system looks easy to dismiss, and dismissing it would be a mistake — for the same reason that dismissing Aristotle because he denied creation would have been a mistake. The system’s errors are not random. They are the errors that a culture makes when it has lost a particular set of doctrines and retained the corresponding appetites.

Look at the list again and notice the shape.

The manifest space has an intense sense of agency and no doctrine of providence. It has an intense sense of desire and no doctrine of the good. It has an intense sense of the interior life and no doctrine of sin or grace. It has an intense sense of signs and no doctrine of revelation. It has an intense sense of practice and no doctrine of the Church. It has an intense sense of now and no doctrine of the last things.

Every one of those pairs is a Christian pair, broken in half. The manifest space is not the opposite of Christianity; it is Christianity with one half of each doctrine removed, so that the remaining half becomes monstrous. Agency without providence becomes technique. Desire without the good becomes idolatry. Interiority without grace becomes self-salvation. Signs without revelation become divination. Practice without the Church becomes a market. Now without last things becomes the denial of death.

That is the diagnosis, and it is the reason the cure cannot be a simple “no.” When a person presents with half a doctrine, you do not remove the half. You supply the other half.

· · ·

There is a name for the mood that results, and it is worth naming because it explains the hold the system has on intelligent people. Call it providential atheism: the conviction that reality is responsive, plus the conviction that nothing personal is on the other end of the response.

It is a very modern position, and it is not stupid. It is what remains when a culture retains the experience of prayer and loses the doctrine of God. The experience does not evaporate. It gets reassigned. The sense that the world is addressed to me — which is, in its origin, the sense that I am a creature — gets relocated into a law of attraction. The sense that my interior life matters beyond my interior life — which is, in its origin, the doctrine of the soul — gets relocated into “vibration.” The sense that words are not neutral — which is, in its origin, the doctrine of the word and the sacraments — gets relocated into affirmations.

The result is a spirituality with all of the phenomenology of faith and none of its object. It feels, to the person inside it, exactly like religion, which is why arguments that assume irreligion will miss entirely. And it explains the strange testimony of so many people who leave the manifest space for the Church: not that they stopped having the experiences, but that the experiences suddenly had somewhere to go.

· · ·

One more observation before the audit begins, because it will matter in Part Three.

The manifest space is often described as a form of materialism, and in one sense it is: it promises things, and it measures success in things. But in a deeper sense it is the opposite. It is a form of idealism — the doctrine that reality is at bottom mental, and that the mental is therefore the only lever worth pulling. Christianity, by contrast, is the religion in which God became flesh, in which matter mediates grace, in which water and oil and bread and wine and bodies and places and history are the chosen instruments of the divine.

Which means that, on the question of matter, the Church is more materialist than the manifest space, and this is one of the great unused arguments in its arsenal. The person who has been taught that everything is a projection of consciousness has not been taught to be worldly; she has been taught to be trapped in her own head, with a universe made of it. The Church offers her the scandalous alternative: a God who made a world that is not her, who entered it in a body, and who gives himself to her in things she can touch.

That is not a smaller promise than the manifest space makes. It is a larger one. But it will not be heard until the diagnosis is made in the right order — and the diagnosis is not “you are too attached to the world.” It is “you have been given a universe made of yourself, and you are suffocating in it.”

The point

The manifest space is a complete rival account of God, creation, person, sin, salvation, revelation, church, sacrament and last things — with a hole where the creator should be.

Do this

Write down which of its nine positions you have heard preached, approvingly, from a Catholic pulpit.

What this sets up

It spreads because it works. Not as it claims — but really.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 4

Why It Works

The system succeeds because it meets four real needs badly, in a culture that stopped meeting them well. An answer that does not meet them better will lose, regardless of its truth.

There is a way of writing about the manifest space that is satisfying and useless: to explain, at leisure, why it cannot work. The explanation is easy to construct. Thoughts are not a physical force. Like does not attract like. The universe has no preferences. The mechanism is a category error dressed in quantum vocabulary.

All of that is true, and none of it explains why the practice spreads, why intelligent people defend it, and why a person who has been told it is nonsense will go home and write in the notebook anyway.

The honest answer is that the manifest space works — in the only sense that matters to the person using it. It does something. It does not do what it claims, but it does something, and the something is not trivial. This chapter tries to say what.

· · ·

First, it restores agency in a condition of real powerlessness.

Consider the material conditions of the people most drawn to it. Rents that consume half of a salary. Entry-level work that requires a degree and offers no security. A housing market that has closed. Fertility that has become a medical project. Climate anxiety. A pandemic that demonstrated, to everyone under thirty, that the adults in charge were not in charge.

In that condition, the ordinary levers of agency are not merely difficult; they are largely imaginary. You cannot affect the interest rate. You cannot affect the hiring committee. You cannot affect the diagnosis. And a culture that has no doctrine of providence has nothing to say to a person in that position except “try harder,” which is insulting, or “accept it,” which is unbearable.

The manifest space says something else: there is a lever, and it is inside you, and it is available now. The claim is false. The experience of having a lever is not false, and it is the experience that keeps the practice alive. A young woman who spends twenty minutes a day writing a future she believes she is choosing is not deluded about the interest rate. She is refusing to be a passenger. The refusal is right. The lever is wrong.

Second, it gives the interior life a practice.

Traditional Catholic piety at its best is extraordinarily rich in practice: the examen, the Rosary, lectio divina, novenas, fasting, the liturgical year, the veneration of saints, the Stations, the Angelus, the aspirations, the examination of conscience, the direction of a soul. At its worst — and the worst is common — it is a set of obligations with no method, offered to people who have never been taught to pray and who are told, in effect, to figure it out.

The manifest space is all method. It tells you what to do at 11:11, how many times, with what feeling, in what posture, with what words. It has a morning routine and an evening routine. It takes the most nebulous human activity — hoping — and gives it a shape. This is not a small gift, and its absence in the lives of most Catholics is a scandal of catechesis. We have been out-practiced.

Third, it takes desire seriously.

There is a strain of Catholic piety that treats desire as a problem to be managed. It is not the whole tradition; it is a deformation of it, but it is common enough that a generation has absorbed it: wanting things is slightly shameful, asking for them is slightly worse, and the mature Christian is the one who has stopped wanting. This is not the Gospel. The Gospel is full of people who ask for things and are not rebuked for asking. “What do you want me to do for you?” is a question Jesus asks twice in the same Gospel.

The manifest space asks the question and waits for the answer. It takes seriously the possibility that a person’s desires are information — about what she loves, what she lacks, what she is for. The information is unreliable, as we shall see, and the discernment of desire is a whole chapter of the spiritual life. But the first move, the move of asking the question at all, is a move the Church should have made first and didn’t.

Fourth, it is beautiful, and free, and immediate.

This is not a small matter. The manifest space has excellent design: soft light, quiet voice, a notebook, a candle, an aesthetic of calm competence. It is available at 2 a.m., in bed, for nothing. It asks nothing of you, requires no membership, imposes no schedule beyond the one you choose, and never makes you feel like an outsider at a meeting where everyone else knows the responses.

Compare: a parish young-adult group that meets on a Tuesday when you work, run by a volunteer with three other jobs, in a room with fluorescent lights; a Mass in a language you half-know, at a time you cannot make; a catechesis that ended at fourteen. The comparison is embarrassing, and it is the actual competitive situation.

· · ·

None of this makes the system true. It makes it intelligible, which is a different and more useful thing. And it lets us say precisely what the Church is up against. The manifest space is not winning because it has better arguments. It is winning because it has better answers to four questions, and the Church has been answering different questions:

The question actually being askedThe manifest space’s answerThe answer too often given instead
Can I do anything at all?Yes: change your interiorOffer it up
How do I pray?Here is a method, at 11:11, for nine daysJust talk to God
What do I actually want?Write it down, in the present tenseWanting is dangerous
Where can I belong, for free, tonight?Here, on your phoneTuesday, in the hall, if you can make it

The right-hand column is not the Church’s teaching. It is the Church’s default pastoral practice in a lot of places, which is a different thing, and which can be changed.

· · ·

Now the wounds. If the manifest space meets four needs, it also inflicts three, and the three are severe enough to make the whole system a net harm — which is the book’s judgment, and which should be argued for rather than assumed.

The wound of blame. This has been said already and will be said again, because it is the centre of the moral case. A system of interior causation has no innocent suffering. The suffering person is therefore either a failure or a lesson, and in neither case is she permitted to be simply a person in pain who is loved by God. The pastoral consequence is exact: the manifest space cannot accompany the dying. It can only recruit them.

The wound of dependence on technique. A practice that promises results produces a particular kind of anxiety: the anxiety of the operator. Did I do it right? Was my feeling real enough? Did I doubt? Anyone who has spent time in the space has met this anxiety, and it is structurally identical to scrupulosity — which is a well-known spiritual affliction with a well-known cure, and the cure is not more technique. The manifest space manufactures the disease it claims to heal.

The wound of the vanished other. This is the deepest and the least noticed. If everyone is you pushed out, then the person in front of you is not a person. She is a mirror, a messenger, an echo of your assumptions. You cannot love such a being, because love requires an other who can refuse you. You can only manage her. And a world of managed mirrors is a world in which loneliness is not a problem to be solved but a metaphysical condition to be accepted. The manifest space’s answer to loneliness is to deny that there is anyone there.

· · ·

There is one more thing to say in this chapter, and it is not comfortable for the Church.

The manifest space did not appear in a vacuum. It appeared in a culture that the Church had largely stopped catechizing, at the exact moment when the practices that had formed Catholics for centuries — the rhythms of the liturgical year, family prayer, the examination of conscience, the regular reception of the sacraments — were dissolving. A generation grew up with the vocabulary of the faith and none of its grammar. When they went looking for a grammar, they found one, and it was not ours.

That is not a failure of the young. It is a failure of transmission, and it is the failure that Fides et Ratio warned about in another register: a culture that loses its philosophical and catechetical formation does not become neutral. It becomes available. Something will fill it, and whatever fills it will be better adapted to the medium than the thing that was lost.

The rest of this book is about filling it with something true. But the first part of the program is not intellectual at all. It is the recovery of practice — the ordinary, daily, unglamorous formation of Catholics in the grammar of prayer — because a grammar is the only thing that can answer a grammar.

The point

It succeeds because it meets four real needs badly, in a culture that stopped meeting them well. An answer that does not meet them better will lose.

Do this

Identify the one need your parish meets worst, and write one thing you could do about it this month.

What this sets up

The Church has faced a rival account of everything before, and it did not begin with a ban.
