Chapter 5

Paris, 1277

What actually happened when Aristotle arrived, why the first answer was a ban, and why the ban failed.

The story usually told is too tidy. In the tidy version, Aristotle’s works were rediscovered, Thomas Aquinas read them, saw that they were compatible with the faith, and wrote the Summa. The Church was pleased, and philosophy has been Catholic ever since.

The actual story is messier, longer, and far more useful. It involves three rounds of bans, a faculty strike, a vendetta between two bishops, a Dominican order defending its controversial brother, a condemnation that hit him after his death, a canonization that vindicated him fifty years later, and a revival six hundred years after that. It is, in other words, the normal shape of a real intellectual integration: not a seminar but a fight.

· · ·

Aristotle’s works came west in waves. The Categories and De Interpretatione had been known through Boethius; the rest — the Physics, the Metaphysics, De Anima, the Ethics, the Politics — arrived in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, translated from Arabic, often by way of Hebrew, in Toledo and Sicily, and accompanied by Islamic commentaries of extraordinary sophistication: al-Farabi, Avicenna, and above all Averroes, whose reading of Aristotle was so powerful that Latin scholars called him simply “the Commentator.”

By 1250 the Latin West possessed a complete, coherent, and philosophically superior account of nature, causation, the soul, and human happiness, written by a pagan who had never heard of Moses. The implications were not subtle. Aristotle’s cosmos was eternal, not created. His God was a self-thinking thought that did not know the world, let alone love it. His soul was the form of the body and, on the most rigorous reading, did not survive it. His ethics delivered flourishing without grace, and his politics delivered the good life without the Church.

The first institutional response was, predictably, prohibition. The statutes of the University of Paris forbade the teaching of Aristotle’s natural philosophy in 1210 and 1215; a papal commission in 1231 ordered that the offending books be “purged of errors” before use. The prohibition did not hold, because the books were too useful and too interesting. By 1255 the arts faculty had made them required texts. You cannot ban a better tool.

· · ·

The crisis that followed was not really about Aristotle. It was about autonomy — whether there is a domain of truth that philosophy can settle on its own, with conclusions that theology must then accommodate.

The figure who pressed this hardest was Siger of Brabant, a master of arts in Paris, whose positions were read as teaching that what is true in philosophy may be false in faith, and vice versa. The “double truth” formula is probably a caricature — Siger’s actual position was more like a professional restriction: the philosopher reports what reason concludes, and leaves the faith aside. But the practical effect was the same. It created a class of Christian intellectuals who taught, six days a week, a cosmology that contradicted the Creed, and who regarded this as a matter of academic method.

Three responses formed, and it is worth naming them, because they recur in every crisis of this kind, including ours.

The first was the traditionalist refusal. Bonaventure, the Franciscan general, preaching in Paris in 1273, warned against the “waters of Aristotle” and treated philosophical autonomy as a spiritual danger. His instinct was not obscurantist; it was pastoral. He had watched the arts faculty turn the study of nature into a substitute for the study of God.

The second was compartmentalization. The arts masters who taught Aristotle’s cosmos while professing the Creed, on the understanding that the two belonged to different registers and need not be reconciled. This is the position of every Catholic who says “I’m Catholic on Sunday and I manifest on Monday; they’re different things.”

The third was transformative integration. Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican, a fat and slow-moving man who wrote at dictation speed and was, by all accounts, socially awkward, spent his life on the problem. He did not begin with a verdict. He began by commissioning translations.

· · ·

That detail is worth pausing on, because it is the least romantic and most revealing fact about the whole enterprise. Thomas did not read Aristotle in snippets from a florilegium. He asked his friend William of Moerbeke to produce literal, word-for-word Latin translations of the Greek, and he worked from those. He wrote commentaries on the Physics, the Metaphysics, De Anima, the Nicomachean Ethics, the Posterior Analytics, and the De Caelo. He wrote a Summa contra Gentiles that is, among other things, a manual for arguing with philosophers on their own ground. Only then did he use Aristotle in theology.

The sequence matters. Description preceded judgment by about fifteen years. Every serious failure in Catholic engagement with the manifest space that I have seen — and I have seen many — fails at this exact point. The critic has read the summary, not the source; the verdict has preceded the description; and the person in front of him, who has actually done the practice, can tell.

· · ·

Thomas’s integration had a structure, and the structure is what this book borrows. Part Two sets out the method in detail; here it is enough to see the shape.

He took Aristotle’s instruments: the logic, the four causes, the analysis of change in terms of act and potency, the psychology of habit and virtue, the account of the passions, the distinction between the speculative and practical intellect. These were tools, and tools do not have a religion.

He refused Aristotle’s framework: the eternity of the world, the necessity of all things, the denial of providence, the mortality of the soul, the self-enclosed God who does not know particulars. He refused them not as “pagan errors” but as philosophical errors, and he argued against them philosophically, often using Aristotle’s own distinctions.

He subordinated the whole to revealed principles. This is the meaning of sacra doctrina: theology is a science whose principles are given, and philosophy is its instrument. The instrument is not despised — a good instrument is precious — but it does not set the questions.

And he accepted that this would cost him. It did.

· · ·

On 7 March 1277, Étienne Tempier, Bishop of Paris, issued a condemnation of 219 propositions. The immediate occasion was a request from Pope John XXI, who was worried about divination and determinism; the deeper occasion was a long-running conflict between the bishop and the arts faculty, and between the secular clergy and the mendicant orders. The propositions condemned included a great deal that Thomas had never taught, a good deal that he had, and several that were the common property of the schools.

The most famous is the claim that God cannot make a vacuum, or that he cannot move the heavens in a straight line, or that he cannot create several worlds — the “absolute power” questions. The condemnation was aimed at protecting divine freedom from Aristotelian necessity. In the process it also hit propositions about the unity of substantial form and about the intellect, which were close to Thomas’s own positions.

Thomas had died in 1274, on his way to the Council of Lyon. He could not answer. The Dominican order did: the provincial chapters defended his teaching, and the order made his doctrine its own. He was canonized in 1323. In 1325, the Bishop of Paris’s successor revoked the condemnation of the propositions that were understood to be his. By the sixteenth century his Summa was the standard textbook of Catholic theology. In 1879, Aeterni Patris made his doctrine the norm of Catholic philosophical formation. In 1998, Fides et Ratio called him “an authentic model for all who seek the truth,” while insisting that the Church “has no philosophy of her own nor does she canonize any one particular philosophy in preference to others” (§§44, 49).

Two things about this timeline should be pressed into the reader’s mind.

First, the condemnation was not simply a mistake and not simply a persecution. It was the institutional immune system doing what immune systems do: responding to a real threat (necessitarian philosophy claiming autonomy) with a blunt instrument (a list of forbidden sentences) that damaged some healthy tissue (Thomas’s own positions) and missed some of the disease (the condemned propositions continued to be taught, in subtler forms, for centuries). The Church’s magisterium is not a truth-machine. It is a living authority that sometimes acts badly and sometimes corrects itself, and both facts belong in the account.

Second, the integration took roughly fifty years from Thomas’s first commentary to the general acceptance of his doctrine, and six hundred to the point where it became a monument — at which point it began to function as a constraint rather than a resource, which is why John Paul II had to say what he said in 1998.

· · ·

Now the translation.

The manifest space is not Aristotle. It is not a science, it is not written in a language that requires a Moerbeke, and it does not have a Siger of Brabant. But the structure of the crisis is identical, and the three responses are already forming.

The traditionalists are already here: the priests and writers who say it is all New Age, all dangerous, all the same thing, and who are sometimes right about specific practices and always wrong about the people. They will produce a ban, or the local equivalent of one, and the ban will fail for the same reason the 1210 statutes failed: the thing is too useful and too interesting to the people who need it, and a prohibition does not supply an alternative.

The compartmentalizers are already here, and they are the majority. They are the Catholics who pray the Rosary and script their manifestations and see no contradiction, because they have been formed by a culture in which the two occupy different rooms and never meet. They are not hypocrites. They are the direct product of a catechesis that taught them doctrine in one register and left practice to the market.

The integrators are barely here. There are a few books, a handful of podcasts, some well-meaning syntheses that keep the metaphysics and add holy water. Nothing yet that has done the Moerbeke work — that has read the sources closely enough to describe them without contempt, and then rebuilt the practice inside a different causality.

Which means the field is open, and the timetable is long, and the first thing to do is not to write a refutation. It is to do what Thomas did in the fifteen years before he wrote a single theological sentence about Aristotle: to read the thing, in its own language, until you can say what it says better than its own defenders can.

That is what the next part of this book attempts. It will be uncomfortable for readers on both sides, which is the ordinary sign that the work is being done honestly.

The point

Aristotle arrived as a complete system and the first institutional response was prohibition. The prohibition failed, because you cannot ban a better tool.

Do this

Read one primary text of the movement you are tempted to dismiss, all the way through, before you say another word about it.

What this sets up

What replaced the ban was a method — six moves, in order.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 6

The Method of the Angelic Doctor

Six moves, in order, with the manifest-space translation of each. This is the operating manual for everything that follows.

A method is not a mood. It is a sequence of operations that can be repeated by someone else and checked at each stage. What follows is an attempt to state Thomas’s method in that form — six moves, in order — and to translate each one into the work that this book is trying to do.

The sequence matters. Move four is useless without move one, and move six is a fantasy without move five. Most Catholic engagements with the manifest space attempt move five first, which is why they fail.

· · ·

Move one: describe the thing in its own terms

Thomas wrote commentaries before he wrote theology. He translated the Greek rather than relying on the anthology. He could state Aristotle’s position so accurately that modern historians still use his commentaries as evidence for what Aristotle meant.

The principle behind this is not politeness. It is the old principle salvare apparentias — save the appearances. If your account of a phenomenon cannot reproduce the phenomenon, your account is wrong. If your description of manifestation cannot be recognized by a person who manifests, you have described something else, and your refutation is a refutation of your own caricature.

Translation. Read Neville Goddard’s Feeling Is the Secret and The Power of Awareness before writing about him. Read The Secret, which is a different and cruder system. Read the Abraham-Hicks material if you can stand it, because it is the most metaphysically explicit version and therefore the most useful. Spend time with practitioners, not with their critics. Ask what they do on a Tuesday, not what they believe in the abstract. And when you write, state their position in a form they would accept — the “steel man,” in the current idiom.

This is the stage at which most Catholic writing on the subject fails, and it fails in a specific way: it describes a version of manifestation that no serious practitioner holds (thoughts are magic, you can get anything with no effort), refutes it triumphantly, and is then unable to understand why nobody changes their mind.

Move two: separate the instrument from the metaphysics

Thomas took act and potency, the four causes, and the treatise on habit. He left the eternal cosmos and the unmoved mover who does not love.

The distinction is not always easy to draw, because in a mature system the instrument and the metaphysics are fused. But it can be drawn, and the test is functional: does this piece of the system do work that survives the removal of the framework? The analysis of change in terms of act and potency survives the loss of the eternal cosmos. The claim that like attracts like does not survive the loss of a sympathetic cosmos, because the attraction is the cosmology.

Translation. The manifest space contains instruments that work and a framework that does not.

Instruments that survive: the observation that attention and expectation shape perception and action; the observation that imagined scenarios rehearse and form desire; the observation that gratitude changes the one who is grateful; the observation that words shape the speaker; the observation that a person’s self-concept constrains what she will attempt; the observation that habit is formed by repetition and by feeling; the observation that the interior life is not private.

Framework that does not survive: resemblance-causation; the responsive universe; the identification of the self with God; the denial of innocent suffering; the technique-guarantee.

The distinction has a practical test: strip the method of its metaphysics and see whether the practice still makes sense. Gratitude journalling without the law of attraction still makes sense — it is a form of examen. Scripting without the law of attraction makes sense as a way of clarifying and presenting a petition, or as a way of rehearsing a resolution. The 369 method without the law of attraction is a timer. What does not survive is the claim that the practice compels the outcome, and that claim was never an instrument; it was the framework.

Move three: subordinate the instrument to revealed principles

Sacra doctrina uses philosophy but does not take its starting points from it (ST I, q. 1, a. 5, ad 2). The technical name for the relationship is instrumental causality: the tool is genuinely the tool’s own thing, doing its own work, but the shape of the whole is set by the science that uses it.

This is the move that distinguishes integration from syncretism, and it is the one that is easiest to fake. A syncretist also “uses” the borrowed material; the difference is that in syncretism the borrowed framework quietly sets the agenda. You can tell which one you are looking at by asking: when the two conflict, which one yields?

Translation. A Catholic practice of manifestation must be one in which, when the technique and the faith conflict, the technique loses — not by being suppressed, but by being reconceived. If the novena “works” and the doctrine of providence is adjusted to explain why, you have syncretism. If the doctrine of providence governs what the novena is understood to be doing, you have integration.

The concrete test: does the practice still make sense if the outcome does not arrive? A Catholic practice must be intelligible and good even when the petition is refused. If it only makes sense when it succeeds, it is a technique wearing vestments.

Move four: correct the master from within

Thomas’s most elegant move was to use Aristotle’s own distinctions to reach conclusions Aristotle did not reach. Act and potency, taken seriously, yield a creator. The analysis of the soul as subsistent form, taken seriously, yields an immortality that Aristotle’s own text seems to deny.

This is more than rhetorical jujitsu. It is a claim about how error works: a system’s errors usually sit at its edges, in the places where it has not applied its own best insight. Find the insight, apply it ruthlessly, and the error often falls out.

Translation. The manifest space has a best insight, and it is this: the interior life is real, and it is causally connected to the exterior life. It does not apply that insight consistently. If the interior life is causally connected to the exterior life, then it must be connected through something — through action, through relationship, through the body, through the structures of the world, through time. The manifest space wants the connection to be immediate and magical, because immediacy is the selling point. But immediacy is not required by the insight. The insight is preserved, and in fact deepened, by a mediated account: interior states → habits → actions → relationships → circumstances, all under providence.

The same move works on desire. The manifest space says desire is authoritative. Its own best insight is that desire is revelatory — it tells you what you love. But if desire is revelatory, it can be wrong about its object, which is exactly what the tradition says: amor is the weight of the soul, and the weight can be misplaced. The manifest space’s own premise, taken seriously, demands a doctrine of disordered love. It has none, and so it must deny the evidence of every human life.

Move five: reject by name, not by category

Thomas did not say “Aristotle is a pagan.” He said: the world is not eternal (ST I, q. 46, a. 2); the soul is subsistent (ST I, q. 75); God knows singulars (ST I, q. 14, a. 11); not all things happen by necessity (ST I, q. 22; q. 116). Each rejection is a specific thesis with an argument attached.

The reason this matters is not taxonomic neatness. It is that a category-level rejection cannot be answered, and therefore cannot persuade. “It’s all New Age” is true of some of it and false of much of it, and the person who hears it knows that it is false of her, and concludes that the speaker does not know what he is talking about.

Translation. Part Two of this book does this work: fourteen claims, each with a verdict and a reason. The verdicts are not all negative. Four are accepted, three are corrected, seven are rejected. A response that rejected all fourteen would be as useless as one that accepted all fourteen.

Move six: institutionalize

Thomas’s synthesis survived because it was taught. It entered the curriculum of the mendicant studia, then the universities, then the seminaries. It had a second generation (his students), a third, a revival in the sixteenth century, and a magisterial endorsement in the nineteenth. The Summa is not a bestseller; it is a textbook, and that is why it is still read.

An idea without an institution is a conversation. The manifest space has institutions — publishers, coaches, platforms, courses, algorithms — and they are extraordinarily effective. The Catholic response will need institutions of its own, or it will be a series of articles that everyone agrees with and nobody uses.

Translation. Part Five sets out the institutional programme: a centre, a journal, a formation module, a publisher, a community, and the pastoral tools that a parish can actually use on a Tuesday.

· · ·

There is a seventh move, and it is not a technique.

Thomas wrote the Summa as an act of prayer. The tradition reports that he said, toward the end of his life, that everything he had written seemed to him like straw compared with what had been shown to him — a sentence that is either the most humble thing in medieval literature or the most terrifying, and possibly both. He did not finish. He stopped writing in December 1273 and died three months later.

The lesson is not that scholarship is worthless. It is that the integration of a rival account of reality is not, at bottom, an intellectual operation. It is a work of love, and love requires the purification of the one who loves. A person who has not been converted by the thing he is trying to integrate will produce a synthesis that is technically correct and spiritually dead — and everyone will be able to tell.

Which is why the next chapter is about the cost, and why the last part of this book is about institutions, and why neither of them is the most important part. The most important part is the one that cannot be put in a method: the practitioner has to become the kind of person who can hold the thing without being held by it.

The point

Thomas described before he judged, separated the instrument from the metaphysics, subordinated the instrument, corrected from within, refused by name, and institutionalised. Six moves, in that order.

Do this

Apply move one to a practice you dislike: state it in a form its practitioners would accept. If you cannot, you are not ready for move five.

What this sets up

The method has a bill, and it is usually presented to the person who did the work.

Chapter 7

The Cost of Integration

Three case studies in what happens to the person who tries this — Thomas, Faustina, and the ordinary catechist — and the rules that follow for anyone attempting the same work.

Every integration has a bill, and the person who presents it is rarely the one who ordered the work.

This chapter is about the bill. It is placed early, before the audit and before the theology, for a reason: anyone who reads this book and decides to attempt something like it should know what they are purchasing. The pattern is remarkably consistent across eight centuries, and it has three parts.

· · ·

Case one: Thomas, 1277.

The facts are in the previous chapter and can be compressed. A man spends twenty-five years describing, correcting, and rebuilding a rival system; he dies; two years later a bishop condemns a list of propositions that includes some of his; his order defends him; he is canonized forty-nine years after his death; his condemnation is partly revoked; and six centuries later his method becomes the Church’s official philosophy — at which point it stops being a method and becomes a monument, and has to be rescued from its admirers.

Notice the shape. The condemnation came not from the enemy but from the guardians. It came not during his life, when he could answer, but after his death, when he could not. It was aimed at something real (necessitarian philosophy claiming autonomy) and it hit something adjacent (his own carefully guarded positions). And it was reversed by the same institution that had issued it, on a timescale that no individual could have survived.

The lesson is not “the Church is oppressive.” The lesson is that institutions protect themselves with categories, and a genuinely new synthesis does not fit the existing categories, and therefore looks, from inside the institution, like the thing it is trying to answer.

Case two: Faustina, 1959.

In 1938 a Polish nun died, leaving a diary of claimed revelations and a devotion to Divine Mercy: an image, a chaplet, a feast, and a set of promises. The devotion spread, especially in Poland and among Polish émigrés. In 1959 the Holy Office issued a notification forbidding the spread of the devotion “in the forms proposed by Sister Faustina,” on the basis of Italian translations that made parts of the diary read as doctrinally alarming, and of exaggerated promises being propagated with it.

The ban lasted nineteen years. During that time the devotion was not destroyed; it went underground, sustained by the Marians and by ordinary people, and its cause was promoted by the Archbishop of Kraków, Karol Wojtyła, who opened a process in 1965 while the works were still censored in Rome. In 1978 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith lifted the prohibition, having examined better texts. Wojtyła became pope that year. Faustina was beatified in 1993 and canonized in 2000, and the Second Sunday of Easter was given the title Divine Mercy Sunday for the whole Church.

The lesson here is sharper than the first, because the 1959 decision was not made by enemies of the faith and was not correcting a real doctrinal error. It was made, in good faith, on bad information, by an institution with a legitimate duty of vigilance, and it silenced a genuine devotion for two decades. The guardians can be wrong in the direction of caution, and the cost of that error is borne by the faithful. Anyone who plans to exercise vigilance over the manifest space should have this case in front of them, because it is the case that shows what vigilance looks like when it is mistaken.

Case three: the catechist, now.

The third case is not famous and happens every week. A parish catechist, or a campus minister, or a youth leader, decides to take the question seriously. She reads the sources. She builds a session in which she takes the manifest space’s claims apart and offers Catholic practice as the alternative. She is careful, and she is fair, and she is not a heresy-hunter.

Three things happen.

Some of the young people are relieved. They had been carrying an intolerable burden — the belief that their fear had caused their mother’s illness — and they had never heard it named. This is the part that is never reported.

Some of the parents are alarmed. A parent who practises manifestation, or who has paid for a coach, hears that the parish is teaching against it, and complains to the pastor. The complaint is not usually about doctrine. It is about the implication that the parent has been doing something wrong.

And some colleague tells her that she is “polarizing,” that the Church should be “accompanied rather than judged,” and that perhaps this is not the moment. Which is true — it is never the moment — and which has the effect of ensuring that the work is done by people with fewer institutional constraints and less accountability.

· · ·

The three cases give three rules, and they are the rules this book tries to follow.

Rule one: stay inside. Thomas did not found a movement. He remained a Dominican, submitted his work to the order and the Church, and let them judge it. The integration that survives is the integration that can be corrected. The moment the integrator becomes the founder of a school that cannot be corrected, he has become the problem.

Rule two: publish the method, not just the conclusion. Thomas’s Summa shows its work to an almost absurd degree: objections, authorities, arguments, replies. This is not a stylistic quirk. It is what makes the work corrigible. A conclusion can only be accepted or rejected; a method can be tested. And a method that can be tested is a method that can be improved by people who do not like the author.

Rule three: do not monetize it. The Church’s own norms for the discernment of claimed revelations list, among the negative criteria, “evidence of a search for profit or gain” (1978 norms, I.B.c). The manifest space is a market. A Catholic response that is also a market will be indistinguishable from it at the level that matters, which is the level of the person deciding whether to trust you. Whatever this work becomes, it should be free at the point of use.

· · ·

The four asymmetries

The analogy with 1277 is the spine of this book, and it has limits. Four of them matter enough to state plainly, because a reader who has spotted them and found them unaddressed is right to distrust everything that follows.

First: Aristotle arrived as a philosophy; this arrives as a practice. The Stagirite came in as a corpus — a body of texts with a school behind it, argued over in Latin by men who had taken vows of obedience. You can dispute with a text. You cannot dispute with a habit that someone performs at eleven at night because it is the only thing that has ever made her feel less alone. The consequence is a change of method: the argument has to be carried by a practice, not by a refutation, which is why Part Four exists and why it is the longest part of the book.

Second: Aristotle’s system had no theodicy of personal misfortune, and this one does. The Physics and the Metaphysics do not tell a grieving woman that her grief is her own fault. The manifest space does, constantly, in the gentlest possible voice, and that changes the timetable. A doctrine can wait fifty years for a correct formulation. A sentence that is telling a dying woman she caused her cancer cannot wait a week.

Third: Thomas had institutions with jurisdiction, and we have platforms without memory. The studia, the chairs, the disputations, the order, the bishop — these were instruments that could decide something and make it stick. The contemporary equivalent is a feed that forgets, a publisher with no doctrinal responsibility, and a diocese that has never heard of the question. We do not get to assume the institutional machinery will do the work, because the machinery is exactly what is missing.

Fourth, and most important: the rival in this case is derived from us. Aristotle was a stranger; New Thought is a descendant. It speaks our vocabulary — word, spirit, abundance, thanksgiving, manifestation — with the meanings quietly inverted, and it borrows the shape of our liturgy while denying the God it is addressed to. That makes it far easier to sell to Christians and far harder to distinguish from the faith once it is inside. The discernment required is therefore finer than anything the thirteenth century needed, and the risk is not that the Church will reject the practice. It is that the Church will absorb it without noticing what it has absorbed.

None of these asymmetries destroys the analogy. Each of them changes what the analogy licenses. The method transfers; the timetable does not; the opposition is not a stranger but a cousin; and the instruments have to be built rather than borrowed.

· · ·

There are two errors to avoid, and they look like opposites but they come from the same place.

The error of the ban treats the phenomenon as a contamination. It is the error of 1210 and of 1959. It assumes that the way to protect the faithful is to remove the dangerous object, and it forgets that the dangerous object is meeting a need that will then be met in some less visible and less corrigible way. When you ban the practice, you do not remove the desire. You remove your own ability to shape it.

The error of credulity treats the phenomenon as a dialect. It is the error of the well-meaning synthesis that keeps the metaphysics and adds a crucifix. It assumes that because the practice is moving and the people are sincere, the framework must be basically sound. It forgets that a system can be internally coherent, psychologically effective, and spiritually ruinous, and that the ruin is usually invisible because it happens slowly, in the way that a person slowly stops expecting anything from God.

Between these two errors there is a narrow path, and the Church has a procedure for walking it. It was issued in 1978, revised in 2024, and it is worth describing here, because it is one of the most useful and least known instruments the Church possesses.

· · ·

The 1978 norms for judging claimed apparitions and revelations set out a procedure with three stages and two sets of criteria.

The positive criteria included: moral certitude about the facts; the personal qualities of the recipients (psychological balance, honesty, moral rectitude, docility to authority); the soundness of the doctrine; and “healthy devotion and abundant and constant spiritual fruit (for example, spirit of prayer, conversion, testimonies of charity).”

The negative criteria included: manifest error about the facts; doctrinal error; “evidence of a search for profit or gain”; grave immorality; and psychological disorder.

And the procedure had three steps: first, judge the facts; second, if the judgment is favourable, permit some public devotion with the formula pro nunc nihil obstare — “for now, nothing stands in the way”; third, after time and experience, and especially “with special regard to the fecundity of spiritual fruit,” express a judgment about authenticity.

The 2024 revision kept the logic and made it more supple, replacing the binary verdict with a graded scale of six possible conclusions: nihil obstat (nothing stands in the way, without any judgment about supernatural character); prae oculis habeatur (keep it before your eyes — there are elements to note); curatur (it needs to be healed or corrected); sub mandato (entrust it to a designated authority); prohibetur et obstruatur (forbid and block it); and declaratio de non supernaturalitate (declare that it is not supernatural).

Read that list again and notice what it is. It is a graded taxonomy for the pastoral handling of a live spiritual phenomenon, running from “leave it alone, it is bearing fruit” to “this is a fabrication.” It is precisely what the manifest space needs and what the current Catholic conversation lacks, because the current conversation has only two settings: it’s fine and it’s demonic.

The taxonomy is translatable. Applied to manifestation practices, it might look like this:

VerdictApplied to a manifestation practice
Nihil obstatgratitude journalling, goal-setting, self-examination, ordinary petition
Prae oculis habeaturvisualization of a desired good, affirmations about one’s own capacities, “manifesting” as colloquial hope
Curaturpractices with sound instincts and unsound framing — most “Catholic manifestation” content
Sub mandatogroup practices, retreats, anything with a guide and a fee
Prohibetur et obstruaturchanneling, mediumship, attempts to control others’ wills, “reality shifting,” curses
Declaratio de non supernaturalitatespecific claims to guaranteed results, verified failure, fraud

This is not a solution to the theological problem. It is a way of not making the theological problem worse while it is being solved. It is the difference between a triage nurse and a surgeon, and the Church needs both.

· · ·

The last cost is the one nobody warns about, and it is the reason this chapter ends where it does.

If you do this work seriously — if you read the sources, learn the vocabulary, sit with the people, and try to build something true — you will find that you have become strange to both sides. The people in the manifest space will hear the critique in your voice even when you are being generous, because they have heard it before from people who were not generous. And the people in your own community will hear the sympathy in your voice and wonder whose side you are on.

That is the ordinary condition of the integrator, and it is not a sign that something has gone wrong. Thomas was suspected by the Augustinians and by the Averroists, and by the bishop, and by the Franciscans, and by some of his own brethren. He kept working, kept submitting, kept praying, and died before the verdict came in. The verdict, when it came, was not the one he would have written, and it took six hundred years, and it was right in the end.

The work is not to be understood by your own generation. The work is to be correct enough that a later generation can use it, and humble enough that it can be corrected, and free enough that nobody has to pay to hear it.

The point

Every integration is condemned by the guardians before it is received by the institution. Thomas in 1277, Faustina in 1959, and the catechist in your parish on Tuesday.

Do this

Decide now, in writing, what you will do when you are misrepresented: stay inside, publish the method, do not monetise.

What this sets up

The audit begins. Four tests, then fourteen verdicts.
