Part Two

The Audit

Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God.

1 John 4:1

A verdict is only as good as the test that produced it. This part builds four tests from the Thomistic tradition, applies them to the manifest space as a system, and then works through fourteen of its central claims one by one, assigning each a verdict: integrate, correct, or reject. It closes with a lexicon, because the argument will be won or lost at the level of vocabulary, and with a chapter on why argument alone cannot win it.

Chapter 8

Four Tests

An audit needs criteria that are prior to the thing being audited. These four are not invented for the occasion; each is a load-bearing principle of the Catholic tradition, and each can be applied to a practice as easily as to a proposition.

Every tradition has its heresy tests, and every tradition’s tests are shaped by the heresies it has actually fought. The Church’s tests — the ones that recur from the councils through the Catechism — are not arbitrary. They are the four places where the tradition has learned, at enormous cost, that it can be bent out of shape.

This chapter states them in a form that can be used on the manifest space. They are: Creator and creature; nature and grace; cross and glory; Church and self. Each corresponds to a principle that the Church has defended against a specific kind of collapse, and each can be applied twice — to the system’s claims and to its practices.

· · ·

Test one: Creator and creature

The principle is the analogia entis — the analogy of being. God is not a being among beings, not the largest item in the universe, not a force alongside other forces. When we say that God is good, and that a creature is good, we do not mean the same thing in both cases; we mean something related but infinitely different. This is not a piece of metaphysical fastidiousness. It is the difference between worship and technique.

The test asks: does this account preserve the infinite difference between God and the world, and therefore the gratuity of everything the world receives?

The manifest space fails this test at its foundation, and it fails in the specific way the tradition has seen before. It makes the divine continuous with the human: the universe is a field, and the self is a center of the field; imagination is God in us; the law is a law of the self’s own nature. The result is a system in which there is no gift, because there is no giver who is other. What looks like grace in the manifest space is always the return of one’s own investment.

The Council of Nicaea faced a version of this in Arius: a Christ who is not God but the highest creature is a Christ who cannot save, because he is on our side of the line. The manifest space faces a version of it in the opposite direction: a self that is not a creature but a creator is a self that cannot receive, because it has nothing above it to receive from.

Test two: nature and grace

The principle is gratia non tollit naturam, sed perficit — grace does not destroy nature but perfects it (ST I, q. 1, a. 8, ad 2). It has two halves, and both are essential. The first half protects nature: the created order is good, human effort is real, the virtues are real, the world is not a prison to be escaped. The second half protects grace: nature cannot complete itself; the thing that saves is not a natural capacity but a gift.

The test asks: does this account leave nature its real causality, and grace its necessity?

Most systems fail one half. The manifest space fails the second half spectacularly: it has an enormous doctrine of human agency and no doctrine of grace at all. Everything is nature, and nature is enough. This is Pelagianism, and it is not a mild error, because a Pelagian universe has no forgiveness in it — only performance, and the failure of performance.

But notice: a great deal of Catholic preaching fails the first half, and has done for a long time. A piety that treats all human desire as suspect, all worldly effort as vanity, and all suffering as something to be offered rather than healed is not orthodox; it is a different error, and it is one of the reasons the manifest space looks, to a young person, like the only religion that thinks anything can be done. The test must be applied to us as well, or we will have no standing to apply it to them.

Test three: cross and glory

The principle is that the Cross is not an interruption of the good news but its centre, and that the resurrection does not cancel the Cross but transfigures it. The technical name for the alternative is a theology of glory — a system in which suffering is a problem to be solved rather than a place where God is found.

The test asks: does this account have a place for innocent suffering?

Not a place for explained suffering. A place for innocent suffering — for the child with leukemia, for the woman who was raped, for the man who lost his faith along with his wife. The test is not whether the system can generate a sentence about suffering. It is whether the sentence allows the sufferer to be innocent.

The manifest space fails this test completely and cannot be repaired, because the failure is not a bug in its theodicy but the theodicy itself. If interior states cause exterior circumstances, then suffering is caused by interior states, and the sufferer is the author. Every softener — “soul contract,” “lesson,” “growth,” “the universe is refining you” — is a euphemism for the same sentence, which is: you did this.

Against this, the Church has two sentences that are worth more than the whole system. The first is from the Gospel: “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him” (John 9:3). The second is from Job, and it is a refusal to answer: God does not tell Job why, and Job is vindicated for demanding an answer and then accepting that there is one he cannot have.

Test four: Church and self

The principle is that grace is mediated, and that the mediation is communal and sacramental. The Christian does not relate to God as an isolated unit; she is a member of a body, and the body has a structure, a history, a liturgy, and authority. This is not an administrative arrangement. It is a claim about what salvation is: not a private achievement but an incorporation.

The test asks: is this practice constitutively communal and embodied, or is it solitary and mental?

The manifest space fails on both counts at once. It is solitary by design — one person, one journal, one phone — and it is mental by metaphysics, since the lever is interior and the world is a projection. The famous phrase “everyone is you pushed out” is not an eccentricity of Neville Goddard’s; it is the logical consequence of the system’s premises, and it makes the other person into a mirror. A mirror cannot be loved, because it cannot refuse you.

The Church’s alternative is not “be more social.” It is the sacramental principle: that God gives himself through matter, in a body, in a place, at a time, through hands that have been ordained and water that has been blessed. This is the point at which the Church is more materialist than the manifest space, and the point at which the manifest space is revealed as a form of idealism — a religion for people who have been persuaded that the only real thing is their own interior.

· · ·

Now the second use of the tests, which is the one that matters most in practice.

These four are usually applied to propositions, and that is why they are so ineffective in pastoral care. Nobody in a parish presents with a proposition. They present with a practice, and the practice has a metaphysics embedded in it that they have never articulated and would deny if you attributed it to them.

So apply the tests to the practice, by asking four questions that a person can actually answer.

On Creator and creature: “When you do this, are you asking someone, or operating something?”

On nature and grace: “If you do everything right and nothing happens, whose fault is it?”

On cross and glory: “What would this say about a friend of yours who got sick and died?”

On Church and self: “If you had to do this in front of another person, and they could say no to you, would it still work?”

The answers are diagnostic to a degree that surprised me when I began using them. A person can hold a false metaphysics in the abstract and still answer these questions in a Catholic way, in which case what they have is a vocabulary problem, not a faith problem. And a person can recite the Creed and answer these questions in a manifest-space way, in which case the problem is exactly where the clergy do not look.

· · ·

One warning about tests in general, and then we can begin the audit proper.

A test is not a weapon. The moment it becomes a way of classifying people rather than claims, it has failed — not morally only, but epistemically, because the person will sense the classification and stop telling you the truth. The tests in this chapter are meant to be used on sentences, in public, where they can be argued with. Used on souls, in private, without invitation, they are an instrument of the very thing this book is trying to cure.

There is a name for a person who applies the four tests to everyone he meets: a heretic-hunter. The tradition has a word for him too, and it is not a compliment.

The point

Four tests — Creator and creature, nature and grace, cross and glory, Church and self — and each can be asked as a question a real person can answer.

Do this

Ask the four questions of your own practice, not of someone else’s.

What this sets up

The first test is the deepest, and it is the one that dissolves the whole vocabulary.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 9

Creator and Creature

The analogy of being is the single most useful instrument in this book. It is also the least understood. Here is what it does, and why the manifest space cannot survive it.

If this book has one technical argument, it is this chapter, and the argument can be stated in a sentence: the manifest space’s errors are almost all instances of one error, which is the refusal of analogy.

That sounds like the sort of claim a scholastic makes to annoy people. It is not. The refusal of analogy is the most common intellectual mistake of the modern period, and it produces the most characteristic modern disasters, from scientism to pantheism to the belief that the universe is a vending machine with a mood.

· · ·

Begin with a puzzle that any child can pose and no one can answer quickly.

God is good. My mother is good. Are they good in the same way?

If yes — if “good” means the same thing in both cases — then either God is good in the way my mother is good (which makes him a creature, a very large and kindly one), or my mother is good in the way God is good (which makes her divine). Both conclusions are absurd, and both have been held by serious people.

If no — if the word means something entirely different in each case — then the sentence “God is good” tells us nothing at all. It is a noise we make in the direction of the mystery. This is the position of a certain kind of apophatic theology and of a certain kind of modern atheism, and it has the same practical result: what we say about God is not true, only pious.

Thomas’s answer is neither. The word is used analogically: in the same order of meaning, but not in the same mode. My mother’s goodness is a participated goodness, received, limited, and mixed with its opposite. God’s goodness is the source of hers, unlimited, and identical with his being. The word is not equivocal (it means something) and not univocal (it does not mean the same thing). It is stretched — and the stretching is not a failure of language but the only honest thing language can do when it speaks of the source of everything.

This is the analogia entis, and it does an enormous amount of work. It is what allows the Church to say that creatures are like God without being bits of God, and that God is other than the world without being unrelated to it.

· · ·

Now apply it to the manifest space, and watch the whole system come apart at one seam.

The manifest space speaks of energy. What does the word mean?

In ordinary usage it means one of two things. In physics it means a quantity: the capacity to do work, measured in joules, conserved. In ordinary speech it means vitality: “I don’t have the energy today.” The manifest space uses the word in a third way, which is neither: a quasi-substantial, quasi-personal, quasi-moral force that is transmitted by thought and feeling, that can be high or low, blocked or flowing, and that attracts like to like.

That third meaning is not an analogy. It is not even an equivocation, because an equivocation is at least aware of the two senses. It is a univocal concept with a mystical job: a single thing, imagined on the model of a physical quantity, which is then asked to perform the work that the tradition assigns to grace, providence, love, and the sacraments. The universe has a voltage, and so do you, and the trick is to match them.

The same structure appears in every load-bearing word of the system. Abundance is a quantity, so more is better and the spiritual life is a supply curve. Alignment is a spatial relation, so the moral life is a matter of getting the pieces to line up. Vibration is a physical motion, so the interior life is a frequency. Block is an obstruction, so sin is a plumbing problem. Frequency is a rate, so prayer is a tuning exercise.

Each of these words is doing something the tradition knows how to do, and doing it by the wrong means. The tradition says: grace. The system says: energy. The tradition says: conformity of will. The system says: alignment. The tradition says: sin. The system says: block. The tradition says: the presence of God. The system says: the frequency.

A word about quantum. The system’s most respectable-looking argument is that physics has caught up with it: the observer effect, entanglement, the collapse of the wave function, “consciousness creates reality.” None of it survives contact with the physics. The “observer” in the observer effect is a measurement interaction, not a mind; entanglement is a correlation, not a channel for intention; the measurement problem is a live dispute about how to interpret the formalism, not a licence to say that your feelings select outcomes. What the appeal accomplishes is a transfer of prestige: technical vocabulary is borrowed to do metaphysical work, and the borrowing is invisible to a reader who has studied neither. That is univocity in its purest form — one word, two domains, no acknowledgement of the gap — and it is worth naming, because a young person who has been told that quantum physics proves manifestation will not be answered by being told that manifestation is unbiblical. She will be answered by someone who can say, in three sentences and without contempt, what the word actually means.

· · ·

Why does this matter? Three reasons, and they are practical.

First, because a univocal concept cannot be worshipped. You cannot adore a quantity. You can only operate it. This is the deepest pastoral consequence of the error: the manifest space trains people in a relation to reality that has no room for adoration, because adoration is the response to a mystery that exceeds the categories, and there is nothing in the system that exceeds anything. Everything is on the same plane, and so everything is manipulable, and so nothing is holy. The result is a person who has a practice and no reverence, which is a spiritual condition the tradition has a name for: it is the condition of the magician.

Second, because univocity makes the creature infinite and therefore unbearable. If the self is a center of the same energy as the universe, then there is no limit that is not a failure. Every boundary becomes a limitation to be overcome, every illness a resistance, every death a defeat of one’s frequency. The creature is not allowed to be a creature. And a creature that is not allowed to be a creature will spend its life in a war against its own conditions, which it cannot win, and which it will interpret as a personal defeat.

Third, because analogy is what makes gratitude possible. If everything good that happens to me is the return on my own interior investment, then there is nothing to be grateful for, only something to be pleased about. Gratitude requires an other who gives. It requires the asymmetry that analogy preserves and univocity destroys. This is why the manifest space’s gratitude practice, which is its most attractive feature, is also the place where its metaphysics is most clearly false: a person writing “I am grateful for my new job” nine times a day is not thanking anyone. She is filing a claim.

· · ·

Thomas’s own use of analogy was not a debating trick. It was the condition of the possibility of theology. If the words we use of God are univocal, we are idolaters; if they are equivocal, we are atheists who make noises. Analogy is the narrow path, and it is narrow for a reason: it requires the speaker to hold in one mind both the likeness and the greater unlikeness, and to keep holding them, and never to let go of either.

The manifest space lets go of both. It takes the likeness (the universe responds! the interior matters!) and drops the unlikeness (the universe is not you, the interior is not the cause). The result is a spirituality of extraordinary intimacy and no reverence — a God you can text, a cosmos that has your number, and a self that is the only thing in the room that is not a projection.

The Catholic answer is not to drop the likeness in reaction. It is to restore the unlikeness, and with it the whole structure that the unlikeness makes possible: creation, providence, grace, sin, redemption, worship, and the possibility of being loved by someone who is not a mirror.

· · ·

There is a version of this argument that is easier to feel than the technical one, and it is worth stating because most people will meet the idea before they meet the metaphysics.

Imagine two people praying for the same thing — a job, say — and imagine the two prayers.

The first says: I am aligning my energy with the outcome. I release resistance. I am open to receiving. I am grateful in advance. Every sentence is addressed to a mechanism, and every sentence is a technique. If the job comes, the person will feel competent; if it does not, she will feel blocked. In neither case has she spoken to anyone.

The second says: Lord, I need work. I am afraid. I do not know what you are doing. Help me. Every sentence is addressed to a person. If the job comes, she will be grateful to someone. If it does not, she will be angry with someone — and anger with someone is a relationship, and a relationship can survive disappointment, and it can even grow in it.

The difference between the two prayers is the analogia entis. Not as a doctrine in a book, but as the thing that makes the second prayer possible, because it makes it possible for there to be someone on the other end who is not a mechanism and not a mirror.

That is why this apparently technical chapter sits where it does. The rest of the audit is an application of it.

The point

Almost every error in the manifest space is a refusal of analogy: a single univocal word — energy, alignment, frequency — doing the work of a doctrine.

Do this

Take one word. Write what it means in physics, what it means in your speech, and what it means in the Creed.

What this sets up

The second test is about grace, and it is where the system’s Pelagianism shows.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 10

Nature and Grace

The manifest space is Pelagianism with a user manual. The diagnosis is old, precise, and — this is the uncomfortable part — partly true of us.

In 2018, Pope Francis published an apostolic exhortation on holiness that contained a chapter on two “subtle enemies” of the Christian life. One was a kind of neo-Gnosticism: a Christianity reduced to an intellectual elite with a private knowledge. The other was a new Pelagianism, and the Pope described it with a precision that reads as though he had been reading the manifest-space literature:

“Still, some Christians insist on taking another path, that of justification by their own efforts, the worship of the human will and their own abilities. The result is a self-centred and elitist complacency, bereft of true love. This finds expression in a variety of apparently unconnected ways of thinking and acting: an obsession with the law, an absorption with social and political advantages, a punctilious concern for the Church’s liturgy, doctrine and prestige, a vanity about the ability to manage practical matters, and an excessive concern with programmes of self-help and personal fulfilment.” (Gaudete et Exsultate 57)

He was writing about Catholics. He could have been writing about the manifest space, from the other side of the same error.

· · ·

Pelagius was a British moralist of the late fourth century who taught that human beings can fulfil God’s commands by their own natural powers, without the special assistance of grace. Augustine opposed him for a decade, and the controversy shaped the whole Western theology of grace. The core of the objection was not that Pelagius was optimistic about human nature — optimism about human nature is not a heresy. It was that Pelagius had made grace superfluous: if the will can do it, then grace is a decoration, and if grace is a decoration, then the Incarnation is a decoration, and if the Incarnation is a decoration, then the Cross is an example rather than a sacrifice.

Francis’s “new Pelagians” are not teaching that the will can fulfil the commands. They are doing something subtler: they are treating the Christian life as a programme whose success depends on the quality of one’s own execution. The tell is not the doctrine; the tell is the anxiety. A Pelagian is someone who cannot afford to fail, because everything depends on the performance, and who therefore experiences the spiritual life as a series of examinations she is not sure she has passed.

Now read the manifest space through that lens, and the diagnosis becomes exact.

The manifest space is a total Pelagianism, and a cheerful one. It has no doctrine of grace at all — not a diminished one, not a disputed one, none. The universe does not give; it responds. The outcome is a function of the practitioner’s interior state. Success is alignment, failure is resistance, and the whole moral universe is a meritocracy of vibration. It is the most complete Pelagianism the West has produced since the eighteenth century, and it is sold as liberation.

· · ·

The Catholic alternative is not the opposite error, which is a quietism that makes human action irrelevant. It is the doctrine that makes both action and gift possible at once, and the Catechism states it with unusual directness:

“God grants his creatures not only their existence but also the dignity of acting on their own.” (CCC 307)

And, on the cooperation of creatures in providence:

“God is the sovereign master of his plan. But to carry it out he also makes use of his creatures’ cooperation. This cooperation is not a passive one; God grants his creatures the dignity of acting on their own and of being causes for one another.” (CCC 306)

Read that twice. It says that human action is real. It is not a puppet-show, not a decoration, not a mere occasion for divine action. When a woman works for a promotion, her work causes something. When a man forgives his brother, the forgiveness changes the world. The Catholic doctrine of providence is not fatalism; it is the most robust account of human agency on offer, because it grounds agency in the creative act rather than in the creature’s own reservoir.

And then it adds the thing the manifest space cannot say: that the whole of this — the agency, the world it acts in, the good it seeks, the power to seek it — is given. “What have you that you did not receive?” (1 Cor 4:7).

This is the structure that the manifest space parodies. The parody is exact: it keeps the agency and drops the givenness. And a creature with agency and no givenness is a creature that must manufacture its own worth, which is the definition of hell, and which is why the manifest space, at its most successful, produces people who are exhausted.

· · ·

There is a second half to this test, and it is the half that most Catholic writing on the subject skips.

Gratia non tollit naturam — grace does not destroy nature. The first half of the principle is a charter for the natural. It says that human effort, human skill, human planning, human desire, human medicine, human friendship, and human ambition are not the enemies of grace but its material. It says that a Christian may set a goal, work for it, visualize it if it helps, write it down, tell a friend, and pursue it with everything she has, without any of that being Pelagianism — because Pelagianism is not the presence of effort; it is the absence of dependence.

This distinction is the pastoral key to the whole book, and it is worth stating as bluntly as possible.

A Catholic may do almost everything the manifest space recommends. What she may not do is believe what the manifest space believes about why it works.

She may write down her desires, because desire is real and articulable. She may rehearse a difficult conversation in her imagination, because the imagination is a real faculty and rehearsal is a real form of prudence. She may keep a gratitude journal, because thanksgiving is a duty and a medicine. She may speak a hoped-for future aloud, because words shape the speaker. She may work for the promotion with all her strength, because the world is real and effort is a real cause.

What she may not do is attribute the result to the resemblance between her thought and the event, because that attribution is not a harmless piece of folk psychology. It is a claim about who God is — namely, that there isn’t one, only a law — and it will eventually exact its price, and the price will be paid by someone who is sick.

· · ·

Which brings us to the hardest sentence in this chapter.

The manifest space is not wrong because it thinks too highly of human beings. It is wrong because it thinks too lowly of them. It offers a creature a universe made of her own interior, which sounds like a promotion and is actually a demotion: a being who can create reality by assumption is a being with no reality to be given, no gift to receive, no other to love, no death to die into, and no God to adore. In the manifest space, the human person is infinite and alone.

The Catholic account says something that is harder to believe and better to live with: that the person is finite, dependent, limited, and loved — loved by someone whose goodness is not a projection, whose gifts are not returns, and whose providence is not a law but a face.

The next chapter takes up the consequence of that, which is the Cross.

The point

The manifest space is a total, cheerful Pelagianism: agency without givenness, effort without gift, and therefore performance without mercy.

Do this

Identify one thing you do in order to earn what has already been given, and stop doing it for a week.

What this sets up

The third test is the one that decides the verdict, and it cannot be repaired.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 11

The Cross and the Glory

This is the test the manifest space cannot pass, and cannot be repaired to pass: the test of the innocent sufferer. Everything else in the audit could be argued about. This one is a verdict.

There is a room in the basement of the manifest space and I have described it twice already in this book, and I am going to describe it a third time, because it is the reason the book exists.

The room has a bed in it. There is a person in the bed, and the person is dying, and someone who loves her is sitting beside the bed with a book that says that illness is a message from your subconscious, that the body keeps the score, that disease is unexpressed emotion, that you do not get what you want but what you are.

The person in the chair has been reading. She has been trying, in the way that people try when they are desperate, to find the thing she did. She has gone back through the years looking for the resentment, the fear, the moment of low vibration that opened the door. She has apologized to her sister for things she did not do. She has begun to be afraid of her own thoughts, because her thoughts are the only thing in the room that might still be causing this.

The manifest space has no way out of that room. It can only furnish it.

· · ·

This is the chapter where the audit stops being an intellectual exercise, so it is worth stating the thesis plainly and then defending it.

The manifest space cannot account for innocent suffering, and the failure is not an accident of its popularizers but a structural property of its metaphysics. Any version that repairs the failure has stopped being the manifest space.

The argument is short. If interior states cause exterior circumstances by resemblance, then every circumstance has an interior cause. If every circumstance has an interior cause, then every suffering has an interior cause in the sufferer. If every suffering has an interior cause in the sufferer, then there is no innocent suffering. And if there is no innocent suffering, then the Gospel is not merely incomplete but false, because the Gospel is the story of a man who was innocent and suffered, and who said in advance that this would happen to his friends.

Every softening move the system makes is a variant of the same sentence. “Soul contract” — you chose this before you were born. “Lesson” — you attracted it in order to learn. “Mirror” — the universe is showing you your beliefs. “Growth” — the pain is the resistance leaving. “Shadow work” — the illness is the unintegrated material. Each of them sounds gentler than you did this, and each of them means you did this. The difference between them is bedside manner.

· · ·

Now the alternative, and it is not a theory that explains suffering. That is important. The Church does not have an explanation of suffering, and every attempt to supply one has been, sooner or later, condemned — by the Church herself, because the explanations always end up blaming someone.

What the Church has is not an explanation but a set of sentences and a presence.

The first sentence is from John 9. The disciples see a man blind from birth and ask the question that every religious person asks in the presence of suffering: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” It is a manifest-space question. It assumes that suffering has a cause in someone’s interior state, and it offers two candidates. Jesus refuses both: “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him” (John 9:3).

Notice what the answer does and does not do. It does not say that the blindness is good. It does not say that the man chose it. It does not explain the mechanism. It says that the situation is not a verdict about the man, and that God is going to be present in it. That is the entire Catholic theodicy in one verse: the sufferer is innocent, and God is not absent.

The second is from Job. Job’s friends are the manifest space. They have a system — suffering is proportional to sin — and they spend thirty-five chapters explaining to a suffering man why his suffering is his fault, in increasingly gentle tones. Job refuses. He demands an answer, and he is not rebuked for demanding one. When God finally speaks out of the whirlwind, he does not give an answer. He gives a tour: where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? The speech is not an explanation; it is an exposure to a greatness that makes the demand for an explanation look like what it is — the request of a creature to be shown the workings of a wisdom it could not survive understanding.

And at the end, God says something extraordinary about the friends: “My wrath is kindled against you… for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has” (Job 42:7). The ones who defended the system were wrong. The one who screamed at God was right. Every theodicy that consoles by assigning blame is condemned by the book that is supposed to be about the problem.

The third is the Cross. Not the Cross as a transaction — that is another theology, and a good one, but it is not what the Gospels put in front of the sufferer. What they put in front of the sufferer is a man who prayed to be spared and was not. “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt 26:39). That prayer contains both halves of the Catholic answer and neither half of the manifest one. It asks for what it wants, without embarrassment. It accepts that the answer may be no, without pretending that the no is a yes. And it is prayed by God.

There is no way to make that prayer compatible with the law of attraction. The law of attraction says that a petition that is properly aligned is always granted. The Gospel says that the one perfectly aligned petition in history was refused, and that the refusal was the salvation of the world.

· · ·

From these three, a shape emerges, and it is worth naming because it is the thing the manifest space cannot offer.

The Catholic account of suffering is a theodicy of participation, not a theodicy of explanation. It does not tell you why. It tells you who is with you, and what your suffering can become, and — this is the part that is hardest to say without sounding glib — that the transformation is real, and that it is not the same as relief.

Three consequences follow, and they are the pastoral content of this chapter.

First: the sufferer is not asked to be the cause of her own healing. She is asked to consent, to trust, to receive the sacraments, to accept help, to let herself be loved. That is a completely different assignment, and it is one a dying person can actually complete. The manifest space assigns the dying person an impossible task at the worst possible moment; the Church assigns her a possible one.

Second: the fear of one’s own thoughts is lifted. A person who has been taught that her intrusive thoughts are causally efficacious lives in a private hell that looks, from outside, exactly like scrupulosity. The Catholic answer is not “your thoughts are powerless” — thoughts are not powerless; they form the soul. It is that thoughts are not creative, and that the ones that arrive unbidden are not yours in the way that the system says they are. The tradition has a whole vocabulary for this: temptation is not sin; the suggestion is not the consent; the first movement is not the act. A person who learns that vocabulary is set free from a burden she has been carrying in secret, and I have watched it happen, and it is one of the most direct works of mercy available to a catechist.

Third: the sick are restored to innocence. This is the whole of it. Every sentence in the Church’s repertoire that is worth anything in that room says the same thing in a different register: you did not do this, and you are not being punished, and God is not disgusted by you, and you may be angry, and you may ask, and you may not understand.

· · ·

Now the glory, because the test is “cross and glory,” and a chapter that stopped at the Cross would be as false as the system it is answering.

The resurrection is not the reversal of the Cross in the sense of a happy ending appended to a tragedy. It is the revelation that the Cross — the actual one, with the actual death — is not the last thing about God. The wounds are still there in the risen body. Thomas is invited to touch them. This is not a detail; it is the answer to the problem. The risen Christ does not appear as someone who avoided suffering. He appears as someone who went through it and came out the other side with the wounds still in him, glorified and not erased.

Which means that the Catholic promise to the suffering person is not: it will be fine. It is: this will be taken up. The technical word is transfiguration, and it is the only promise in the world that neither denies the reality of the wound nor leaves it as the final truth about you.

The manifest space’s promise, by contrast, is that the wound was never real — it was a misalignment, a belief, a frequency. That is not a hope. It is an erasure, and it is offered to people who have lost children.

· · ·

There is one more thing to be said, and it is the thing that makes this chapter hard to write honestly.

The Church has often failed this test herself. There is a Catholic version of the manifest space’s cruelty, and it is the version that tells the sufferer that her suffering is a punishment, or a test she is failing, or the result of insufficient faith, or — the most refined version — something she should not talk about because it would be a bad witness. The prosperity gospel is not a Protestant invention that stayed in its lane; it has Catholic cousins, and they are just as cruel and rather better dressed.

The test is not “Catholic versus New Age.” The test is: does this allow the sufferer to be innocent? Applied to the manifest space, the answer is no. Applied to a certain kind of Catholic preaching, the answer is also no. The difference is that the Church has a canon by which she can be corrected — Job, John 9, the Cross, the saints who suffered — and the manifest space has only its own premises. That is what a tradition is for. It is not a guarantee that we will get it right. It is a place where getting it wrong can be named.

The point

The system cannot allow the sufferer to be innocent, and the failure is structural. It is refuted by John 9, by Job, and by the Cross.

Do this

Learn the four sentences for the sick by heart, and say none of them until you are sitting down.

What this sets up

The same failure appears in its account of other people.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 12

Church and the Self

“Everyone is you pushed out” is not a curiosity of one writer. It is the logical consequence of the system’s premises — and it is the point at which the manifest space abolishes the other person.

Of all the manifest space’s doctrines, the one that sounds most like a deep spiritual insight and is in fact the most destructive is the one Neville Goddard’s readers summarize as everyone is you pushed out.

The claim is that the people in your life are not independent agents but reflections of your own assumptions. Their behaviour toward you is determined by what you hold in consciousness about them. If someone treats you badly, it is because you assume, at some level, that you deserve it. Change the assumption, and the person changes — not because you have persuaded them, but because you have altered the state of which they are an outpicturing. Goddard is reported to have put it in a sentence that is either mystical or monstrous depending on your metaphysics: “The world is yourself pushed out.”

Read in one mood, this is a counsel of self-examination, and there is a real insight buried in it: our assumptions about other people do shape how we approach them, and how we approach them shapes how they respond. A person who assumes hostility will find it. That much is true, and it is the beginning of wisdom about one’s own contribution to conflict.

Read as the system requires, it is something else entirely: a denial that there is anyone else.

· · ·

The appeal is real, and it should be stated before it is criticized.

If everyone is you pushed out, then you are never actually at the mercy of another person’s freedom. The boss who humiliates you is a state of your own consciousness; the parent who abandoned you is an echo of your assumptions; the man who assaulted you is a mirror. The doctrine offers, to people who have been genuinely powerless, an account in which the power was never really elsewhere. It is the same psychological move as the “soul contract,” and it is the same reason it is so attractive: it converts victimhood into authorship, which feels like dignity.

And it works as a technique of detachment, in the narrow sense. A person who stops needing another’s approval becomes less manipulable, and the doctrine can produce that effect. Some of the people who defend it are defending the only thing that got them out of bed.

But now follow the logic, because the logic is inexorable and it leads somewhere no one wants to go.

If everyone is you pushed out, then the person who harms you has no moral standing of her own. She is not a subject; she is a symptom. She cannot be forgiven, because forgiveness requires someone to forgive. She cannot be confronted, because confrontation requires someone to confront. She cannot be loved, because love requires someone who could refuse you. She can only be managed — which is to say, manipulated at the level of your own interior, which is the exact opposite of the thing the Gospel calls love of neighbour.

And the doctrine destroys the possibility of testimony. If the other person is a projection, then the person who told you about the doctrine is also a projection, and so is the doctrine, and so is your belief in it. The system cannot be defended without assuming the very thing it denies. This is the oldest objection to every form of solipsism, and it is fatal here: the person who taught you that everyone is you pushed out was not you.

And it makes the victims of abuse responsible for their abuse. This is not a hypothetical misuse; it is the doctrine applied consistently. If another’s action toward me is the outworking of my assumption, then the assault was mine. The manifest space has produced, in the last decade, an entire literature of people trying to escape this conclusion while retaining the premise, and the literature is a record of intelligent people performing increasingly elaborate contortions to avoid a sentence that follows from their own first principle.

· · ·

The specific person

If you spend an hour in the manifest space online, you will meet the practice the doctrine was built for. It is usually called SP — “the specific person.” The technique is simple: choose the person you want, whether or not she has chosen you; write the scene in which she has; feel it as already done; persist until the world rearranges. There are communities with acronyms and journals, “SP journeys” with day counts, celebratory posts when the person comes back, and consoling posts about the bridge of incidents when she does not.

This is not a fringe misuse. It is the cleanest test case the system has, because it removes every ambiguity: the desired good is another person’s will.

The metaphysics fails first. If everyone is you pushed out, then the person you are working on has no interior life to consent with. She has a script, and you are editing it. The practice is not an attempt to persuade someone; it is an attempt to replace her. Whatever else it is, it is not a relationship, because a relationship requires two centres of action and the technique has arranged for there to be one.

The ethics fails second, and in a way the system cannot repair. Love wills the good of the other; this wills the other as my good. Love is glad that the beloved is free, because her freedom is what makes her love worth having; the technique treats her freedom as the obstacle to be dissolved. This is why the practice so often ends in the same place: the person returns, and the practitioner discovers that she has won an argument with a mirror. What she wanted was to be chosen by someone who could have chosen otherwise. She has arranged to be chosen by someone who could not.

The pastoral reality is third, and it is not contemptible. Most of the people doing this work are grieving. “SP” is, in the overwhelming majority of cases, an ex — and the practice is a way of not accepting a refusal, which is the oldest and hardest human problem there is. The Church has a word for the place where a refusal is accepted and mourned and survived, and it is not a technique. It is a tomb, and an Easter, and a community that will sit with you in between.

So the transposition is narrow, and it has to be said precisely, because a careless version would be cruel. You may pray for a person, and for her good, and for her conversion. You may not pray for her will — not because God could not move it, but because to ask him to move it against her freedom is to ask him to do the one thing he has bound himself not to do, which is to save a person by force. The prayer that is permitted is harder and better: “Make her happy. Make me the kind of man she would choose freely. And if she does not, make me free of her.” That prayer can be answered. The other one, if it were answered, would destroy the thing it was asking for.

· · ·

The Catholic alternative is not “other people are real and your assumptions don’t matter.” Both halves matter. What the tradition offers is a metaphysics in which the other person is irreducibly other — created, free, capable of refusing you, and therefore capable of loving you — and in which your own interior life is genuinely causally connected to hers without being the cause of her.

The technical name for this is the doctrine of creation, and the practical name for it is the doctrine of the neighbour.

Because the other is created, she is a gift. This is the sentence that the manifest space cannot say and that the Gospel says constantly. The neighbour is not an emanation of my consciousness; she is a work of God, given to me from outside, and the whole possibility of love depends on her not being me. “Love your neighbour as yourself” is a command that presupposes two selves. A philosophy in which there is only one self can produce benevolence — I can be kind to my projection — but it cannot produce love, because love is the act of willing the good of another as other, and there is no other.

Because the other is free, she can refuse, and her refusal is a good. This is the hardest part. The manifest space promises a world in which no one can refuse you, because you control the reflection. The Catholic faith promises a world in which people can refuse you — and in which God himself can refuse you — and it says that this is worth more than a world of compliant mirrors, because a world without refusal is a world without love, and a world without love is a world in which nothing you receive means anything.

Because the other is a member, her good is bound up with yours. The Church’s doctrine of the Mystical Body is the exact inversion of the mirror: “If one member suffers, all suffer together” (1 Cor 12:26). This is not a metaphor for solidarity; it is a claim about the structure of reality. We are not particles projecting onto one another; we are members of one body, and the body has a head, and the head is not me.

· · ·

There is a practice that makes the difference concrete, and it is so ordinary that its metaphysical content is easy to miss. It is the practice of asking someone else to pray for you.

Consider what is happening when a Catholic says to a friend, “please pray for my son.” She is asking a person — an other, free, distinct, with her own relationship to God — to intercede. She is not aligning energies. She is not managing a projection. She is acknowledging, in the most practical way possible, that there are at least two of us, and that the second one can do something the first one cannot do alone.

And the same structure appears, at its highest, in the communion of saints. The Catholic asks the saints to pray for her, which is either the most absurd doctrine in Christianity or the most exact expression of what it means to be a creature among creatures before God. It is absurd if the other is a projection, because you cannot ask a mirror for help. It is the whole of reality if the other is a person.

The manifest space has no intercession. It cannot have intercession, because it has no others. And that absence is, I think, the single most reliable diagnostic question in this whole audit: who do you ask, other than yourself? If the answer is “no one, I just align,” the system has already done its work, and no refutation will reach the person, because the person has been taught that no one is there to reach her.

· · ·

One more layer, and then the audit moves on to the specific claims.

The manifest space’s answer to loneliness is to deny that there is anyone to be lonely for. The Catholic answer is much stranger and much harder: that loneliness is real, that it is a wound in a real communion, that it is the ache of a member separated from a body, and that it will be healed — not by learning that everyone was you all along, but by being incorporated into a communion of persons who are irreducibly not you, and by seeing, at the end, the face of someone who has been looking at you the whole time.

Everything in the manifest space that is beautiful about connection — the synchronicity, the sense that the world is addressed to you, the feeling that strangers are messengers — is true, and is true for a reason the system cannot name. The world is addressed to you. The strangers are messengers. But they are not sent by your assumptions. They are sent by someone, and they are sent as themselves, and the whole drama of salvation consists in learning to receive them as such.

The point

“Everyone is you pushed out” is the logical consequence of the system’s premises, and it abolishes the other person — and therefore love.

Do this

Ask who you ask to pray for you, other than yourself. If the answer is no one, you have found the real work.

What this sets up

With the tests in place, the claims can be judged one by one.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 13

Fourteen Claims, One by One

The audit, applied. Four are true and should be received; three are half-true and must be corrected; seven are false and must be refused. The ratio is the point.

A system is not refuted by being disliked. It is refuted — or received — claim by claim, and the verdicts are not all the same verdict. What follows is the audit in its most concrete form: fourteen claims that between them carry most of the manifest space’s weight, each stated in the strongest form I can give it, each given a verdict, each given an argument, and each given something to do instead.

The verdicts are integrate (the claim is true, and the Church should say so louder), correct (the claim names something real but describes it wrongly), and reject (the claim is false in a way that cannot be repaired inside the system). The whole audit is summarized in a table at the end of the chapter; a reader who wants the shape of the result before the arguments should read that table first.

· · ·

1. Attention and expectation shape action and perception

Integrate. This is not a piece of New Age metaphysics; it is a piece of Aristotelian psychology that the Church received eight centuries ago and that contemporary cognitive science has done nothing but confirm. What we attend to we perceive; what we expect we tend to find; what we rehearse we perform. Aquinas’s treatise on the passions and the vis cogitativa — the estimative power by which we grasp a situation as “good for me” or “threatening” — is a more rigorous account of this than anything in the self-help literature, and it makes the same practical point: the interior life is the proximate cause of action.

The manifest space’s error is to extend this from action to being — to claim that attention shapes not only what we do but what happens. That extension is false. The core is true, and a Catholic who denies it has denied the doctrine of virtue.

What to do instead: examine what you habitually attend to. The examen does this at the level of the day; the doctrine of habitus does it at the level of a life.

2. Gratitude changes the one who is grateful

Integrate. The most defensible claim in the system, and the one most likely to be dismissed by critics who have never kept the practice. Gratitude reorders attention, softens resentment, and makes a person capable of receiving. The Church has known this since the Eucharist — eucharistia, thanksgiving — and has a whole ascetical tradition built on it: the examen’s first point is gratitude, not confession.

The manifest space’s error is not in the practice but in the address. Its gratitude is directed at a mechanism, and a mechanism cannot be thanked. What is being performed, in a great deal of manifestation journalling, is the form of thanksgiving with the object removed — which is why the practice, at its most intense, produces a strange hollow feeling that its practitioners describe and cannot explain.

What to do instead: thank someone. Specifically, by name, for something specific, out loud. The general gratitude of the journal becomes the particular gratitude of the Te Deum and of the thank-you note, and particular gratitude is the kind that changes a person.

3. Words shape the speaker

Integrate. Speech is not the transmission of pre-existing thought; it is one of the ways thought is formed. What we say about ourselves, we come to believe; what we say about others, we come to see. James devotes a chapter to this (“the tongue is a fire”), and the tradition built an entire discipline — custody of speech — around it.

But the manifest space extends the claim in a direction the tradition refuses: from words shape the speaker to words shape the world. The extension has a name in Catholic moral theology, and it is not a compliment: it is the error of the magus, the belief that the correctly formulated word compels.

What to do instead: attend to what you say about yourself in the third person and about others in the second. Bless rather than curse, literally and out loud. And when you notice that you have been speaking a false sentence about yourself for years, go to confession and hear the true one said over you by someone with authority to say it.

4. Imagination mediates knowledge and desire

Integrate. Aquinas holds that the intellect cannot think without the phantasm — the image — and that desire is aroused by what is imagined. Ignatius built a method on it: the composition of place, the application of the senses. The Exercises are the most sophisticated technology of imagination in the Western tradition, and they are aimed at the opposite of the manifest space’s goal: not the manufacture of a desired future, but the contemplation of a given one.

The manifest space’s error is a category mistake about what the imagination is. It treats a medium of encounter as a cause of being. The imagination is the door through which grace and truth come in and through which the affections go out. It is not a pump.

What to do instead: imagine the Gospel. Fifteen minutes with a scene from the life of Christ, in the Ignatian manner, will do more for the imagination than a year of visualization, because the scene is real.

5. Desire is a guide to the good

Correct. Desire is not arbitrary noise; it is the soul’s inclination toward the good, and it is revelatory: it tells you what you love. The tradition takes it seriously — “What do you want me to do for you?” is a question Jesus asks, and he does not treat the answer as an impertinence.

But desire is disordered as well as revelatory, and both halves are essential. Spe Salvi 33 puts it exactly: “In prayer we must learn what we can truly ask of God — what is worthy of God… We must learn to purify our desires and our hopes.” The manifest space keeps the revelatory half and drops the purifying half, and the result is a person who takes her desires as instructions from the universe and has no way of asking whether they are good.

What to do instead: ask of each desire three questions — what is this a desire for? (the object beneath the object), what would it cost someone else?, and would I want it if I had to receive it from God’s hand rather than my own? The third question is the one that does the work.

6. Persistent asking is heard

Correct. This is biblical, and the manifest space quotes the verses correctly: ask, seek, knock; the friend at midnight; the widow and the unjust judge. The tradition has a doctrine of impetration, and it is robust.

What the manifest space gets wrong is the causality of prayer. It makes asking into a technique that compels, and it makes the answer a function of the asker’s state. Aquinas’s account is both more sober and more encouraging: “Divine providence disposes not only what effects shall take place, but also from what causes and in what order these effects shall proceed… we pray not that we may change the Divine disposition, but that we may impetrate that which God has disposed to be fulfilled by our prayers” (ST II-II, q. 83, a. 2). Prayer is a real cause, ordained as a cause, and it does not manipulate.

What to do instead: ask specifically, repeatedly, with the confidence of a child, and then add the clause that makes the prayer Christian: not as I will. And when the answer is no, do not conclude that you asked badly. Conclude that you are being given something else, and go looking for it.

7. You create your reality

Reject as stated; correct to cooperation. The sentence is attractive because it is almost true and the almost is invisible.

You do not create your reality. You act inside a reality you did not create, with a body you did not design, in a history you did not choose, under a providence you do not administer. What you do is cooperate — and the Catechism gives that cooperation a dignity that the manifest space’s version actually diminishes: “God grants his creatures not only their existence but also the dignity of acting on their own” (CCC 307).

The difference is not verbal. A creator is responsible for the whole; a cooperator is responsible for her part. If you create your reality, then every disaster in your life is your fault and every disaster in your neighbour’s life is hers. If you cooperate in a reality that is given, then your part is real, your responsibility is proportionate, and the parts you do not control are not your guilt.

What to do instead: distinguish, in any situation, what is yours to do from what is not. Then do the first with all your strength and entrust the second — which is the structure of every Catholic prayer ever written.

8. Everyone is you pushed out

Reject. Treated at length in the previous chapter, and rejected there for three reasons that bear repeating in one line each: it makes the other person a symptom rather than a subject; it makes love impossible; and it refutes itself, since the person who taught it to you was not you.

What to do instead: assume that the person in front of you is more real than your idea of her. Then ask her a question and listen to the answer, which is the only known method of discovering that someone exists.

9. The universe responds to your vibration

Reject as stated; transpose. There is no such thing as vibration in this sense. The word borrows the authority of physics and delivers a metaphor, and the metaphor is doing the work of a doctrine — specifically, the doctrine of providence — while denying everything that makes providence providence: that the one who orders is personal, free, and not under our control.

The transposition is real, though, and it is this: reality is responsive, and not merely mechanically. Grace answers prayer. Sacraments effect what they signify. The saints intercede. Providence orders events, including the free acts of creatures, without compelling them. The world is not a machine. But the responsiveness runs from a person to a person, and the initiative is not ours.

What to do instead: replace the question “what am I vibrating?” with the question “to whom am I speaking, and what has he promised?”

10. You are God; you are Christ-conscious

Reject. This is the claim that cannot be softened, because it is the metaphysical centre of the system, and because the Church has a true doctrine that looks similar from a distance and is the exact opposite.

The true doctrine is divinization: “The Son of God became man so that we might become God” (CCC 460, quoting Athanasius and Augustine). But the Catholic doctrine is that we become God by grace, by adoption, by participation, receiving a life that is not ours by nature. The manifest space’s doctrine is that we are God by nature, and that the task is to realize it. The first is the most extravagant gift in the history of religion. The second is the oldest lie in the book: you shall be like God.

What to do instead: say the truth out loud, in the first person, once a day: I am not God, and I am not nothing. I am a son in the Son. The sentence is harder to believe than the lie, which is why it has to be practiced.

11. Illness and misfortune are attracted by the sufferer

Reject. The most harmful claim in the system, and the one for which there is no softening. It is refuted by John 9, by Job, and by the Cross, and it is refuted experientially by every hospital ward in the world.

There is a version of this claim that is true and modest: some illness is behaviourally mediated, some suffering is the fruit of sin, and the connections are worth studying. That version is medicine and moral theology. The manifest-space version is different in kind: it says that the interior state is the efficient cause of the disease, which makes the sick person the author of her illness and turns the care of the sick into an investigation.

What to do instead: whenever you are tempted to explain someone’s suffering to them, do not. Sit down. Ask what would help. Bring food. Pray. If you must say something, say the thing that Job’s friends should have said and didn’t: I don’t know why, and I am not going anywhere.

12. The past can be revised

Correct. There is a real experience here, and it is one of the most striking in the whole system. People who practise “revision” report a genuine change in their relation to a past event: the memory loses its sting, the story changes shape, the identity built on the old version becomes available for revision.

That is real. It is also not what the system says it is. The system says the past itself is altered, that the event is rewritten in the fabric of reality, that one’s history becomes a different history. That is false, and it is false in a way that costs the practitioner something important: a past that can be rewritten cannot be forgiven, because forgiveness presupposes that the thing happened.

The Catholic alternative is much stronger. Confession does something to the past that no amount of reimagining can do: it removes the guilt while leaving the fact intact, and it does so by the authority of another. The healing of memories, where it is authentic, does not delete the event; it heals the wound the event left, by bringing Christ into the memory rather than replacing it.

What to do instead: go to confession. Name the thing. Receive absolution. Then, if the memory still wounds, pray the event with Christ present in it — not instead of it.

13. Signs and numbers decode the future

Reject. “All forms of divination are to be rejected… Consulting horoscopes, astrology, palm reading, interpretation of omens and lots, the phenomena of clairvoyance, and recourse to mediums all conceal a desire for power over time, history, and, in the last analysis, other human beings, as well as a wish to conciliate hidden powers” (CCC 2116). The 11:11 is an omen; it is a small one, and the Catechism’s sentence covers it.

The reason the Church is severe here is not fussiness. It is that the practice trains a person to relate to reality as a code to be broken rather than a gift to be received, and it produces a permanent low-grade anxiety that is the opposite of faith. The alternative is not “ignore providence.” It is discernment: the tested reading of interior movements and external events, ordered to action rather than to prediction.

What to do instead: when you notice a coincidence, do not decode it. Thank God for it, if it moved you to gratitude, and then do the next right thing. If you are trying to decide something, use the Ignatian rules for discernment, a trusted adviser, and the ordinary means — and then decide.

14. A technique guarantees the outcome

Reject. This is the claim that makes the rest operational, and it is the one the Church has a precise name for: tentare Deum, tempting God.

Aquinas treats it as a species of superstition (ST II-II, q. 97): it is the attempt to put God to the test, to require a specified result as the price of belief. And the Catechism names the underlying error with great precision: superstition “can even affect the worship we offer the true God, e.g., when one attributes an importance in some way magical to certain practices otherwise lawful or necessary” (CCC 2111).

Notice: the Catechism’s target is not the pagan. It is the Catholic who treats the practice as a mechanism. Which means that the most dangerous version of this error is not in the manifest space at all. It is in the parish, in the person who says nine novenas to get the result and is quietly certain that the tenth will work if the first nine were said properly.

What to do instead: do the practice, then say, out loud, thy will be done. If the sentence sticks in your throat, you have found the thing that needs healing, and it is not the outcome.

· · ·

Fourteen claims, and the tally is four integrate, three correct, seven reject.

That tally is the argument of this book in miniature. A response that rejected all fourteen would be false, unjust, and useless. A response that accepted all fourteen would be a surrender with incense. The Church’s response has to be the one thing that is harder than either: discriminate, name, receive, refuse, and then build the alternative so beautifully that the refusal becomes attractive.

VerdictClaimsDisposition
Integrate1 attention and expectation · 2 gratitude · 3 words shape the speaker · 4 imagination mediates knowledgeTeach them louder, and give them their true object
Correct5 desire as guide · 6 persistent asking · 12 revision of the pastKeep the experience, replace the causality
Reject7 you create your reality · 8 everyone is you pushed out · 9 the universe answers vibration · 10 you are God · 11 illness is attracted · 13 signs decode the future · 14 technique guarantees the outcomeName them, refuse them, and supply the alternative

Four, three, seven. The proportion is the argument: a response that rejected all fourteen would be as false as one that accepted them, and a response that accepted the four has to mean it, which means teaching them better than the movement does.

The next chapter does the same work at the level where it is actually decided: the level of vocabulary.

The point

Four claims are true and should be taught louder; three name something real and must be corrected; seven are false and cannot be repaired inside the system.

Do this

Pick the one claim you actually hold, and test it against its verdict. Do not pick the one you find easiest to reject.

What this sets up

The argument will be won or lost at the level of vocabulary.

Chapter 14

The Lexicon

Inculturation is won or lost at the level of vocabulary. Thirty words carry the manifest space — fifteen at length, fifteen in brief — and most of them are equivocal, and the equivocation is where the metaphysics hides.

There is a reason the Church’s missionary history is full of fights about words. Filioque. Theotokos. Substance. Person. The fights were not about pedantry; they were about whether a word could carry the faith without smuggling in a rival metaphysics. A term borrowed from the surrounding culture is a vessel, and vessels have shapes, and a shape that is wrong will deform whatever is poured into it.

The manifest space has a vocabulary of its own, and it is a good vocabulary — vivid, concrete, emotionally intelligent, and almost entirely equivocal. Each of its key words carries two meanings at once: a Catholic meaning, which is usually true, and a manifest-space meaning, which usually is not. The person using the word is usually holding both, and does not know it.

This chapter takes the most important of those words and does four things with each: gives the manifest-space meaning, names the equivocation, gives the Catholic transposition, and issues a verdict.

· · ·

Manifest. Manifest-space meaning: to cause a desired thing to appear in the external world by interior work. Equivocation: the word in Christian usage is passive and divine — Christ “was manifested in the flesh” (1 Tim 3:16); the Spirit is “manifested” for the common good (1 Cor 12:7); the children of God will be “manifested” (Rom 8:19); the believer’s life is “hidden with Christ” until it is manifested in glory (Col 3:1–4). In every case the manifesting is done by God, or done to the believer, and never by the believer to the world. Transposition: keep the word and reverse the direction. Verdict: retain, re-oriented.

Abundance. Manifest-space meaning: material and experiential plenty, measured in goods. Equivocation: the Gospel’s abundance is the superabundance of grace — “I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly” (John 10:10) — which is compatible with poverty, and which the saints have usually experienced in poverty. Transposition: abundance is a property of the gift, not of the inventory. Verdict: correct.

Alignment. Manifest-space meaning: the matching of one’s inner state to a desired outcome. Equivocation: the tradition’s word is conformity — the conforming of the will to God’s — and its model is Gethsemane, where the alignment was perfect and the outcome was the Cross. Transposition: alignment is with a person, not with an outcome. Verdict: correct.

Block. Manifest-space meaning: an interior obstruction preventing the result. Equivocation: the tradition has three quite different words for what stops a person: sin (which is chosen), disordered attachment (which is habitual), and illness (which is suffered). Collapsing all three into “block” makes the first two invisible and the third a moral failing. Transposition: name which of the three you are dealing with. Verdict: refuse, replace with the three.

Energy. Manifest-space meaning: a quasi-physical force transmitted by thought and feeling. Equivocation: energeia in the tradition means act, operation, activity — the operation of a nature — and in the Greek Fathers the uncreated energies of God are God himself, not a force in the world. Transposition: there are real energies: grace, charism, virtue, the virtus of a sacrament. They are personal and gratuitous, and none of them is measured in units. Verdict: refuse as substance, retain as act.

Frequency, vibration. Manifest-space meaning: the medium by which like attracts like. Equivocation: metaphor borrowed from acoustics, used as though it were physics. Transposition: none — there is nothing to transpose, because there is no referent. The underlying experience (that a person’s habitual state is perceptible and contagious) is real and has better names: temperament, habit, atmosphere, the sensus fidei of a community. Verdict: refuse.

The universe. Manifest-space meaning: an impersonal-responsive agency that hears, answers, and arranges. Equivocation: “the universe” in Catholic speech means creation, which is not an agent and cannot hear. The functions assigned to it belong to providence, which is personal, free, and cruciform. Transposition: creation is real, providence is real, and neither is a mechanism with a mood. Verdict: correct, sharply.

Higher self. Manifest-space meaning: the divine core of the person, the true identity beneath the ego. Equivocation: the tradition has imago Dei (a real dignity, wounded by sin), conscience (a real voice, which can be mistaken), and the indwelling Spirit (a real presence, which is not a part of the self). None of them is a “higher self,” and all of them are better news, because all of them involve someone who is not me. Transposition: the self is not deep enough to save itself. Verdict: refuse.

Shadow. Manifest-space meaning: the disowned material of the psyche, which must be integrated. Equivocation: there is a real phenomenon here — the tradition calls it the passions, the wounds, the fomes, the tinder of sin — and a real practice, which is the examination of conscience and the confession of what one would rather not see. But the Jungian frame makes the shadow a project of integration, whereas the Christian frame makes it a mercy to be confessed. Transposition: you do not integrate the shadow; you bring it into the light and it is judged and healed. Verdict: correct.

Limiting belief. Manifest-space meaning: the sole obstacle to the desired outcome. Equivocation: some beliefs are indeed false and limiting, and the tradition cares about them (it calls the cure faith, and the disease despair). But the frame makes every limit a belief, and therefore makes creaturely limits — finitude, illness, death, other people’s freedom — into errors of the mind. Transposition: there are real limits and there are false beliefs, and the discernment between them is most of the spiritual life. Verdict: correct.

Affirmation. Manifest-space meaning: a formula repeated to impress the subconscious. Equivocation: the tradition’s parallel is the aspiration — a short prayer, often scriptural, repeated through the day (“Jesus, have mercy on me”). The difference is the addressee: an affirmation speaks into a mechanism; an aspiration speaks to a person. Transposition: keep the repetition, change the object. Verdict: correct.

Scripting. Manifest-space meaning: writing the desired future in the present tense as though it had happened. Equivocation: the tradition’s parallel is the written petition and the spiritual journal — both real practices with a long history, and both addressed to God rather than to the subconscious. Transposition: write it, date it, and offer it. Then, when it is answered or refused, write that down too; the record of God’s dealings with you is worth more than the record of your wishes. Verdict: correct.

Detachment. Manifest-space meaning: not needing the outcome, so that the outcome can arrive. Equivocation: the tradition’s word is indiferencia — Ignatius’s “indifference,” which is not apathy but a freedom from inordinate attachment such that one is ready to receive either health or sickness, riches or poverty, provided it serves God’s glory (SpEx 23). The manifest version is a technique for getting the thing; the Ignatian version is a freedom from needing it. Transposition: detachment is not a strategy. Verdict: correct, and the correction is the whole difference.

Signs. Manifest-space meaning: confirmations from the universe. Equivocation: the tradition reads signs too — but by discernment, with criteria, under obedience, and with a strong bias against novelty. Transposition: the rules for the discernment of spirits (SpEx 313–336) are a tested method for exactly this, and they are better than 11:11. Verdict: correct.

Gratitude. Manifest-space meaning: a technique that raises vibration and attracts more. Equivocation: gratitude in the tradition is a virtue — a habit of the will by which one acknowledges a debt to a giver — and its highest form is the Eucharist. Transposition: gratitude requires a someone. Verdict: integrate, with the object restored.

· · ·

A second tier of words can be handled more briefly, but each has the same structure — a true experience, a false frame, a transposable core.

WordManifest-space senseCatholic disposition

focusconcentration that magnetizesattention as a moral act — keep

· · ·

One observation about this chapter, and it is the reason it exists.

If you remove the manifest space’s vocabulary from a person and give her nothing in its place, you have not converted her; you have silenced her. She will still have the experiences — the sense that her interior life is connected to the world, the sense that the world is addressed to her, the sense that words matter, the sense that gratitude changes her — and she will have no words for them, and the experiences will either fade or return under a different brand.

The Church’s vocabulary is better. It is older, more precise, more beautiful, and it has been tested in every century by people who were about to die. But it is not available to a person who has never heard it, and it is not attractive when it is delivered as a correction.

So the lexicon is not a weapon. It is a translation table, and the work of translation is the work of a culture — slow, patient, and done one conversation at a time.

The point

Inculturation succeeds or fails at the level of the lexicon: thirty words carry the system, and most of them are equivocal.

Do this

Choose one word from the lexicon and learn its Catholic meaning well enough to explain it to a fourteen-year-old.

What this sets up

None of which changes anyone by itself, because refutation is not conversion.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 15

Why Refutation Fails

The audit is finished, and it changes nothing by itself. This chapter is about the difference between winning an argument and converting a person — and about the only two things that have ever done the second.

If you have followed the argument this far, you are in a dangerous condition: you may believe that the case has been made, and that the case being made is the same as the case being won.

It is not. The history of Catholic engagement with popular spirituality is a long record of excellent arguments that changed nothing. The arguments against spiritualism in the 1920s were correct. The arguments against the prosperity gospel in the 1980s were correct. The arguments against The Secret in 2007 were correct. And the movements went on, because a movement is not a proposition, and refutation is a technique that works on propositions.

This chapter tries to say why, because a book that ends Part Two without saying it would be a book by someone who has never tried.

· · ·

The first reason is that people do not hold beliefs in the way the word suggests.

Newman made the distinction between notional assent — agreement with a proposition considered abstractly — and real assent — the assent of a person whose imagination and affections have been seized by the thing. A notional assent can be refuted. A real assent cannot, because it is not held as an argument; it is held as an experience, and experiences do not respond to syllogisms.

The manifest space is almost entirely a matter of real assent. Its adherents do not believe in the law of attraction in the way they believe that Wellington is the capital of New Zealand. They believe it because they did the practice and something happened — a coincidence, a shift in mood, a job — and because the practice gave them, for the first time in years, a way of being in the world that felt like agency. You cannot refute that with a paragraph about efficient causation.

The second reason is that the system is unfalsifiable by construction. Every failure is evidence of insufficient alignment; every success is evidence of the law. A belief system with that structure is immune to the only evidence that could disconfirm it, and it is also immune to the argument that would, because the argument rests on evidence of the same kind.

The third reason is identity. For a great many people, the manifest space is not a hobby; it is the community that took them in when the Church did not, the language in which they learned to hope, and the thing that distinguishes them from their parents.
