To give it up is not to change an opinion; it is to lose a self. Any argument that does not reckon with this will be heard as an attack, and it will be resisted for reasons that have nothing to do with its premises — which is exactly what the person making the argument will then call irrationality, and which is not irrationality at all.

The fourth reason is that the system’s practices work, in a limited and real sense. Twenty minutes a day of focused attention on a desired future, combined with gratitude and a refusal to rehearse failure, will change a person’s behaviour, and changed behaviour changes outcomes. The person who reports that it works is not lying. She is misattributing the mechanism. And misattribution, when the effect is real, is almost impossible to correct by argument, because the argument appears to deny the effect.

The fifth reason is the credibility of the arguer. This is the one that hurts. A Church whose members are known to have committed grave abuses, whose institutions have protected themselves, and whose ministers sometimes speak of suffering in ways that suggest they have never suffered, does not begin the argument with credit. The manifest space’s claim to be the only spirituality that takes your desire seriously is believed partly because the alternative is believed to be indifferent. That belief is often unjust. It is not baseless.

The sixth reason is beauty. The manifest space is beautiful. The Church, in many places, is not — or rather, the Church’s beauty is stored in its liturgy and its art and its saints, and is not available on a Tuesday night on a phone. An argument that is true and ugly loses to a falsehood that is beautiful, over the length of a life.

· · ·

If refutation does not work, what does?

The honest answer is: two things, and neither of them is an argument.

The first is a practice. People change their metaphysics when they change their practice, not the other way around. The person who begins to pray the examen every night for a month will discover, from the inside, that her interior life is being observed by someone; the theology follows the practice, and it follows it slowly, and it does not need to be argued. This is why the Catholic tradition is a tradition of ascetical practices rather than a tradition of propositions to be believed in the abstract. It has always known that the way in is through the body and the day.

Which means that the pastoral answer to “is it okay if I manifest?” is, at the level of practice, almost always the same: here is something to do instead, and then a concrete, small, beautiful, repeatable thing. The examen, five minutes, tonight. A novena with a real intention. Adoration, twenty minutes, with a question. The Rosary, badly, in the car. It does not matter much which one, so long as it is real, and so long as the person is not left with the void.

The second is a person. Nobody is argued into the Church by a book; people are drawn in by someone whose life has a shape they cannot account for. This is not a counsel of anti-intellectualism. It is a description of the ordinary means: the friend who prays, the priest who is patient, the mother whose grief is not despair, the catechist who takes the question seriously instead of flinching. The argument matters, and it matters mostly after: it explains, retrospectively, what the person has already begun to live.

There is a name for this in the tradition, and it is witness. It is the reason the martyrs converted more people than the apologists, and the reason the Church’s intellectual achievements have always followed her saints rather than the reverse.

· · ·

There is a further implication, and it is not comfortable for the institution.

If practice and witness are the means, then the reform that matters most is not a reform of documents. It is the reform of the ordinary: better catechesis, better homilies, better availability of confession, better formation of catechists, more beautiful liturgy, and a clergy and laity who are not exhausted. These are unglamorous things, and they are the actual front line. A parish that teaches one young person to pray the examen, well, for a year, has done more against the manifest space than a conference of theologians writing against it.

None of which makes this book useless. A practice without a theology drifts, and a witness without an argument becomes a personality. The argument is necessary; it is simply not sufficient, and the failure to say so has produced a great deal of writing that is correct and inert.

· · ·

One last thing, and it is a warning about the reader’s own condition.

The most dangerous outcome of an audit like this one is contempt. It is possible to learn the manifest space’s grammar, see through its metaphysics, and come away with a sense of superiority that is itself a spiritual disease — the disease of the man in the Gospel who thanked God that he was not like the other man. Contempt is not a theological virtue. It is not even an intellectual one, since it prevents the holder from learning anything further from the people he has decided to look down on.

The test of whether this book has been understood is not whether the reader can now refute a manifestation video. It is whether the reader can sit with the girl at 11:11, take her seriously, refuse to lie to her, and give her something better — and whether he can do it without needing her to be wrong.

Part Two ends here. The audit has done its work: four claims received, three corrected, seven refused, thirty words translated, and one honest admission that none of it is enough.

Which means the burden now shifts. If refutation cannot do the work, something has to be built. And a thing that has to be built needs a foundation, and the foundation is the subject of Part Three: not what the manifest space gets wrong, but what the Church actually has.

The point

People are not changed by arguments. They are changed by a practice and by a person — and mostly in that order.

Do this

Stop arguing with someone about manifestation, and hand her one practice with a time attached.

What this sets up

And so we turn from what is wrong to what we actually have.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Part Three

The Reclamation

You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.

Colossians 3:3\u20134

The audit has told us what to refuse. It has not yet told us what we have. This part builds the positive theology — not as a set of restrictions on the manifest space but as the thing the manifest space was reaching for and could not name. It begins with a word: manifestation is not a New Age term that the Church must tolerate. It is a biblical word, and in the Bible it is something God does. From there it develops the four scriptural pillars, the sacramental principle, the practice of manifestation of conscience, the engine room of providence, the anthropology of desire and habitus, and the discipline of hiddenness. By the end, the reader should be able to say not merely what is wrong with the law of attraction but what the truth is that the law of attraction is a parody of.

Chapter 16

Manifestation Is a Divine Word

The word the manifest space borrowed belongs to God. Reclaiming it is not a rhetorical trick; it is the whole argument in miniature.

Begin with the word, because the word is where the battle is.

Manifest comes into English from the Latin manifestus — “caught in the hand,” hence palpable, evident, plain. It is the opposite of hidden. In the New Testament it renders a family of Greek words: phaneroō, to make visible or known; phanerōsis, a making-visible; epiphaneia, an appearing, from which we get Epiphany. None of these words, in any of their occurrences, means what the manifest space means. Not one of them describes a human being causing an event to appear by the power of thought.

They describe something else, and the something else is the subject of this chapter.

· · ·

Manifestation is what God does.

“He was manifested in the flesh” (1 Tim 3:16). The sentence is a hymn fragment, quoted by Paul as something already familiar, and it is one of the densest Christological statements in the New Testament. What is being said is not that a divine idea became vivid. It is that the eternal, invisible, unimaginable God entered a particular human life at a particular time in a particular place, and could be seen, heard, and touched.

John says the same thing with the authority of a witness: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and touched with our hands, concerning the word of life — the life was made manifest, and we saw it” (1 John 1:1–2). The accumulation of senses is deliberate. He is insisting on the physicality, because the physicality is the point.

And the prologue of the fourth Gospel states the principle that governs everything else: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The manifestation of God is not a thought that becomes clearer. It is a person who becomes present.

Now notice the shape of this. Something hidden becomes visible. Something interior becomes external. Something eternal enters time. Something invisible takes on flesh. A word becomes a body.

That is exactly the shape of the manifest space’s grammar — hidden becomes visible, interior becomes external, word becomes fact — and it is the exact inversion of it in every respect that matters. In the Gospel, the one who manifests is God, the means is a person, the result is a gift, and the effect on the recipient is worship. In the manifest space, the one who manifests is the self, the means is a technique, the result is a possession, and the effect on the recipient is satisfaction.

The same shape, turned inside out. That is what a parody is.

· · ·

Manifestation is what God does to the believer.

“To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” (1 Cor 12:7). The Greek is phanerōsis tou pneumatos — the making-visible of the Spirit — and the sentence is a bombshell, because of the last three words.

The manifestation is given, not achieved. It is given to each, not earned by the exceptional. Its content is the Spirit, not a result. And its purpose is the common good, not the private benefit of the recipient.

Every one of those four points is a direct contradiction of the manifest space, and they arrive in a single clause of a letter written to a quarrelsome community in a port city. The Corinthians were, among other things, a congregation of spiritual overachievers — proud of their gifts, ranking them, using them for status — and Paul’s response was not to deny the gifts but to reorient them. The manifestation is real. It is spectacular. And it is not yours.

This is the chapter of Scripture that should be printed on the wall of every Catholic retreat centre, because it settles the whole question of what a manifestation is for. If the Spirit is manifested for the common good, then a practice whose entire structure is private benefit has not merely got the metaphysics wrong. It has got the direction of the gift wrong.

· · ·

Manifestation is what creation is waiting for.

“For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God” (Rom 8:19). The Greek is apokalypsis — an unveiling — and the passage it belongs to is the most important passage in the New Testament for this book.

Paul has been describing a world in bondage: creation subjected to futility, groaning in travail, waiting. And what it waits for is not a delivery. It is a revelation — the appearance, in glory, of what the children of God actually are. “It does not yet appear what we shall be, but we know that when he appears we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2).

Put these together and something remarkable emerges. The manifest space’s central desire — that the invisible become visible, that the interior become external, that what is hidden in me be made real in the world — is not a false desire. It is the desire of creation. It is the groaning of Romans 8. It is precisely what the Gospel promises.

What the manifest space has done is take the deepest desire of the human person and shrink it to the size of a personal outcome. The thing we are waiting for is not the job. It is the revelation of who we are in Christ, and the creation is on tiptoe for it.

· · ·

Manifestation is presently hidden.

“Your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life is manifested, then you also will be manifested with him in glory” (Col 3:1–4).

This is the sentence that makes the whole thing bearable, and it is the sentence the manifest space cannot survive.

The Christian’s manifestation is deferred. It is real — as real as the risen body, as real as the glory that will be revealed — but it is not now, and the not-now is not a failure. It is the structure of the life of faith. The Christian is hidden: in Christ, in the Church, in the ordinary, in the sacraments, in a life that often looks like nothing at all. And the hiddenness is not a problem to be solved by technique. It is a place to live.

The manifest space cannot say this, because the manifest space exists to eliminate the gap. Its whole premise is that the delay is a malfunction — resistance, misalignment, low vibration — and that the technique closes it. But the delay is not a malfunction. It is the space in which faith, hope, and love become possible. If everything were manifested now, there would be nothing to hope for, and hope is the one thing that makes a human life livable.

· · ·

Now the reclamation, stated as a proposal.

Stop conceding the word. Every time a Catholic writer uses “manifestation” in quotation marks, as though it were a term belonging to the phenomenon under critique, the Church loses a little ground. The word is ours. It has been ours for two thousand years. The phenomenon borrowed it, as the phenomenon has borrowed everything else — the sense of providence, the power of words, the reality of the interior life, the practice of gratitude, the hope of transformation — and it borrowed them because it had nothing of its own.

Teach the direction. The single most useful catechetical sentence in this whole area is: manifestation is something God does. Everything follows from that. If God manifests, then the appropriate posture is receptivity, and the appropriate practices are prayer, sacrament, and obedience. If the self manifests, then the appropriate posture is technique, and the appropriate practices are methods. Two spiritualities, two postures, two kinds of person.

Recover the feast. The Church already has a liturgy of manifestation: Epiphany, the showing-forth of Christ to the nations; the Presentation, the meeting in the temple; the Transfiguration, the glory briefly visible; the Resurrection appearances; the Ascension; Pentecost. These are not decorations on a doctrinal system. They are the Church’s annual school of manifestation, and a person who has prayed them for twenty years knows more about the subject than any coach.

Name the desire correctly. When someone says, “I want to manifest a better life,” the accurate translation is usually: I want to become the person I am supposed to be, and I want it to show. That is not a bad desire. It is Romans 8 in colloquial English. The pastoral task is not to suppress it but to name it, and then to say where it is actually fulfilled.

· · ·

There is a risk in this proposal, and it should be named.

If you tell people “manifestation is a Catholic word,” some of them will hear “so my practice is fine.” That is why this chapter cannot stand alone. The reclamation of the word only works together with the audit — with the fourteen verdicts, the four tests, the lexicon, the refusals. The word is ours because the thing the manifest space does with it is a parody, and a parody is only corrected by the original, not by the abandonment of the term.

The two halves of this book belong together. Part Two without Part Three is a demolition. Part Three without Part Two is a surrender with better vocabulary. What is wanted is the thing that is hardest to hold: the word, the doctrine, and the refusal, in one hand.

The point

“Manifestation” is a biblical word, and in Scripture it is something God does. The manifest space has the shape of revelation turned inside out.

Do this

Read Romans 8:19 and Colossians 3:3–4 today, slowly, out loud.

What this sets up

The purpose clause is three words long, and it reorders everything.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 17

For the Common Good

Three words at the end of 1 Corinthians 12:7 settle the purpose of every manifestation — and they are the words the manifest space has never once quoted.

“To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.”

The sentence is one clause long, and it is the most politically explosive thing Paul ever wrote, because it does three things at once that no spiritual market can survive.

It says that the manifestation is given, which removes the technique. It says that it is given to each, which removes the elite. And it says that it is for the common good, which removes the private benefit. Every one of the three is a direct contradiction of the manifest space, and together they constitute a complete alternative program.

· · ·

The Corinthian community was, by the standards of the ancient world, embarrassingly gifted. They had tongues, prophecy, healing, discernment, teaching, generosity, and a lively sense that these things were evidence of their own spiritual attainment. Their worship was chaotic; their social life was stratified; their theology was a mess; and they were proud.

Paul’s response is not to dampen the gifts. It is to re-describe them. A gift is not an achievement; it is a charisma, a grace-gift, given by the Spirit as he wills, distributed variously, and ordered — this is the new element — to the building up of the body. The body has many members, and the members do not choose their function, and no member can say to another “I have no need of you.”

Three marks of an authentic manifestation follow, and they function as a test:

Givenness. It comes from outside; it is received; it is not a technique. The moment a manifestation can be produced on demand by a method, it has stopped being a charism and become a skill — which is not a sin, but it is a different thing, and the difference matters enormously for how we treat the person who has it and the person who doesn’t.

Diversity. Not everyone has the same gift, and the absence of a particular gift is not a defect. This is a direct refutation of the manifest space’s implicit claim that the successful life is available to anyone who applies the method correctly. In the body, some are apostles and some are hands and some are ears, and the ear does not become an eye by believing harder.

Order to the whole. The purpose is the common good, the building up of the body. A gift that does not build up is, on Paul’s account, not a gift being used but a gift being consumed.

· · ·

Now the contrast, which is exact.

The unit of the manifest space is the individual: one person, one notebook, one desired outcome, one life improved. The unit of the charismatic economy is the body: the gift is given to a member for the sake of the others, and its authenticity is tested by what it does to the whole.

The unit of the manifest space is the outcome: the thing desired, obtained. The unit of the charismatic economy is the person: built up, consoled, taught, healed, sent.

The unit of the manifest space is the sealed interior: the assumption held in secret, the wish not told to anyone. The unit of the charismatic economy is the assembly: the gift exercised in public, tested by others, subject to discernment.

It is not an exaggeration to say that these are two different religions. And the difference is not a matter of emphasis. It is a difference about what a human being is for.

· · ·

The practical consequence is a diagnostic question, and it is one that can be asked gently, in a conversation, without a lecture.

“Who is this for?”

Take the person who is manifesting a spouse. Ask who the spouse is for. If the answer is “for me, to complete my life,” the practice is a form of consumption dressed as hope. If the answer is “for the person he or she is, whom I would want to love well,” something has already changed, and the change did not come from the technique.

Take the person manifesting money. Ask who it is for. If the answer is “so I can stop being afraid,” that is a real need and it deserves a real response — but the response is providence and detachment, not a frequency. If the answer is “so I can look after my mother and give more away,” the desire has already begun to take a form that the Church can bless, and the practice that follows is stewardship, not attraction.

Take the person manifesting a healing. This is the hardest case, and it needs to be handled with the greatest care, because the desire is holy and the presumption is dangerous. Ask who the healing is for. If it is for the suffering person’s own relief, it is a legitimate petition and may be brought to God without embarrassment. If it is for the manifestation of God’s glory, it is the prayer of the Gospel. And if it is for the sake of the manifester’s own record of success, it has become something else, and the Church’s long and painful experience with faith-healing ought to make us very slow to promise outcomes.

· · ·

There is a temptation on the Catholic side at this point, and it is the mirror image of the manifest space’s error. It is the temptation to make the gifts safe by making them clerical, ceremonial, and rare — to insist so strongly on order that the manifestation of the Spirit becomes a thing that happens to other people, in a church, at a scheduled hour, administered by a professional.

Paul’s sentence forbids this. To each is given. Not to the Twelve. Not to the ordained. Not to the exceptional. To each. The Church has always insisted, against every attempt to confine the Spirit to an institution, that the sensus fidei, the charisms of the laity, the gifts of the young, the prophetic witness of the poor and the suffering are real manifestations, and that the body is crippled when they are suppressed.

The charismatic renewal is the great modern test case. It produced, and produces, real gifts of healing, prophecy, intercession, and joy; it also produced, in places, extravagance, manipulation, and a culture of spiritual one-upmanship that did real damage. The Church’s response was neither to endorse everything nor to shut it down, but to do what she always does at her best: to test, to regulate, to insist on submission to the local ordinary, and to let the fruit decide over decades. That is the model for how any renewal of manifestation in Catholic life should be handled.

· · ·

Now the transposition, in concrete form. The point of this chapter is not to replace private desire with public service — that would be a new legalism. It is to place private desire inside a body, where it can be healed and where it can become a gift.

Private petition becomes intercession. The person who wants to manifest a future spouse can begin, tonight, to pray for that person by name — even without a name — for their conversion, their safety, their healing, their vocation. This is not a trick to speed up the arrival. It is a change in what the desire is: from a want directed at the universe to a love directed at a person.

Self-improvement becomes service. The drive to become a better version of oneself is real, and the Church has a word for it — vocation — which locates improvement in a call rather than in a project. Ask not “what do I want to become?” but “what am I being asked to become, and for whom?”

The vision board becomes an intention list that is prayed over and then acted on. The difference is not in the paper. It is in the third column: for each item, write who it serves, and what the first concrete act would be. Half the items will not survive that column, and the half that does will be real.

The secret becomes the confessional and the direction of a soul. The manifest space’s insistence on secrecy (“tell no one, or the energy dissipates”) is one of its most revealing features, because it is the exact opposite of the Catholic practice of manifestation of conscience — the disclosure of one’s interior to a director precisely so that it can be tested, corrected, and prayed for. What the manifest space calls protection is, functionally, isolation.

· · ·

A last word on the “common good,” because it is a phrase with a long history and it does not mean “charity.”

The common good, in Catholic social teaching, is not the sum of private goods and not the aggregate of individual preferences. It is the good of a people, a good that is shared and that is only possessed together: peace, justice, worship, the flourishing of families, the care of the poor, the possibility of a good life for everyone. A manifestation is for the common good when it makes the manifester more capable of contributing to that, and less capable of being consumed by her own project.

Which is a way of saying that the test of a genuine manifestation is not whether the thing arrived. It is whether the person, in the process, became more available.

That is a standard no technique can meet, and it is the standard by which every practice in this book should eventually be judged.

The point

The manifestation of the Spirit is given, to each, for the common good — three words that no spiritual market can survive.

Do this

Ask “who is this for?” about the thing you most want, and write the answer down.

What this sets up

The world itself is waiting for the same thing.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 18

The Groaning Creation

Romans 8 gives the manifest space’s desire a cosmic scope and a different object. The world is not a mirror; it is a fellow creature, in labour, waiting with us.

There is a passage in Romans 8 that reads, if you come to it from the manifest space, like a message in a bottle from a better version of the same longing.

Paul has been arguing that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed. Then he does something unexpected: he puts the world into the sentence. “For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God… we know that the whole creation has been groaning in travail together until now; and not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Rom 8:19, 22–23).

The manifest space has a cosmology. It is a projection theory: the world is an outpicturing of consciousness, a mirror, a screen. Romans 8 has a cosmology too, and it is not that. The world is a creature: made, good, wounded, subjected to futility, groaning, waiting. And it is waiting for the same thing we are — the manifestation of the children of God.

· · ·

Two cosmologies, and the difference between them is not academic.

In the manifest space, the world has no independent standing. It is a reflection, and a reflection has no rights. You cannot owe anything to a mirror. This is why the manifest space, for all its talk of energy and connection, has no real doctrine of creation, and therefore no real doctrine of the environment, and no real doctrine of the body, and no real doctrine of the neighbour. A world that is a projection can be used without limit, because there is nothing there to use.

In Romans 8, the world is a fellow creature. It has been subjected to futility — note that Paul does not say by whom; the passive is careful — and it groans, and it waits, and its fate is bound up with ours. “The creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.”

This is one of the strongest possible grounds for a Christian ecology, and it is also the strongest possible ground for saying that the manifest space’s relationship to the material world is not “too material” but “not material enough.” A person who believes the world is a mirror will treat it as a surface. A person who believes the world is a creature will treat it as a companion.

· · ·

There is a second thing in Romans 8, and it is the answer to a question the manifest space raises and cannot answer.

The manifest space has a great deal to say about the present and almost nothing to say about the future. Its eschatology is realized: the thing is now, or the technique is wrong. Romans 8 is the opposite. It says that the whole creation — and we with it — is in labour, and that the labour is not a malfunction but a birth.

The image of childbirth is exact and it does no sentimentalizing. Labour is real pain, it is not chosen in the moment, it is not a punishment, and it ends. The one giving birth does not “manifest” the child by aligning her frequency; she undergoes something that is happening to her and through her, and the thing that comes out is not a projection of her consciousness but a person.

This is the structure of Christian hope, and it is what makes the manifest space’s optimism look like what it is: a refusal to wait. Optimism says the pain is not real or is about to end. Hope says the pain is real, the birth is real, and the two are connected, and the connection is not visible yet.

· · ·

Now the warning, because Romans 8 is also the chapter that the manifest space’s cousin, the “cosmic Christ” movement, uses for its own purposes. The 2003 Pontifical Council document flagged this precisely: in New Age thought, “Christ” is a title for a state of consciousness, and Jesus of Nazareth was one of many who attained it (§2.3.4.2; §3.3). The cosmic Christ becomes a principle of universal energy, and the historical Jesus evaporates into an example.

The Catholic doctrine of the cosmic Christ is entirely different and much more concrete. “He is the image of the invisible God, the first-born of all creation; for in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible… all things were created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together” (Col 1:15–17). And then, the sentence that makes it Christian: “For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross” (Col 1:19–20).

Notice the difference. The New Age cosmic Christ is a principle that explains the universe. The Catholic cosmic Christ is a person through whom the universe was made and is being reconciled, and the reconciliation happens “by the blood of his cross” — which is to say, through a particular death at a particular time, under a particular empire. The principle is available to anyone with the right consciousness. The person is available to anyone who will receive him.

The manifest space’s “universe” is a degraded version of this doctrine. It has the universality and the responsiveness and the sense that everything is connected — all of which are true — and it has lost the person, the cross, and the creation. What is left is a cosmos that feels like God and has none of the properties of God: no will, no face, no history, no wounds.

· · ·

Which brings us to the practical point of this chapter, and it is unexpectedly ordinary.

If the world is a creature — if it groans, if it waits, if it is a fellow and not a screen — then the way you treat the material world is a spiritual matter in a much stronger sense than “stewardship.”

The food you eat is a creature. The body you inhabit is a creature, and it is not a projection of your beliefs about it; it is a gift with its own integrity, its own limits, its own mortality. The person who cleans your office is a creature. The weather is a creature. None of them is a mirror, and none of them exists to tell you about your vibration.

This is why the Church’s materiality — water, oil, bread, wine, incense, stone, stained glass, fasting, feasting, pilgrimage, relics, bodies laid in the ground — is not a lower stage of religion from which a mature person graduates into pure spirituality. It is the religion of the Incarnation, and the Incarnation is the doctrine that matter can carry God.

The manifest space’s ideal is a world you can influence without touching. The Catholic ideal is a world you touch, and that touches you back, and in which God is present in a piece of bread.

That is not a smaller vision. It is the only vision in which the groaning of Romans 8 makes sense, because it is the only vision in which the world is real enough to groan.

The point

The world is a creature in labour, not a mirror of your interior. Which is why the Church is more materialist than the market.

Do this

Treat one created thing this week as a companion rather than a surface: a body, an animal, a piece of ground, a person who serves you.

What this sets up

And the manifestation you are waiting for is currently hidden.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 19

Hidden with Christ

The Christian’s manifestation is deferred, and the deferral is not a failure. This is the doctrine that makes the whole practice of hope possible — and the one the manifest space cannot survive.

There is a sentence in Colossians that ought to be printed on the inside of every manifestation journal in the world, and if it were, the practice would collapse in a week:

“You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life is manifested, then you also will be manifested with him in glory.” (Col 3:3–4)

Three clauses. Your life is hidden. It is hidden with Christ. It will be manifested, later, with him.

The manifest space is built on the elimination of the gap between the hidden and the manifested. That is its product, its promise, and its entire reason for existing. Colossians says the gap is the structure of the Christian life, and that the attempt to close it is not a technique but a refusal of the cross.

· · ·

Begin with the pastoral case, because it is the case that matters and it is the case that nobody writes about.

There is a woman in your parish who has done everything right. She prayed, she went to Mass, she received the sacraments, she raised her children, she cared for her husband through a long illness, she buried him, she kept going. Her life, from the outside, looks like nothing. No promotion, no platform, no visible fruit, no story that would make a good testimony at a conference. If she had been formed by the manifest space, she would have concluded, somewhere in her fifties, that she had failed at the interior life, because the exterior did not match.

Colossians says her life is hidden with Christ in God. That is not a consolation prize. It is a description of where her life actually is. It is stored, kept, held — in the place where Christ is, which is to say, in the safest place there is — and it will be manifested, and the manifestation will be glory, and it will be hers.

The manifest space has no category for this woman. It can only tell her that she did not align. The Church can tell her the truth: that she is not a failure, she is hidden, and hiddenness is not the absence of a manifestation; it is its location.

· · ·

Now the doctrine, in three steps.

First: the Christian has died. Paul is not being poetic. Baptism is a burial; the old self is gone; the life that is now lived is “Christ living in me” (Gal 2:20). This is the most radical claim in the New Testament, and it is the reason the manifest space’s anthropology cannot be reconciled with it. The manifest space says: you are an unlimited creative power who has forgotten it. The Gospel says: you are a dead person who has been raised, and the life you have is not yours.

Second: the life is hidden, with Christ, in God. The location is specified with a precision that is almost comic. Not “hidden in your potential,” not “hidden in your subconscious,” not “waiting to be unlocked.” Hidden with Christ, in God. It is a fact about where you are, not a fact about what you have not yet realized, and it is therefore not something a technique can reach or a feeling can confirm.

Third: the manifestation is future and it is certain. “When Christ who is your life is manifested, then you also will be manifested with him in glory.” The Christian’s manifestation is not a possibility to be optimized. It is an event in the future of the world, as certain as the resurrection, and it is not under our administration.

· · ·

The contrast with the manifest space’s secrecy is worth drawing carefully, because the two look alike and are opposites.

The manifest space instructs people to keep the wish secret — do not tell anyone what you are manifesting, or the energy dissipates, or you will introduce doubt. The secrecy is a technique of protection: the desire is kept in a closed system so that nothing can interfere with it.

The Christian’s hiddenness is not a technique and not a secret. It is not that you know something you are not telling; it is that the truth about you is not yet visible, and cannot be made visible by effort. It is hidden in God — which means it is known, and known perfectly, by the one in whom it is hidden. The Christian is not keeping a secret from the world. The Christian is being kept.

The practical difference is enormous. The person with a secret is alone with it. The person who is hidden is accompanied.

· · ·

There is a whole theology of the hidden life in the tradition, and it is one of the Church’s great gifts to a culture of performance.

The thirty years at Nazareth are the foundation of it. The Son of God spent three decades doing nothing that anyone would have written down: working, eating, praying, being a son. The most important life ever lived was, for ninety per cent of its duration, entirely unremarkable. If the manifest space were true, those years were wasted.

Thérèse of Lisieux built an entire spirituality on this — the “little way” — and she did it in a convent at nineteen, with no achievements, no platform, no influence, and a slow death from tuberculosis. Her autobiography is a manual for people whose lives are hidden, and it is one of the most widely read books in the history of the Church, which tells you how many people need it.

And the tradition’s word for the virtue that makes hiddenness livable is humility, which is not thinking less of yourself but being free from the need to be seen. The manifest space is, at bottom, a technology for being seen — by the universe, by others, by yourself — and it is therefore, at bottom, a technology of pride. Not the crude pride of vanity; the subtle pride of needing your interior life to produce visible results that confirm you exist.

· · ·

Now the hard part, because this doctrine can be abused and has been.

The doctrine of hiddenness has been used, by cowards and by institutions, to keep people quiet. “Your suffering is hidden with Christ” has been said to people who needed to be defended, and it has been said by people who wanted them to stop complaining. “Offer it up” is a true sentence and a terrible sentence, depending on who is saying it and to whom.

The distinction is this: hiddenness is a description of where your life is, not a prohibition on speaking about your life. The one whose life is hidden with Christ is not required to pretend that nothing hurts, and is not required to accept injustice in silence, and is not required to be invisible to the people who ought to see her. Christ himself wept in public, and argued in public, and was executed in public.

What hiddenness rules out is not speech. It is the demand that the world confirm you now. It rules out the project of making your interior life visible on your own terms, on your own schedule, as evidence that you are real. That is the project the manifest space exists to serve, and it is a project that cannot succeed, because the thing it is trying to prove cannot be proved by results.

· · ·

One last image, and it comes from the liturgy.

On Holy Saturday, the Church does nothing. The tabernacle is empty, the altar is stripped, the bells are silent, and the faithful are told, in effect, to go home and wait. There is no Mass. The most important thing that has ever happened is happening out of sight, in the dark, in a tomb, and no one is watching, and nothing can be done.

That is the shape of the Christian life for most of its duration. The manifestation is real. It is happening. It is hidden, and it is hidden in God, and it will be shown, and the showing will not be a technique but a resurrection.

The person who can live in Holy Saturday without trying to force Easter is the person who has understood the doctrine. And the Church, which has been keeping Holy Saturday for two thousand years, is the only institution in the world that has any practice for it.

The point

Your life is hidden with Christ in God. The hiddenness is not the failure of the manifestation; it is its location.

Do this

Name one hidden thing in your life and thank God for it, out loud, without asking him to make it visible.

What this sets up

Hidden things are carried by matter, and matter is the Church’s speciality.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 20

The Sacramental Principle

The Church is not less material than the manifest space. It is far more. That is the argument nobody is making, and it is the one that wins.

Here is a claim that sounds wrong and is exactly right: the manifest space is a form of idealism, and the Catholic Church is the materialist option.

The manifest space says that reality is at bottom mental, that the world is a projection of consciousness, that the lever is interior, and that matter is a surface on which the inner state writes. The Church says that God made matter, that God entered matter, that God gives himself through matter, and that the body will be raised. One of these is a spirituality for people who are tired of the physical world. The other is a religion of the Incarnation.

This is not the argument the Church usually makes. The usual argument is that the manifest space is worldly — too attached to money, to outcomes, to the goods of this life. And it is true that the manifest space is attached to outcomes. But its attachment is not to the world as such. It is attachment to a result, which is a very different thing, and which leaves the world itself untouched, uninteresting, and unreal.

· · ·

The technical heart of the Catholic position is a phrase that is badly misunderstood: ex opere operato.

The Council of Trent defined it against the Reformers: the sacraments confer grace ex opere operato, “by the work worked” — by the fact of their being performed — provided the recipient does not place an obstacle. The phrase sounds, to modern ears, like magic. It is the opposite of magic, and the difference is the entire argument of this chapter.

Magic is a technique. It works by the correct performance of the correct formula, regardless of who performs it, and its power is in the formula. Ex opere operato also says that the effect does not depend on the minister’s worthiness — but for a completely different reason: because the one who acts in the sacrament is Christ. The minister is an instrument. The efficacy is the fidelity of a person who has promised.

Put the two side by side and the structural difference is plain:

Magic / techniqueSacrament
Who actsthe operatorChrist
Why it worksthe formula is correctthe promise is kept
What is guaranteedthe resultthe gift
What the recipient must doperform correctlyreceive without obstacle
Failure meansyou did it wrongnothing, or not yet

The manifest space is on the left. It is not on the left because it uses rituals — the Church uses rituals. It is on the left because its efficacy is located in the correctness of the operator’s interior state. Which is why the manifest space is the most anxious spirituality in the modern world: the operator is always the one who might have failed.

· · ·

Now the sacraments themselves, read as the Church’s answer to the manifest space’s seven hungers.

Baptism answers the hunger for a new identity. The manifest space says: assume a new self-concept until it hardens. The Church says: you were buried and raised, once, at a font, and the fact does not depend on your feeling. The identity is not assumed. It is given, and it is indelible.

Confirmation answers the hunger for power. The manifest space says: raise your vibration. The Church says: receive the Spirit who gives gifts, and the gifts are for the common good, and they are not under your control.

Eucharist answers the hunger for abundance. The manifest space says: attract more. The Church says: here is the body and blood of God, given for you, under the appearance of bread and wine — the most abundant thing in the universe, in the least impressive form. And note the form. The manifest space would have made it a spectacle. God made it food.

Confession answers the hunger for a revised past. The manifest space says: rewrite the memory. The Church says: the sin is forgiven, the guilt is removed, the fact remains, and you are sent away with a penance and a fresh start. This is the only real revision of the past on offer, and it works because someone with authority says so, not because you feel it.

Anointing answers the hunger for healing. The manifest space says: illness is misalignment, so realign. The Church says: this body is anointed, this suffering is united to Christ’s, this person is strengthened, and the outcome is entrusted to God, and death is not a failure of faith.

Orders answers the hunger for a guaranteed channel. The manifest space says: learn the method. The Church says: here are men set apart whose ministry does not depend on their talents, so that the gift is not for sale.

Marriage answers the hunger for a life that is not alone. The manifest space says: everyone is you pushed out. The Church says: here is a person who is not you, who has promised to stay, and whose otherness is the sacrament.

Seven hungers, seven material signs. Not one of them is a technique, and every one of them is physical.

· · ·

The same logic governs the sacramentals — a category almost entirely unknown to ordinary Catholics and directly relevant to this book.

A sacramental is a blessing, an object, an action of the Church that disposes a person to grace without conferring it the way a sacrament does: holy water, the sign of the cross, a medal, a rosary, the blessing of a home, a candle, salt, oil, the blessing of fields and engines and animals. They are the Church’s everyday material spirituality, and they are exactly the kind of thing the manifest space invents for itself: crystals, charms, salt lamps, oils, “protection” practices.

The difference is not that one is rational and the other superstitious. Both are material practices with spiritual claims. The difference is the theology of the object. A sacramental is a creature that has been blessed — it points beyond itself, it is used in faith, and its power, such as it is, is the power of the Church’s prayer and God’s goodness. A crystal in the manifest space is a reservoir — it stores and emits a force, and its efficacy is quasi-physical and independent of any relationship.

And here is the sting: the Church warns about the misuse of her own sacramentals in exactly the terms she uses against the manifest space. “Superstition,” says the Catechism, “can even affect the worship we offer the true God, e.g., when one attributes an importance in some way magical to certain practices otherwise lawful or necessary. To attribute the efficacy of prayers or of sacramental signs to their mere external performance, apart from the interior dispositions that they demand, is to fall into superstition” (CCC 2111).

So the Catholic who wears a medal to ward off bad luck, and the manifest-space practitioner who carries a crystal to raise her vibration, are committing the same error, and the Church names it first against her own.

· · ·

There is a final inversion in this chapter, and it is the one I would put on a poster.

The manifest space promises that the universe responds to your interior state. The Church promises something stranger and better: that God responds to matter — that he gives himself in water and oil and bread and wine and human hands, and that the material world is not a screen for the spiritual but its chosen medium.

Which means that the person who has been taught that everything is in her mind has not been taught to be spiritual. She has been taught to be trapped. The Church’s answer is not “think differently.” It is: get up, go to a building, touch water, eat bread, let a man put oil on your forehead, and be told by someone with authority that you are forgiven. Every one of those is a physical act, and every one of them is a refusal of the idealism that is quietly ruining the spiritual life of a generation.

The manifest space offers a universe made of your own interior. The Church offers a world you can touch, in which God has already touched back.

The point

The sacraments are efficacious signs, not techniques: the one who acts is Christ, and the efficacy is a promise kept, not a formula performed.

Do this

On Sunday, touch the water on the way in deliberately, and know what you are doing.

What this sets up

The word itself runs the other way: disclosure, not projection.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 21

The Manifestation of Conscience

There is a Catholic practice called the manifestation of conscience, and it runs in the exact opposite direction from the manifest space: not projecting the interior onto the world, but exposing it to another so that it can be healed.

The phrase manifestatio conscientiae — the manifestation of conscience — is one of the oldest technical terms in the Church’s spiritual vocabulary, and almost nobody has heard of it.

It means the disclosure of one’s interior state to another person: to a confessor, a spiritual director, a superior, a trusted guide. It is not a metaphor and it is not a mood. It is a practice with a procedure, a history, and a set of rules, and the tradition regards it as one of the principal means by which a soul is healed.

Set it beside the manifest space’s central act — the interior state held in secret and projected onto reality by technique — and you have two practices that use the same word for opposite operations.

The manifest space manifests the interior outward, onto the world, without a witness. The manifestation of conscience manifests the interior outward, to a person, in order to be judged, healed, and directed. One projects. The other discloses. One is a technology of influence. The other is an act of humility.

· · ·

The scriptural warrant is not obscure. “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16). Note the sequence: confession, intercession, healing. The healing is attached to the disclosure, not to the technique.

The practice took institutional form early — the penitential discipline, the monastic exagoreusis (the daily disclosure of thoughts to the abba), the office of the confessor, the rise of spiritual direction. By the Middle Ages the Church had made annual confession a requirement, and by the Counter-Reformation the directed retreat, above all the Ignatian Exercises, had turned the manifestation of conscience into a method.

Ignatius’s Exercises are, among other things, a manual for this. The retreatant is told to keep nothing back from the director — “the more familiar the soul is with its director, the more easily and fruitfully will it be able to speak” — and the director is told to be careful, to ask about the movements, to test them, and not to impose his own inclinations. The whole apparatus exists because of a conviction that the interior life, left to itself, is unreliable: it can be moved by God, by one’s own disordered affections, or by the enemy, and the three are hard to tell apart from the inside.

The manifest space’s conviction is the opposite. The interior is the oracle. It does not need a witness; it needs to be trusted, clarified, and unleashed. The tradition’s conviction is that the interior needs a witness precisely because it is the place where self-deception is most persuasive.

· · ·

Why does disclosure heal? Three reasons, and each of them is a direct answer to a manifest-space wound.

Because shame lives in secrecy. The thing that is not said grows. This is not a pious platitude; it is a reliable observation of every confessional and every therapy room. A person who has carried something for twenty years and finally says it out loud to another human being discovers that the thing was smaller in the light — not because the act was smaller, but because the isolation was larger. The manifest space, with its injunction to keep the wish secret, is a machine for manufacturing exactly this kind of isolation. Its secrecy is not protection. It is confinement.

Because the word from outside does something the word from inside cannot. “I absolve you” is not a report about the penitent’s feelings. It is an act of authority, performed by a man who has been given the power to bind and loose, and it changes the penitent’s standing before God. Nothing in the manifest space has this structure, because nothing in the manifest space has an outside. You cannot forgive yourself; the attempt to do so is one of the characteristic modern miseries, and it fails for a reason: forgiveness is a transaction between persons, and a person cannot be her own offended party.

Because counsel requires another. The manifest space’s guidance is a feed: an algorithm shows you what you already want to see. Direction is the opposite. It is a particular person, with a particular charism and a particular knowledge of you, telling you something you did not want to hear, which turns out to be true.

· · ·

Now the diagnostic use of all this, because it is the most practical thing in the book.

When a person presents with a manifestation practice, the most useful question is not “do you know that’s not Catholic?” It is: “Who knows about this?”

If the answer is “nobody — you’re not supposed to tell anyone,” then you are looking at a structure of isolation, and the first work is not doctrinal correction but the restoration of a witness. The doctrine can wait. The person needs to be known.

If the answer is “my spiritual director knows, and we talked about it,” then whatever else is going on, the practice is inside a structure that can correct it, and the situation is much better than it looks.

If the answer is “my coach knows, and I pay her,” then you are looking at a commercial relationship in which the guide has an interest in the practice continuing, and the question of authority is live.

This is why the practice of spiritual direction is, I think, the single most important institutional response to the manifest space — more important than any book, including this one. A person with a director is a person who cannot be alone with a technique. The technique will be named, tested, and, over time, either purified or abandoned. And it will be abandoned in the only way that lasts: not because it was refuted, but because something better took its place.

· · ·

There is a risk in this chapter and it should be named, because the tradition has been wounded by it.

The manifestation of conscience can become an instrument of control. A director who uses what he is told to manage the directee, a superior who requires disclosure of thoughts as a tool of obedience, a confessor who is curious rather than holy — these are real abuses, and they have done real damage. The Church’s own law has, over centuries, built safeguards: the seal of confession is absolute; a director may not command the interior; the Exercises explicitly warn the director not to interfere with the retreatant’s liberty.

The safeguard is the same as the one that governs every sacrament: the one who acts is Christ, and the minister is an instrument. A director who forgets that he is an instrument becomes a technician of souls, which is to say, a mirror image of the thing this book is criticizing. The difference between direction and manipulation is not the technique. It is who is in charge.

· · ·

Which brings us back to the word.

The manifest space has taken a Catholic word and reversed it. In Catholic usage, to manifest is to become visible in the presence of another, and the highest form of it is the manifestation of conscience, where a person becomes visible to God through the mediation of a witness. In the manifest space, to manifest is to make the world visible to yourself, by an operation that requires no witness and no God.

Part Three has been arguing that the Church should reclaim the word rather than surrender it. This chapter is where the reclamation is most exact, because here the two meanings meet face to face and one of them is a parody of the other.

The remedy is not to stop manifesting. It is to manifest in the right direction: not the projection of the interior onto the world, but the disclosure of the interior to God, through the Church, in the presence of a witness who can say the words that the interior cannot say to itself.

That is what confession is. It is also, and this is not a coincidence, the only practice in the world that does what “revision” claims to do.

The point

The manifestation of conscience is the exact inversion of the manifest space: not the interior projected onto the world, but the interior disclosed to a witness.

Do this

Tell one person one true thing about your interior life this week. Not a confession of sin necessarily — a disclosure.

What this sets up

Which brings us to the engine room of the whole doctrine.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 22

Providence and Secondary Causality

This is the engine room. Get this doctrine right and the manifest space loses its market; get it wrong and you produce either fatalism or magic.

Every spirituality has a doctrine of how things happen. The manifest space’s doctrine is a law of resemblance. The Church’s doctrine is providence, and providence is the most misunderstood word in popular Catholicism.

It is misunderstood in two directions at once, and both misunderstandings are common in the same parish.

The first is fatalism: providence as a script written in advance, in which human action is a decoration. On this view, praying is pointless because the outcome is fixed, and the only piety is acceptance. This is not the Catholic doctrine; it is a version of it that has done enormous damage, particularly to the sick and the grieving.

The second is deism with a religious vocabulary: providence as a general supervision, in which God set things going and now watches, and the actual working of the world is done by laws and by us. On this view, God is real but remote, and the daily texture of life is administered by second causes with no particular divine involvement.

Aquinas’s doctrine is neither, and the difference is technical, and the technique matters.

· · ·

Begin with the definition. Providence, for Aquinas, is the ratio — the plan, the ordering — of things to their end, existing in the divine mind (ST I, q. 22, a. 1). Governance is the execution of that plan (q. 103). And the crucial move comes in the next step: God governs the world through secondary causes, not instead of them.

“Divine providence disposes not only what effects shall take place, but also from what causes and in what order these effects shall proceed” (ST II-II, q. 83, a. 2). That sentence is the whole doctrine in one line. God does not merely decide the outcome; he decides the causal order by which the outcome arrives, and that order includes real creatures doing real things.

The Catechism puts it in language a child can follow: “God is the sovereign master of his plan. But to carry it out he also makes use of his creatures’ cooperation. This cooperation is not a passive one; God grants his creatures the dignity of acting on their own and of being causes for one another” (CCC 306). And then: “God grants his creatures not only their existence but also the dignity of acting on their own” (CCC 307).

Read those two paragraphs slowly, because they contain the answer to the manifest space and to fatalism simultaneously.

Against fatalism: your action is not a decoration. It is a cause, ordained as a cause, and the outcome genuinely depends on it. When you work, the work does something. When you ask, the asking does something. When you forgive, the forgiveness changes the world. God has chosen to govern a world in which creatures are causes, and he does not bypass them.

Against magic: your action is not the only cause, and it is not the first cause. It operates inside an order you did not establish, alongside causes you cannot see, under a wisdom you cannot audit. You are a real cause and you are not the cause, and the difference between those two sentences is the difference between a creature and a god.

· · ·

Now the part that is hardest and most important: chance.

The manifest space cannot tolerate chance. If something happens, something caused it, and if something caused it, you can find it, and if you can find it, you can use it. A world with genuine contingency is a world in which some things happen that are not about you, and that is intolerable to a system whose entire promise is that everything is about you.

Aquinas has room for chance, and he has it precisely because he has room for real secondary causes. A thing is accidental or fortuitous with respect to its secondary causes — the man who happens to be at the well when the other man passes by — and it is nevertheless foreseen and ordered by God, who includes the accidents in the plan (ST I, q. 22, a. 2, ad 1; q. 116, a. 1). Chance is real at the level of creatures and not ultimate at the level of God.

This is a doctrine with immense pastoral value, and it is almost entirely absent from contemporary preaching. It means that the flat tire is not a message. It means that the illness is not a verdict. It means that the fact that two events coincided does not oblige you to find a meaning, and that the refusal to find one is not a failure of faith but an act of humility. The manifest space’s sign-reading and the over-pious Catholic’s sign-reading are the same error: the refusal to let anything be merely contingent.

· · ·

Which brings us to the hard question, the one every pastor is asked in a hospital corridor: if God governs, why this?

The tradition’s answer has three parts, and none of them is “God wanted this.”

First: God does not will evil. The language of “God’s will” needs to be broken into three senses, which are routinely conflated and which produce most of the cruelty in this area. There is God’s prescriptive will — what he commands, which is always good. There is his permissive will — what he allows, which includes the free acts of creatures and the workings of nature, and which he allows for reasons that are often not given to us. And there is his particular will for an individual — the vocation, the path, the thing he is asking of you. Saying “God took your child” confuses permission with prescription, and it is not the Church’s teaching; it is a pastoral malpractice with a pious accent.

Second: God can bring good out of evil, and does. “God permits evil only to draw a greater good from it” (CCC 324 is close to this; the tradition states it in many forms, and the Catechism is careful to add that we often do not see the good). This is not an explanation of the evil. It is a promise about its limits. The evil remains evil; the Cross remains a murder; and the resurrection does not make the murder acceptable, it makes it defeated.

Third: the answer to the question is a person, not a proposition. Job’s question is answered by a tour of creation and, for us, by the Incarnation. God does not tell us why. He tells us who is with us, and he does it by being born, and suffering, and dying. Any theodicy that is more satisfying than that is less true.

· · ·

There is one more consequence, and it is the one that makes this chapter the engine room of the whole book.

If providence is real, then the outcome of your action is not your responsibility, and the action is. This is the exact distribution of burden that the manifest space gets wrong in both directions: it makes you responsible for the outcome and it makes the action a technique. The Catholic distribution is the reverse, and it is the only one a human being can carry for a lifetime.

You are responsible for what you do: for the prayer, the work, the honesty, the courage, the fidelity. You are not responsible for what happens: for the diagnosis, the hiring committee, the interest rate, the other person’s freedom, the timing of God. You are called to act as if everything depended on your action, and to trust as if nothing did, and the two together are not a contradiction but the definition of a creature who knows what she is.

That is what providence is for. Not to explain the world, but to make action possible without despair and without delusion.

· · ·

The manifest space’s “universe” is a second cause with the first cause deleted. It has the responsiveness of providence and none of its personhood, the order of governance and none of its freedom, the intimacy of a Father and none of his face.

The Catholic doctrine keeps all three, and it adds the one thing no system of attraction can offer: a God who is not a mechanism, who can say no, who has said no, and who in saying no to his Son said yes to us. That is not a law. It is a story, and it is the only story in which a creature can act with all her strength and then sleep.

The point

Providence governs through real secondary causes, which is why your action is serious and why the outcome is not your responsibility.

Do this

Divide your current worry into two columns: mine to do, and not mine. Do the first; hand over the second.

What this sets up

Providence makes room for desire — and desire needs purifying.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 23

Desire and Its Purification

The manifest space takes desire as an oracle. The tradition takes it as a signpost — one that must be read, tested, and purified. This chapter is about the difference, and about what happens to a person when the desire is not granted.

Augustine began the Confessions with a sentence that every spiritual writer since has had to reckon with: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

It is a sentence about desire, and it makes three claims at once. Desire is constitutive — we are made for something. Desire is disordered — the heart is restless, which is not a compliment. And desire has an object that is not any of the things it appears to want — it rests only in God.

The manifest space affirms the first, denies the second, and denies the third. It says that desire is the compass (true), that it needs no purification (false), and that its object is the thing desired (false). Three claims, two errors, and the errors are the ones that turn a spiritual practice into a machine for producing disappointment.

· · ·

Start with what is true, because the manifest space’s insight here is real and the Church has often been slow to say so.

Desire is revelatory. What you want tells you what you love, and what you love tells you who you are. This is not a modern insight; it is the structure of the whole moral theology of the Summa, which begins its treatment of human action with the question of beatitude and derives everything from the fact that the will is ordered to the good (ST I-II, qq. 1–5). A person who does not know what she wants does not know herself.

Desire is a form of prayer. “Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart” (Ps 37:4) is a verse the manifest space quotes constantly and the tradition reads more carefully: the promise is attached to the delight, not to the desire. But the desire is not the enemy. It is the material.

Desire is not to be shamed. This needs saying because a certain Catholic formation produced the impression that wanting things is faintly indecent. It is not. The Gospel is full of people who ask for things — a healing, a child, a place in the kingdom, a sign — and Jesus, who rebukes a great deal, almost never rebukes the asking.

· · ·

Now the two denials.

Desire is not authoritative. The manifest space’s move is to treat the desire as an instruction from the universe: if you want it, it is yours; the work is to clarify and release. The tradition’s move is to treat the desire as a datum that must be interpreted. Some desires are true and point to real goods. Some are true in their object and disordered in their intensity — a legitimate love of family become an idolatry of family. Some are false in their object: the desire for revenge, for another person’s spouse, for a greatness that would destroy the one who got it. And some are true at a deeper level than their surface: the desire for a promotion that is really a desire to be seen, which is really a desire for the love that only God can give.

Telling a person that her desire is an instruction is like telling her that a pain is a diagnosis. It may be; it may not; either way, someone has to read it.

Desire is not satisfiable by its apparent object. This is the claim that the manifest space must deny and cannot avoid, and it is the claim with the most evidence behind it. Every honest person who has obtained the thing she wanted knows what happened next: a brief satisfaction, a strange flatness, and then a new want. The manifest space calls this “expanding your vibration” and treats it as progress. The tradition calls it what it is — the infinite disproportion between a finite object and a desire that was made for the infinite — and treats it as evidence.

Spe Salvi 33 makes the point in the context of prayer, and it is worth quoting again because it is the whole chapter in one paragraph:

“In prayer we must learn what we can truly ask of God — what is worthy of God. We must learn to purify our desires and our hopes. We must free ourselves from the hidden lies with which we deceive ourselves.”

Note what Benedict does not say. He does not say that we should stop desiring. He says that we must learn what we can ask — which means that the first thing a prayer teaches us is that we were asking for the wrong things, and that this discovery is part of the answer.

· · ·

How is desire purified? The tradition has a great deal to say, and three instruments do most of the work.

Ignatian indifference. Not apathy: a freedom from inordinate attachment such that one is not enslaved by any outcome. “We ought to be indifferent, not only to the choice of a state of life, but also in all that concerns our own persons, so that we do not prefer health to sickness, riches to poverty, honour to dishonour, a long life to a short one” (SpEx 23). This is not a counsel to want nothing. It is a discipline of holding everything in an open hand, so that the will is available to God and not captive to a result.

The manifest space has a counterfeit of this — “detachment” as a technique to make the thing arrive — and the counterfeit is exactly the thing that the real practice forbids, because the real practice is not a technique for getting what you want. It is the freedom to be given something else.

The dark night. John of the Cross described, with a precision that still startles, what happens when a person who has been praying with sweetness stops being given sweetness. The senses lose their consolations; the imagination loses its images; the desire loses its object; and the person is left in a darkness that feels exactly like failure. It is not failure. It is the purification of desire, and its function is to detach the desire from the consolation so that it can rest in the Beloved.

This is the most important thing in this book that the manifest space has no answer to, and it is the question that its practice cannot survive: what do you do when the thing does not come?

The manifest space’s answer is: you did not align. The tradition’s answer is: you may be in the dark night, and the dark night is a gift, and the fact that it feels like abandonment is the evidence that something is being taken away that needed to be taken away.

The offering of desire. The practice that turns a want into a prayer is not the suppression of the want but its presentation. “Lord, this is what I want. I want it very much. I am not sure it is good for me. I am not sure it is good for anyone. I am asking for it, and I am asking to be made able to receive your answer.” This is a completely different act from the manifest space’s scripted affirmation, and it produces a completely different person: the one is a technician of her own desire, the other is a child with a Father.

· · ·

Now the pastoral cases, because this is where the doctrine has to prove itself.

The woman who wants a child. She has been told by the manifest space that her yearning is the signal that the child is hers, and by a certain Catholic piety that she should stop wanting it and offer it up. Both are cruel. The first sets her up for a devastation that will be interpreted as her fault; the second tells her that the deepest desire of her body is a spiritual defect. The truth is harder and kinder: the desire is good, the grief is real, the outcome is not in her hands, and God is not asking her to stop wanting — he is asking her to keep wanting him while she waits, and to let the wanting be a prayer rather than a program.

The man who wants recognition. His desire is real and its object is a lie, because what he wants is not the recognition but the love that he believes the recognition would prove. The manifest space will help him get the recognition, and he will be as empty as Daniel in the first chapter. The tradition will ask him to name the deeper want, and then to bring it where it can be answered.

The person who has got what she wanted and feels nothing. This is the most common outcome of a successful manifestation, and it is almost never discussed in the manifest-space literature. The tradition has a word for it — acedia, or the noonday demon, the sorrow that arises when the good thing does not satisfy — and a treatment: not more goods, but a re-ordering of love.

· · ·

There is a last thing to say, and it is the hinge to the next chapter.

The manifest space is right that desire is central to the spiritual life, and it is right that most Christians have not been taught to desire well. Where it goes wrong is in thinking that desire is a force to be used rather than a faculty to be formed.

A force is spent. A faculty is cultivated. And the cultivation of a faculty — the slow, repeated, unglamorous transformation of what a person loves — has a name in the tradition, and it is the subject of the next chapter.

The point

Desire is a signpost, not an oracle: it tells you what you love, and what you love may be false.

Do this

Take one desire and ask the three questions: what is this for, who else does it touch, would I take it from God’s hand.

What this sets up

What forms a person is not the desire but the habit.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 24

Habitus; or, The True Law of Assumption

The manifest space’s most famous doctrine — persist in an assumed state until it hardens into fact — is a real doctrine with the wrong metaphysics. Aquinas has the same insight, better, and calls it habitus.

If there is a single chapter of this book that a philosopher should read, it is this one, because it is where the manifest space comes closest to being right and where the cost of its being wrong is clearest.

The claim is Neville Goddard’s most quoted sentence, and he wrote it in 1952: “An assumption, though false, if persisted in, will harden into fact” (The Power of Awareness, ch. 4).

Taken as a claim about reality, it is false, and this book has spent fifteen chapters showing why. Taken as a claim about persons, it is one of the most important truths in moral psychology, and the tradition has a technical account of it that is far richer than Goddard’s. The account is the doctrine of habitus, and it is the instrument by which the manifest space’s best insight can be saved.

· · ·

Begin with Aquinas’s definition, which is dry and repays patience. A habit — habitus — is a disposition by which a being is disposed well or ill, either in relation to itself or in relation to its operation (ST I-II, q. 49, a. 1). It is a quality, not an action; it is stable, not fleeting; it is formed by acts and it forms acts.

Four features matter here.

A habitus is stable. It is not a mood or an episode. It is a state — the very word the manifest space uses, and uses correctly. To have a virtue is to be the kind of person from whom certain acts come easily, and the state persists through changes of feeling.

A habitus is formed by acts. We become just by doing just things, brave by doing brave things, temperate by doing temperate things. This is not a slogan; it is a mechanism. Repeated acts leave a disposition, and the disposition makes the next act easier, and the easier act makes the disposition stronger.

A habitus disposes acts. Once formed, it shapes perception and desire before deliberation: the generous person notices the need; the coward notices the exits. The habit operates at the level of attention, which is why it is so powerful and so hard to see.

A habitus perfects a power. It does not add a new faculty; it makes an existing one work well. The virtue of courage does not give you a new will; it heals the will’s relation to fear.

· · ·

Now put Goddard beside this.

“Assume the feeling of the wish fulfilled, persist in it, and it will harden into fact.”

What has he noticed? He has noticed that an interior state, held with feeling and repetition, becomes a durable disposition, and that a durable disposition changes what a person does, how she appears, what she notices, and therefore — very often — what happens to her. That is a real observation. It is the observation that the habitus tradition has been making for twenty-three centuries, and the reason his writing has traction is that it is true at that level.

What has he got wrong? Two things, and they are enormous.

First, he has made the state into a cause of events rather than a cause of acts. The habit does not reach out and rearrange the world. It reaches in and rearranges the person, and the person then acts, and the acts have consequences, and the consequences are ordered by providence. The chain is longer than Goddard’s, and every link is real. What he has done is to delete the middle links and attach the state directly to the outcome, which is not a stronger claim but a magical one.

Second, he has made the state something you pretend rather than something you receive. This is the deeper error, and it is the one that produces the exhaustion. For Goddard, the assumed state is a fiction you inhabit until reality catches up — “an assumption, though false.” For Aquinas, the fundamental state of the Christian is not an assumption at all. It is a fact: you are a son, you are justified, you are indwelt. The task is not to pretend it until it becomes true.
