The task is to live out of what is already true, which is a completely different psychological operation and produces a completely different person.

· · ·

This is where the theological virtues enter, and they are the answer to the whole book.

Aquinas distinguishes acquired virtues, which are formed by our acts, from infused virtues, which are given by grace (ST I-II, q. 62; q. 63, a. 3). Faith, hope, and charity are not produced by practice; they are poured in. They are habitus in the strict sense — stable dispositions that perfect the powers of the soul — but their cause is God, not us.

Which means that the Christian already possesses the thing the manifest space is trying to manufacture. The manifest space says: assume the state of the wish fulfilled until it hardens into fact. The Gospel says: the state has been given, at Baptism, and it is not a wish fulfilled but a sonship conferred, and the work of a life is to let the acts flow from it.

This is what Paul means by “walk by the Spirit” and what the tradition means by “living in grace.” It is not a feeling. It is a state, in the precise sense: a habitus, infused, stable, and prior to your feelings about it.

The pastoral consequence is enormous, and it is the single best answer to the manifest space’s anthropology that I know. You do not have to become someone. You have to become who you are. The manifest space’s version — become the person who has the thing — is a treadmill, because the state is always counterfeit and always needs maintenance. The Gospel’s version is rest, because the state is real and does not depend on your performance.

· · ·

There is a modern corroboration worth noting, not because sociology proves theology, but because it shows that the structure is not exotic.

The empirical literature on habit formation says, roughly, what Aquinas said: behaviour is governed less by decisions than by dispositions; dispositions are formed by repetition in a stable context; and the most durable change comes not from willing harder but from changing the environment and the identity in which the behaviour is embedded. The self-help industry has absorbed this and repackaged it — “identity-based habits,” “become the kind of person who” — and the packaging is often closer to the truth than the manifest space’s version, because it keeps the causality inside the person.

What none of it can supply is the ground of the identity. It can tell you to adopt an identity; it cannot tell you which identity is true. That is a question for metaphysics and for revelation, and the answer the Church gives is the one that makes the practice livable: the identity is not adopted, it is received, and it is received from someone who does not change his mind.

· · ·

So what does the practice look like?

It looks like a rule of life — a small, stable, repeatable set of acts, ordered to the virtues, reviewed and adjusted. Not a vision board. A rule.

It looks like the examen, daily, because the examen is the instrument by which a person notices the movements that are forming her, which is the empirical half of the doctrine of habitus.

It looks like the virtues taken one at a time — patience for a season, then humility, then courage — because habits are formed by focused repetition and not by generalized aspiration.

It looks like the sacraments, because the infused virtues are increased by them, and because a habitus that depends on my performance is not a habitus at all but an anxiety with a schedule.

And it looks like the acceptance of slowness, which is the hardest part for a generation formed by the manifest space. Habits are formed over months and years. The manifest space promises a result in a week. The Church promises a character in a lifetime, and then a resurrection.

· · ·

One last formulation, and it is the thesis of Part Three in a sentence.

The manifest space’s law of assumption is true about persons and false about the world. The doctrine of habitus is true about both, because it puts the person where the person belongs — as a creature whose interior life really does shape her action, whose action really does shape her world, and whose whole life is held in a providence that does not need to be tricked.

Which means the true law of assumption is not a technique. It is a grace. Assume the state of the son, because the son is what you are; and then, over a lifetime, the assumption will harden into fact — not because the universe rewards persistence, but because grace perfects nature, and the thing that is being perfected is you.

The point

The law of assumption is true about persons and false about the world. Aquinas’s account of habitus is the true version, and grace is the true assumption.

Do this

Write a rule of three practices: one daily, one weekly, one monthly. Small enough that you will actually keep them.

What this sets up

Which is why the rest of the book is practice.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Part Four

The Practice

But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.

James 1:22

A theology that does not become a practice will be defeated by a practice that has no theology. This part is therefore the most concrete in the book, and the most exposed to being wrong, because practices can be tested and doctrines can only be argued.

It sets out why practice beats doctrine in the formation of human beings; what the grammar of Catholic practice actually is; the transpositions, in four groups — word and image, time and body, memory and desire, signs and guidance; a worked rite, the Novena of Desire, that can be prayed as written; and a triage for the ordinary pastoral case, in which the only question is what to do on Monday.

Chapter 25

Why Practice Beats Doctrine

Human beings are not formed by what they believe but by what they do repeatedly. The manifest space knows this. That is the real reason it is winning — and the reason the response has to be a practice, not a pamphlet.

There is a fact about Catholic life that is embarrassing to state plainly, and this chapter is going to state it.

The Church possesses the most sophisticated, most beautiful, most tested system of spiritual practice in the history of the human race: a daily sacrifice, a cycle of readings that covers the whole of Scripture, seven sacraments, a Liturgy of the Hours that has been prayed without interruption for fifteen centuries, a thousand years of monastic discipline, the Rosary, the examen, lectio divina, fasting, pilgrimage, the veneration of relics, the liturgical year with its fasts and feasts, and a library of ascetical theology that no other tradition can approach.

And a generation of Catholics has grown up knowing almost none of it as practice, having received it instead as obligation — a list of things one must do, with no instruction in how, no explanation of why, and no experience of the effects.

The manifest space arrived in that vacuum with twelve pages of method and took the field.

· · ·

This is not a failure of doctrine. It is a failure of formation, and the distinction matters because the remedy is different.

Doctrine is transmitted by teaching. Practice is transmitted by apprenticeship: you do it with someone who knows how, badly at first, and you get better. The Church has always known this — it is the entire logic of the liturgy, of the novitiate, of the Exercises, of the family rosary — but in the last sixty years the apprenticeship has collapsed in many places while the teaching has continued, so that Catholics can now explain transubstantiation and cannot pray for twenty minutes.

The manifest space did not win by having better doctrine. It won by having an apprenticeship: a video shows you exactly what to do, tonight, in ten minutes, with your own hand and your own pen. That is a form of transmission, and it is thousands of years older than the printing press.

· · ·

There is a principle behind this, and it is the one this book has already used: lex orandi, lex credendi — roughly, the law of prayer establishes the law of belief. What a community does in worship shapes what it can believe. Doctrine is not the opposite of practice; it is the sediment that practice leaves.

This has two consequences, and they cut in opposite directions.

The first is encouraging. You do not need to win the argument first. If you can get a person to pray the examen for a month, the doctrine will follow, because the practice will have taught her something that no argument could. She will have discovered, from the inside, that her interior life is observed; that her desires are mixed; that she is capable of being moved by something that is not her; that gratitude changes her. None of that needs to be argued. It needs to be done.

The second is sobering. The reverse is also true: a bad practice teaches a bad doctrine, whatever the catechism says. A parish that celebrates the liturgy carelessly teaches, without a single word, that the Eucharist is not the body of Christ. A devotional life that consists of anxious bargaining teaches that God is a mechanism. A catechesis that consists of worksheets teaches that the faith is a school subject. The manifest space does not need to argue with us; it only needs to be more formative than we are.

· · ·

Which is why this part of the book is not an appendix. It is the heart of the proposal, and if it fails, everything before it was a long way of saying nothing.

The test of the transpositions that follow is not whether they are doctrinally correct. It is whether a person will do them, and whether, having done them for a month, she is more free. If the practice is correct and nobody does it, it has failed. If the practice is done and the person is unchanged, it has also failed, and the doctrine is not to blame; the design is.

So the criteria for a good transposition are severe, and they are worth stating before we look at any of them:

  1. It must be small enough to start tonight. Five minutes, not an hour. A person in crisis does not have an hour.
  2. It must be repeatable. Daily or weekly, at a fixed time, with a fixed form, because formation happens through repetition.
  3. It must be embodied. Posture, place, object, breath. A practice that exists only in the head is a practice that can be abandoned without noticing.
  4. It must be addressed to a person. Not to a mechanism, not to the self in the abstract. “Lord” or “Father” or “Jesus,” said, not thought.
  5. It must be open to refusal. A practice that promises a result is a technique. A practice that can be answered with “no” is a prayer.
  6. It must be intelligible without a lecture. The person should be able to grasp the shape of it in a paragraph, even if its depths take years.
  7. It must be given, not sold. The manifest space is free at the point of use. So must this be.
· · ·

There is one more reason to put practice at the centre, and it is the reason that is easiest to miss.

The manifest space’s hold on people is not primarily intellectual. It is experiential: people have had experiences in the practice — of focus, of hope, of a strange coincidence, of a shift in mood — and those experiences are the anchor. You cannot argue a person out of an experience. You can only offer her a deeper one.

This is why the transpositions in the next four chapters are not “Catholic alternatives” in the sense of consolation prizes. They are attempts to put a person in the way of the experiences that the manifest space counterfeits: the experience of being heard, of being known, of being changed, of being spoken to, of receiving what one did not earn.

Those experiences are real. They are available. They are, in fact, more available than the counterfeit, because they do not depend on the practitioner’s performance and they do not stop working when the outcome does not arrive.

The only thing they require is a form of life in which they can happen — and the provision of that form is what a Church is for.

The point

Human beings are formed by what they do repeatedly. Doctrine alone has never displaced a devotion, and it will not displace this one.

Do this

Pick one practice and one time, and put it in your calendar as an appointment you cannot move.

What this sets up

But not every practice is Catholic. Six marks tell the difference.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 26

The Grammar of Catholic Practice

Six marks distinguish a Catholic practice from a technique with a Christian veneer. Every proposed transposition should be tested against all six.

A practice is not Catholic because it has a saint’s name attached or because it is performed in a church. The manifest space has already proved that you can attach holy words to a mechanism and produce something that looks devout and is not. What makes a practice Catholic is a structure, and the structure can be specified.

There are six marks. They are not arbitrary; each one follows from a doctrine established in Part Three. A practice that lacks one of them may still be good, but it is not yet Catholic in the full sense, and if it lacks three it has become something else.

· · ·

1. It is addressed to a person.

The doctrine: the analogia entis, and the personal God of revelation. A Catholic practice says you, not it. It speaks to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit — or to a saint, or to the Blessed Virgin, who is a person and who can be asked. It does not address a field, a frequency, a law, or the universe.

This is the mark that most clearly separates a Catholic practice from a manifest one, and it is not a matter of vocabulary. A person can say “Lord” and address a mechanism; a person can say “the universe” and address a Father. The test is whether the practice can survive an answer that is no. A practice addressed to a person can. A practice addressed to a mechanism cannot, because a mechanism that does not respond is simply broken.

2. It is mediated by the Church.

The doctrine: the Mystical Body and the sacramental economy. A Catholic practice is not a private invention. It comes from the Church’s tradition, it is done in communion, and where it involves the sacraments it involves a minister with authority.

This does not mean that every prayer must be liturgical. It means that the practice has a provenance: someone gave it to you, and the someone stands in a line that goes back. The manifest space’s practices have no provenance; they have an author, who is usually selling something. The difference shows up in the corrections: a tradition can correct its practices, a market cannot.

3. It is embodied.

The doctrine: the Incarnation and the resurrection of the body. A Catholic practice involves the body: kneeling, standing, walking, fasting, singing, touching water, eating bread, holding beads, making a sign on the forehead. Not because the body is a machine for producing spiritual states, but because the body is part of the person and cannot be left out of the person’s prayer.

This is the mark that makes Catholic practice resistant to the manifest space’s idealism. You cannot do the Rosary in your head alone for very long; the beads bring you back. You cannot fake a pilgrimage. The body keeps the practice honest.

4. It is rhythmic.

The doctrine: providence and the liturgical year. A Catholic practice has a time: daily, weekly, annually. It is not performed when one feels like it, or when a need arises, but on a schedule that is older than one’s feelings — which is precisely the point, since the feelings will not cooperate.

The manifest space has methods, not rhythms. Its practices are deployed when a desire appears, and abandoned when the desire is satisfied or the technique fails. A rhythm is different: it forms the person whether or not the person is getting anything out of it, which is what formation means.

5. It is non-manipulative.

The doctrine: grace, and the freedom of God. A Catholic practice does not compel. It asks, it offers, it waits. It is compatible with the answer “no,” “not yet,” and “something else.”

This is the most important mark and the most easily faked. A novena can be prayed as a technique; a Rosary can be recited as a spell; a pilgrimage can be undertaken as a transaction. The Church’s own tradition warns about this constantly — CCC 2111 on superstition, the prophets on sacrifice without obedience, the whole critique of “vain repetition.” The test is not the form of the words but the posture of the one saying them, and the posture is revealed by what happens when the request is refused.

6. It is ordered to communion.

The doctrine: the common good, and the nature of the Church as a body. A Catholic practice makes the practitioner more available to others, or it is not finished. This is why the Church’s practices are almost all public in their orientation even when they are private: the Divine Office is prayed on behalf of the whole Church; the Rosary is a share in the prayer of the communion of saints; fasting is ordered to almsgiving; the examen ends in a resolution about how to love better tomorrow.

The manifest space’s practices are complete in themselves: the practitioner and the outcome. A Catholic practice is never complete in itself, because there is always a body to which it is ordered.

· · ·

Now the inventory, briefly, because most Catholics know the names and not the grammar.

The Mass is the paradigm of all six: addressed to the Father, mediated by the Church and the ordained minister, embodied in gesture and matter, rhythmic (daily and weekly), non-manipulative (it is a sacrifice of praise, not a transaction), and ordered to communion (it is communion).

The Liturgy of the Hours is the Church’s public prayer, and it is the single most underused resource in the Catholic world. A layperson can pray Morning Prayer and Night Prayer in ten minutes a day and be inserted into a rhythm that the Church has kept for centuries. It is also, incidentally, the best available answer to the manifest space’s morning and evening routines: it has the same shape — a fixed time, a fixed form, a text given to you — with the right addressee.

The Rosary is a rhythmic, embodied, non-manipulative contemplation of the Gospel, and its structure is genius: the body does something simple so that the mind can do something difficult.

The examen is the Church’s instrument for noticing the movements of the interior life, and it is the direct counterpart of the manifest space’s journalling.

Lectio divina is the Church’s method for reading Scripture as address rather than information, and it is the counterpart of scripting: the same act of writing down a sentence and letting it enter, with the direction reversed.

Fasting and almsgiving are the Church’s disciplines for the training of desire, and they are the counterpart of the manifest space’s “detachment,” with the crucial difference that they cost something real.

The novena is a nine-day petition, and it is the closest thing the Church has to a manifestation method — which is why it is the subject of chapter 31.

Sacramentals and the liturgical year supply the material and temporal texture that the manifest space supplies with crystals and moon phases.

· · ·

A last word on invention.

None of this means that no new practice can be created. The Church’s practice has always developed: the Rosary is a medieval development; the Divine Mercy chaplet is a twentieth-century one; the Exercises were a sixteenth-century innovation; the novena form is early modern. The tradition is alive, and a living tradition invents.

But it invents inside the grammar. A new Catholic practice will have the six marks, will be submitted to authority, will be tested by fruit, and will be given away rather than sold. That is the difference between development and the thing that happened in the manifest space — which invented a whole liturgy with none of the marks, no provenance, no oversight, and a price list.

The transpositions in the next four chapters are offered in that spirit: not as a new revelation, but as the old grammar applied to a new set of hungers. They should be tested, corrected, and, where they fail, replaced.

The point

A Catholic practice is addressed to a person, mediated by the Church, embodied, rhythmic, non-manipulative, and ordered to communion.

Do this

Test your favourite devotion against the six marks. Where it fails, ask whether the fault is the devotion or your way of doing it.

What this sets up

Word and image come first, because that is where the manifest space is strongest.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 27

Transpositions I: Word and Image

Scripting, affirmations, visualization, vision boards, and the “I AM.” Five practices with real power and the wrong addressee — and what to do with each of them tonight.

The manifest space’s most transferable material is its technology of the word and the image. This is not an accident. Speech and imagination are the two powers by which human beings most directly participate in their own formation, and every spiritual tradition has developed techniques for them. The manifest space developed good techniques and pointed them at a mechanism.

What follows is not a critique but a set of substitutions, each with instructions specific enough to be tried. They should be tried badly, and then better.

· · ·

1. Scripting → the written petition

What the manifest space does. Writes the desired outcome in the present tense, repeatedly, as though it had already happened, in order to impress the subconscious and align with the outcome.

What is true in it. Writing fixes the mind; the present tense concentrates the desire; the act of writing is an act of attention, and attention is formative. All of that survives.

What must change. The addressee, and the tense. A petition is written to someone, and it is written in the tense of a request, not of a possession. The present tense is the one thing that must go, because “I am grateful for my new job” said about a job one does not have is not faith; it is a small lie repeated until it dulls.

The practice. Take a sheet of paper. Write at the top: “Father, this is what I want, and I am asking you for it.” Then write the thing plainly, in the first person, in the present tense of desire: “I want work that does not make me sick with dread.” Then — this is the part that distinguishes it from a wish list — write three further lines:

  • What I think this would give me (the desire beneath the desire)
  • Who else this would affect, and how
  • What I will do this week that is mine to do

Then sign it with a date, and put it somewhere you will find it again. Once a month, take it out and write underneath what has happened. Do not throw away the ones that were not answered. They are the most important part of the record.

Why it works. It converts a technique into a relationship, and it forces the three questions — the object, the neighbour, and the action — that the manifest version is designed to skip.

· · ·

2. Affirmations → aspirations

What the manifest space does. Repeats a sentence about oneself (“I am worthy,” “I am abundant,” “I am loved”) in order to reprogram the subconscious.

What is true in it. Repetition forms the soul. The tradition has always known this, and has a whole genre for it: the aspiration, the short ejaculatory prayer, said many times a day, often while doing something else. “Jesus, have mercy on me.” “My Lord and my God.” “Jesus, I trust in you.” “Mother of God, pray for me.”

What must change. The subject of the sentence. An affirmation is a claim about me, asserted to no one. An aspiration is a claim about God, addressed to him. The first is a form of self-suggestion; the second is a form of love, and it changes the one who says it for the opposite reason: not because repetition impresses the subconscious, but because attention to God is the thing that makes a person.

There is one affirmation that must be refused on principle, and it is the one the manifest space loves best: “I AM.” In the tradition this is not a technique of self-realization; it is the divine name given to Moses (Ex 3:14), which is why the evangelist has Jesus say it and why the crowd picks up stones. To take the name of God and use it as a self-esteem formula is not a small confusion of categories. It is the oldest error in the book, and it is worth naming clearly because it appears, with great sincerity, in a lot of Catholic-adjacent content.

The practice. Choose one short scriptural line — no more than eight words — and say it at three fixed moments: when you wake, at midday, and when you lie down. Say it out loud if you can. Do not evaluate whether it is “working.” It is not a technique; it is a conversation, and the measure is not the feeling but the fidelity.

· · ·

3. Visualization → composition of place

What the manifest space does. Imagines the desired outcome in vivid sensory detail, from the first person, with the feeling of having received it.

What is true in it. Imagination is a real cognitive power and a real form of presence. The intensity, the sensory detail, the first-person perspective — all of this is exactly right, and the manifest space has, without knowing it, reinvented a technique that Ignatius of Loyola codified in 1548.

What must change. The object. Visualization imagines a future that does not exist and tries to make it real. Composition of place imagines a mystery that does exist and tries to enter it.

The practice. Fifteen minutes. Choose a Gospel scene — the storm on the lake, the woman at the well, the road to Emmaus, the raising of Lazarus. Then, in Ignatius’s manner:

  1. See the place. Build it in detail: the light, the water, the dust, the crowd. (SpEx 47)
  2. Hear the sounds. The wind, the voices, the silence.
  3. Smell and taste. The fish, the fire, the wine.
  4. Touch. The wood of the boat, the dust on your feet.
  5. Then enter it. Do not watch from outside. Be a person in the scene. Notice who is looking at you.
  6. Speak. Ignatius ends every contemplation with a colloquy — a conversation, as one friend speaks to another, or as a servant to a master, or as a child to a parent. Say something. Then wait.

Why it works. It gives the imagination what it was made for — the presence of God in his mysteries — and it produces the thing visualization can only counterfeit: the experience of being addressed.

· · ·

4. Vision boards → the altar, the icon, the Mass intention

What the manifest space does. Assembles images of desired outcomes and looks at them daily to focus attention and attract.

What is true in it. The visual environment shapes desire. We become what we look at. The Church has always known this, which is why it built cathedrals.

What must change. What is looked at, and what it is for. A vision board is a portrait of a future self; an altar, an icon corner, or a crucifix is a portrait of God and of the saints, and the difference is not a matter of taste. The board says this is what I will have. The icon says this is who is with me.

The practice. Make a small physical place in your home — a shelf, a corner, a nail — and put on it: a crucifix, one icon or holy card, a candle, and a slip of paper with the intention you are currently praying for. Change the paper when the intention changes. Light the candle when you pray. If you want to keep the visual discipline of a board, make the board an intercession board: photographs of the people you are praying for, with their names.

And then add the practice that has no manifest equivalent, and which is worth more than all of the above: have a Mass offered for your intention. It costs nothing, it involves a priest, it is offered on an altar, and it is the most powerful thing the Church can do for a person — and it is not a technique, because it depends on Christ and not on you.

· · ·

5. “Name it and claim it” → the name of Jesus

What the manifest space does. Speaks a desired outcome as though it were already granted, on the model of the Word-of-Faith preachers: “I declare,” “I decree,” “I claim.”

What is true in it. There is real power in the name of Jesus — “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Phil 2:10) — and the Church has never been embarrassed by it. The Jesus Prayer, the invocation in deliverance, the naming of the name in the litany: all of this is real.

What must change. Everything about the grammar. The name is not a password. It is the name of a person, and it is powerful because the person is, not because the syllables are correct. A decree issued to the universe is magic; a name invoked in faith is prayer. The difference is the same difference as everywhere else in this book: whether there is someone there.

The practice. Learn the Jesus Prayer — “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner” — and say it for ten minutes, with the breath, sitting still. Then use it in the moment of fear, in the moment of temptation, in the moment of the 3 a.m. waking. It is the shortest, oldest, and most portable practice in the Christian tradition, and it has been the whole spiritual life of millions of people who could not read.

· · ·

The common thread in all five is the same thread as in the rest of this book: keep the technique, change the addressee. The manifest space is not wrong that words and images form a person. It is wrong about what they are for, and about who is listening.

And the proof that the change is not merely semantic is what happens when the request is refused. The technique has nothing to say. The prayer has somewhere to go.

The point

Keep the technique and change the addressee: the petition, the aspiration, the composition of place, the altar, the name.

Do this

Write the petition tonight, with the three questions under it, and date it.

What this sets up

Then there is the body, and the clock.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 28

Transpositions II: Time and Body

Eleven-eleven, the moon phases, the state akin to sleep, the 3 a.m. waking — four temporal and bodily practices with real effects, and the Church’s far older discipline of sacred time.

The manifest space is unusually attentive to when and how one practices. There are times (11:11, the new moon, the hour before sleep), postures (lying down, hand on heart), rhythms (morning and night), and bodily techniques (breath, repetition, the state between waking and sleeping). This is not superstition. It is a genuine insight: human beings are temporal and bodily creatures, and a spirituality that ignores time and the body will be a spirituality of the mind only, which is to say, a spirituality that will not survive a bad week.

The Church is, if anything, more attentive to these things than the manifest space. What follows is the transposition.

· · ·

1. Eleven-eleven and the moon → the liturgical calendar

What the manifest space does. Watches for repeating numbers as confirmations, and organizes practice by lunar phases (new moon for intentions, full moon for release).

What is true in it. Sacred time is real. Some moments are different, and a person who marks time is a person whose life has a shape. The manifest space has discovered this and, having no calendar, has improvised one out of clocks and moons.

What must change. The calendar. The Church has a calendar that is two thousand years old and covers the year with fasts, feasts, seasons, saints’ days, and the whole life of Christ. It is the most sophisticated Christian answer to the human need for sacred time, and most Catholics use almost none of it.

The practice. Begin with three days a year, and let them be real: Ash Wednesday (the fast), Good Friday (the silence), and your baptismal anniversary (the feast). Then add the Sunday obligation as what it is — the first day, the day of resurrection, the day that makes the week. A person who keeps the liturgical year for three cycles will find that time has become a story rather than a series of Tuesdays.

· · ·

2. The state akin to sleep → Compline

What the manifest space does. Uses the hypnagogic state — the borderland between waking and sleeping — for “SATS”: the assumption of the wish fulfilled, repeated as one falls asleep, on the theory that the subconscious is most receptive then.

What is true in it. The state before sleep is spiritually significant. The last thing on your mind shapes the night, and the night shapes the morning. Every monastic tradition has known this; Compline exists because of it.

What must change. The content and the addressee. SATS fills the borderland with a manufactured scene. Compline fills it with the Psalms, the Nunc dimittis, the confession, and a blessing — and then the great antiphon of the tradition: Salva nos, Domine, vigilantes; custodi nos dormientes — “Save us, Lord, while we are awake; guard us while we sleep.”

The practice. Night prayer, five minutes, from a breviary app or a printed copy. If you have no book: one psalm (4, 91, or 134), the Nunc dimittis (“Lord, now let your servant go in peace”), an examination of the day in three questions (what went well, what went badly, what will I do tomorrow), and the sign of the cross. Then sleep.

Why it works. Because it does to the night what SATS tries to do and cannot: it puts the night under someone else’s care rather than under the care of your own imagination.

· · ·

3. The 3 a.m. waking → the night office

What the manifest space does. Nothing, mostly. The 3 a.m. waking is a problem for a system that promises peace, and it is usually interpreted as resistance or as a sign that the practice is not working.

What is true in it. The night is when a person is alone with her thoughts, and the tradition has an entire literature for this: the night office of the monks, the psalms of lament, the “dark night” of John of the Cross, the insomnia of the saints.

What must change. The interpretation. The 3 a.m. waking is not a failure of your frequency. It is one of the ordinary conditions of being a creature, and the tradition has a practice for it: get up, or lie still, and say Psalm 63 — “O God, you are my God, for you I long; for you my soul is thirsting” — or the Jesus Prayer, or the Rosary, badly, in the dark, until you sleep.

The point is not to eliminate the waking. It is to make it a place where you are not alone. There are people who have prayed in that hour for fifteen hundred years, and joining them is a real act of communion, and it is available at 3 a.m. in a way that almost nothing else is.

· · ·

4. Breath and repetition → the body at prayer

What the manifest space does. Uses breath work, tapping, bilateral stimulation, humming, and repetition to regulate the nervous system and “raise the vibration.”

What is true in it. The body is involved in prayer, breath is a real instrument, and repetition has real effects on attention and on the nervous system. Anyone who has prayed the Rosary badly and felt calmer knows this.

What must change. Almost nothing at the level of technique, and everything at the level of meaning. The Church has its own embodied repertoire, and it is older and richer:

  • Kneeling — the body’s confession that it is not in charge.
  • Prostration — on Good Friday and at ordinations, the most absolute gesture in the tradition.
  • Fasting — the body’s participation in a desire that is not for food.
  • Pilgrimage — walking as prayer, with a destination that is not metaphorical.
  • Incense, water, oil, candles — the senses enlisted.
  • Silence — the hardest and most bodily of all, because it requires an actual body in an actual room doing nothing.

The practice. Choose one bodily practice and one time. Kneel for the Our Father. Fast on Fridays, in some real way, and give the money saved to someone. Walk to a church once a week rather than driving. The body will complain, which is the point: the complaint is the practice.

· · ·

5. The Sabbath → the great refusal

There is one practice in the tradition that has no manifest equivalent at all, and it is the one most needed by a generation formed in the manifest space.

The Sabbath — the day on which you do not optimize.

The manifest space has no Sabbath, because everything is potentially an opportunity to align, manifest, improve, or optimize. Its logic is total: every hour can be worked, every mood can be adjusted, every outcome can be influenced. This is why its most successful practitioners are exhausted, and why the aesthetic of the manifest space is a strange combination of calm and strain.

The Sabbath is the structural refusal. One day in seven, you do not work, you do not optimize, you do not manifest. You rest, you worship, you eat with people, you do nothing useful. And you do it not because it is efficient but because you are not a machine, and because the world is held by someone else, and because the refusal to be productive is an act of faith.

The practice. Pick a day, or a half-day, and keep it. No work. No self-improvement. No screens if you can. Mass, a meal with people, a walk, a nap, a book. And when the guilt arrives — and it will, because the manifest space has trained you to feel guilty about unproductive time — say the sentence that the Sabbath exists to teach: the world is not mine to run.

· · ·

The pattern in all five transpositions is the same as in the previous chapter. The manifest space is not wrong that time and the body matter. It is wrong about what they are for, and it has improvised a calendar, a night prayer, and a bodily discipline out of almost nothing, while the Church’s versions sit unused in the breviary and the calendar.

Which is an indictment, but also an opportunity, and it is the reason this chapter is practical rather than polemical. The material is already there. Somebody has to hand it to people, with instructions, on a Tuesday.

The point

The manifest space has improvised a calendar, a night prayer, and a bodily discipline out of nothing. The Church has better versions of all three, unused.

Do this

Keep Compline for seven nights. Five minutes. Use a book or an app; do not improvise.

What this sets up

Then the hardest material: memory, and the shadow.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 29

Transpositions III: Memory and Desire

“Revision,” “shadow work,” limiting beliefs, soul contracts — the manifest space’s four attempts to deal with the past. The Church’s answer is older, harder, and actually works.

The past is where the manifest space is most obviously making something up, and where the Church has the most to offer. Four practices, and four substitutions.

· · ·

1. “Revision” → confession and the healing of memory

What the manifest space does. Mentally rewrites a past event — imagining it as it should have been — on the theory that the revision changes the event’s effect on the present, or the event itself.

What is true in it. The past is not finished with us. An event can be carried in a way that poisons the present, and the way it is carried can genuinely change. A memory can lose its sting. A person can be released from a history. All of this is true, and the manifest space is not wrong that something can be done.

What must change. The mechanism, and the honesty. Revision works by denial: it says that the event, in some sense, did not happen as it happened. That is false, and it is also pastorally disastrous, because the person who has denied the event has no way to be forgiven for it and no way to grieve it.

The practice, part one: confession. The sacrament does what revision claims to do, and does it by the opposite means. It keeps the fact and removes the guilt. It names the thing out loud to a witness. It receives a word from outside: I absolve you. And it gives the penitent something to do — a penance — which converts the past into a future act of love.

The theology here is worth stating because it is the whole answer to “revision”: the past of a forgiven sinner is not deleted; it is redeemed. The fact remains, the guilt is gone, and the event is taken up into a story that now ends differently. That is a more radical claim than revision, and it is the only one that can survive contact with the truth.

The practice, part two: the healing of memory. Where a memory still wounds after confession — and it often does, because the wound is psychological as well as moral — the tradition offers a prayer that is simple and has a long pedigree. Take the memory, in prayer, and ask Christ to be present in it. Not instead of the event; in it. Then, in the imagination, let him look at the person you were, and say what he would say. This is not revision. It is the application of the Incarnation to a memory: the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and “among us” includes the worst room in your history.

Caution. This practice is powerful and is not a substitute for therapy. Where the memory involves trauma, it should be undertaken with a competent director and, where appropriate, a clinician — not alone, and not as an attempt to force a feeling.

· · ·

2. “Shadow work” → the examination of conscience

What the manifest space does. Identifies the disowned, rejected parts of the self and integrates them, so that they stop sabotaging the manifestation.

What is true in it. There is a great deal in a person that she does not want to see, and it operates below the level of choice. The tradition calls it the passions, the wounds, the fomes — the tinder of sin — and it has been studying it for centuries with more precision than the modern literature.

What must change. The goal. Shadow work aims at integration: the disowned part is brought into the self and accepted. The Christian practice aims at conversion and confession: the thing is brought into the light, named, judged, forgiven, and healed. Integration leaves you in charge of your darkness. Confession puts you under a mercy.

The practice. The examination of conscience, done properly, is not a scrupulous audit of faults; it is the Ignatian review of the day’s movements. Fifteen minutes, three questions:

  1. What did I feel today, and where did it come from? (Not “what did I do wrong” — first, what moved me.)
  2. Which of those movements led me toward love, and which away?
  3. What is the one thing I will do differently tomorrow?

Once a month, take the pattern to confession. The shadow, named in the presence of a confessor with authority, is a very different thing from the shadow named in a journal at midnight.

· · ·

3. “Limiting beliefs” → the discernment of spirits

What the manifest space does. Treats every sense of limitation as a false belief to be removed, because the only obstacle to the desired outcome is the belief that it is impossible.

What is true in it. Many beliefs are false, and they do limit. A person who believes she cannot learn, cannot be loved, or cannot change is being held by a lie, and the lie should be broken.

What must change. The assumption that every limit is a belief. Some limits are real: finitude, illness, the freedom of other people, the consequences of one’s history, death. A practice that treats these as beliefs to be deleted will produce either a fantasy life or a collapse, and it will do so with the cruelty of a system that says the collapse was your fault.

The practice. Discernment. For any belief that seems to be holding you back, ask: Is this a lie, or is it a truth I do not want? The two are handled completely differently. A lie is renounced and replaced with the truth (which is often a scriptural sentence). A truth is accepted and grieved, and then worked with. The confusion of the two is one of the most common causes of spiritual damage in the manifest space, and it is the reason the Church insists on the discernment of spirits as a discipline rather than a mood.

· · ·

4. “Soul contracts” → the refusal to explain

What the manifest space does. Explains suffering by saying that the soul chose it before birth, for a lesson, in a contract agreed to in another life.

What is true in it. The instinct behind it is good: it refuses to accept that suffering is meaningless, and it looks for a purpose beyond the obvious.

What must change. Everything. The soul contract is a theodicy that assigns the cause of suffering to the sufferer — which is the same move as “you attracted it,” only with a longer timeline and a gentler vocabulary. It is also, pastorally, a closed system: the person cannot argue with a contract she does not remember making.

The practice. Learn to say, and to mean, I do not know why. This is not a failure of faith. It is the answer of Job, of the psalmists, of the Church in the presence of the innocent sufferer. What the Christian has is not an explanation but a presence, a promise, and a future; and the discipline of not explaining is one of the works of mercy.

When someone offers you a soul contract as a consolation, the kind response is: I know you mean to help. I don’t think the reason is available to me. What would help is if you sat with me.

· · ·

5. The journal → the ledger of providence

There is one practice I would recommend above all the others in this chapter, and it is the one nobody teaches.

Keep a written record of your petitions and of what happened.

The manifest space cannot keep such a record, and this is one of its most revealing limitations. Its literature is entirely composed of successes, because its epistemology requires it; the failures are either unrecorded or reclassified as misalignment. This produces the strange effect that a practice used by millions has almost no honest archive.

A Christian can keep an honest archive, because a Christian can survive an unanswered prayer.

The practice. A notebook, one page per month. In one column, the date and the petition. In a second, the date and what happened — granted, refused, different, not yet, I no longer want it. In a third, what changed in me.

Do this for three years and you will possess something that no manifestation journal can contain: a record of providence. You will see patterns you could not have seen in the moment; you will see prayers that were answered in ways you did not recognize; you will see the ones that were refused, and, if you are honest, you will sometimes see why. And you will learn the thing that the whole practice is designed to teach: that you have been dealt with, personally, patiently, over a long time, by someone who was not a mechanism.

· · ·

The four substitutions in this chapter have a common shape, and it is the shape of the whole book. The manifest space takes a real human task — dealing with the past, facing the shadow, breaking false limits, finding meaning in suffering — and offers a technique that avoids the one thing that would actually accomplish it: the presence of another.

Confession requires a confessor. Direction requires a director. The healing of memory requires Christ. The refusal to explain requires a community that can sit with the unexplained. Every one of them is a relationship, and every one of them is therefore slower, harder, and real.

The point

The past is not rewritten; it is forgiven, healed, and recorded. Confession does what revision claims, and keeps the fact.

Do this

Go to confession within the fortnight, and bring one thing you have been carrying for years.

What this sets up

And the signs? They are not a code.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 30

Transpositions IV: Signs and Guidance

The desire to be guided is not superstition; it is one of the deepest human longings. The Church has a tested discipline for it, and it is not reading numbers.

Of all the manifest space’s practices, the reading of signs is the one most likely to be dismissed as silly and most likely to be doing real damage. Both reactions are wrong, and the second is more important.

The practice is not silly, because the desire behind it is not silly. A person who looks for signs is a person who believes that the world is addressed to her — that her life is not a random sequence but a communication. That belief is true. It is one of the things that the doctrine of providence is for. The manifest space has it, badly, and the Church has it, well, and has largely stopped teaching it.

And the practice does damage, because a life spent decoding is a life spent in low-grade anxiety, and because the code is never finished, and because a person who reads signs instead of seeking counsel will eventually read the sign she wants.

· · ·

What the Church forbids, and why

The Catechism is blunt: “All forms of divination are to be rejected: recourse to Satan or demons, conjuring up the dead or other practices falsely supposed to ’unveil’ the future. Consulting horoscopes, astrology, palm reading, interpretation of omens and lots, the phenomena of clairvoyance, and recourse to mediums all conceal a desire for power over time, history, and, in the last analysis, other human beings, as well as a wish to conciliate hidden powers” (CCC 2116).

Two things about that sentence are worth noticing.

First, “interpretation of omens” is in the list. The 11:11 is an omen. It is a small, harmless-looking one, and it belongs to a category the Church has always treated as seriously as she treats anything: because the issue is not the size of the omen but the shape of the relationship it creates. The person who reads omens is trying to obtain knowledge of the future in order to secure power over it. That is the posture the Church refuses, and she refuses it for the person’s sake.

Second, the Catechism diagnoses the desire under it: a desire for power over time, history, and other human beings. This is the same diagnosis as the one this book has been making about the manifest space from the beginning. Divination is not primarily an intellectual error; it is a strategy for managing anxiety by controlling the unknown. And it does not work, which is why it must be repeated.

· · ·

What the Church offers instead: discernment

The alternative is not “stop noticing things.” It is a discipline, and it is one of the Church’s great practical gifts.

Ignatius of Loyola’s rules for the discernment of spirits (SpEx 313–336) are a method for distinguishing, in the movements of one’s own interior life, what comes from God, what comes from one’s own disordered affections, and what comes from the enemy. They are not a theory; they are a set of rules learned by experience, tested in the confessional and in the Exercises, and they are far more reliable than any sign.

The core of the method is a distinction between consolation and desolation.

Consolation is a movement that increases faith, hope, and love; that brings peace; that draws the soul toward God and toward others; that produces “quiet and peace.” It can be intense or quiet, but its fruit is recognizable: it makes a person more herself, more free, more loving.

Desolation is the opposite: darkness, disturbance, disquiet, a pull toward what is low, a loss of hope, a sense of being alone. Ignatius is careful: desolation is not sin, and it is not a sign that God has abandoned you. It is a state to be understood and resisted, not a verdict.

And then the rules that turn the method from a mood into a discipline:

  • Never make a change during desolation. (SE 318) The most important rule in the whole set, and the one most often broken. Decisions made in desolation are almost always wrong, because desolation distorts the field of vision.
  • In desolation, intensify the practice rather than changing course. (SE 319–321) More prayer, not less. Stay where you are.
  • Notice the direction of the movement. (SE 314–315) Consolation draws toward God and the good; desolation draws away.
  • Test by the fruits, over time. (SE 316) Not by intensity, and not by the coincidence.
  • Seek counsel. (SE 326) Not a sign. A person.
· · ·

The three times of election

Ignatius also gives a structure for the larger decisions — the ones that actually need guidance — and it is worth setting out because it is the exact alternative to a life of decoded signs.

He describes three “times” in which a good choice can be made (SE 175–188):

  1. When God moves the will directly and unmistakably. Rare, and not to be presumed.
  2. When enough clarity is given through consolation and desolation — the movements have left a discernible direction.
  3. In tranquility, by reasoning it out: the pros and cons, the advice of wise people, the examination of motives, the consideration of what one would advise another person to do in the same position.

Most decisions are made in the third time. This is a crucial and liberating fact. It means that a Christian is not required to wait for a sign, and is not required to have a supernatural experience, and is not obliged to feel certain. She is required to think, to pray, to seek counsel, to examine her motives — and then to decide, and to trust that God governs the decision she makes in good faith.

That is a form of guidance far more robust than sign-reading, because it can be taught, it can be reviewed, and it does not collapse when the coincidence stops.

· · ·

The practice: the movements log

Fifteen minutes in the evening, five days a week, for a month.

Write three columns:

MovementWhere it came fromWhat I did
A sudden peace about the decisionSeems like consolation — came during prayer, after CommunionWrote it down, did not act yet
A pull to check her social mediaDesolation or habit? Noted, and did not do itWent for a walk instead
Sharp irritation at my brotherOwn disorder — tired, hungryApologized the next day

The point of the log is not to decode the future. It is to learn your own interior, which is the only instrument you have for discerning anything, and which no one has ever taught you to read.

After a month, take the log to a spiritual director or a confessor. What you will discover, in most cases, is that you have been receiving guidance all along, and that the signs you were looking for were mostly noise, and that the movements that actually mattered were quiet, and could bear being tested.

· · ·

The distinction that makes it all work

There is a difference between a sign and a movement, and it is the difference between divination and discernment.

A sign is external, ambiguous, and infinitely interpretable. A movement is internal, particular, and testable. A sign says: something will happen. A movement says: this is drawing you toward love, and that is drawing you away.

The manifest space trains people to look outward for confirmation. The Church trains them to look inward for movement, and then outward for counsel, and then upward for grace. It is a slower method. It is also the only one that produces a person who can decide.

And there is one more rule, which is not in Ignatius but runs through the whole tradition, and which is the simplest answer to the question of signs: if you are looking for a sign about whether to do something you already know is right, the sign is the knowing.

The point

The Church forbids decoding omens and offers something better: the discernment of movements, tested over time and by counsel.

Do this

Start the movements log tonight. Three columns, five days, no interpretation on day one.

What this sets up

Put the pieces together into a rite you can actually pray.
