Chapter 31

The Novena of Desire

A worked rite, nine days, twenty minutes a day — the Church’s native practice of petition, rebuilt for people who have been formed by the manifest space, and offered for testing.

The novena is the Church’s closest structural relative to the manifestation method, and almost nobody notices.

Nine days. A fixed time. A fixed prayer. A specific intention. A repeated act, sustained across a period, with an expectation that something will happen at the end. That is a novena, and it has been a Catholic practice since the nine days between the Ascension and Pentecost, when the disciples waited in the upper room with Mary.

The manifest space reinvented it — 9 days, 9 repetitions, a specific intention — and gave it a mechanism. What follows is the Church’s version, rebuilt deliberately for a person who has been formed by the manifest space: someone who knows how to do a daily practice, who expects it to matter, and who has been told that the result depends on her alignment.

The rite has four parts: the petition, the relinquishment, the listening, and the thanksgiving. The second of them is the one that makes it Catholic.

· · ·

Before you begin

The intention. Choose one thing. Not a list. It should be specific enough that you would know whether it had been granted, and honest enough that you would admit it if it had not. Write it down.

The three questions. Before day one, answer these in writing, briefly:

  1. What do I think this would give me? (The desire beneath the desire.)
  2. Who else does this involve, and have I considered their good? (The neighbour.)
  3. What is mine to do about it, and what is not? (The action and the limit.)

The time and place. Twenty minutes, same time each day, same place. A candle if you have one. A chair, not a bed.

The rule. If you miss a day, do not restart. Continue where you are. The point is fidelity, not perfection, and the person who restarts after every failure is being formed by the very perfectionism this rite is designed to heal.

· · ·

The structure of each day

Twenty minutes, in this order.

1. Silence (2 minutes). Sit. Do not fill it. If it is unbearable, say the name of Jesus slowly.

2. The psalm (3 minutes). One psalm, read aloud. The psalms of petition are the Church’s vocabulary for asking — Psalm 5, 13, 22, 25, 27, 40, 62, 86, 130. Read one slowly, and stop at the line that catches.

3. The petition (5 minutes). Say it out loud, in your own words, as a child would say it. Not “I am grateful for my new job.” Rather: “Father, I am asking you for this. I want it. I am afraid that I will not get it. I am asking you to give it, or to give me what is better.”

4. The relinquishment (5 minutes). This is the heart of it. Say, slowly, three times, with a pause between: “Not my will, but yours.” Then sit in silence for two minutes and let the sentence do what it does. It will be easy on the first day and difficult by the fourth, which is the point.

5. The listening (3 minutes). Ask: “Is there anything you want me to do today?” Then wait. Do not manufacture an answer. If nothing comes, nothing comes, and that is also an answer.

6. The thanksgiving (2 minutes). Thank God for one specific thing from the last twenty-four hours. Not a general gratitude. A specific one — a person, a meal, a moment.

7. The sign of the cross. End it. Do not linger. The practice ends, and you go and live.

· · ·

The nine days

The themes are not magic; they are a structure for the purification of the desire across nine days. Each day has a scripture and a question.

DayThemeScriptureQuestion
1AskMatt 7:7–11What exactly am I asking for?
2The desire beneathPs 37:4What do I think this will give me?
3The neighbourMatt 22:36–40Who else is affected, and how?
4The obstacleMark 10:46–52What in me resists asking plainly?
5The refusal2 Cor 12:7–9What if the answer is no?
6The hiddennessCol 3:1–4Can I live without seeing the result?
7The offeringRom 12:1–2Can I offer the desire itself?
8The trustMatt 6:25–34What am I afraid of?
9The thanksgivingLuke 17:11–19What has already been given?

Day 5 is the pivot. It is the day on which the person discovers whether she is praying or operating. If the question “what if the answer is no?” produces panic, that is not a failure of the novena; it is the novena working. The panic is the sound of a technique being converted into a prayer.

· · ·

The “no” clause

Every day, at the end of the petition, say this, or something like it:

“Father, if this is not for me, then give me the grace to want what you want, and the honesty to admit that I did not get what I asked for.”

Two things are being trained by that sentence. The first is freedom — the capacity to receive a no without concluding that one is unloved. The second is honesty — the refusal to retroactively reinterpret a refusal as a grant, which is the characteristic move of the manifest space and the beginning of a life of self-deception.

A person who can say that sentence and mean it has already received something greater than the thing she asked for, and it is one of the marks of the authentic operation of grace that the gift is often not the requested one.

· · ·

What to do with the outcome

On the tenth day, write down what happened. Use the ledger from chapter 29: the petition, the outcome, what changed in you.

If the thing was granted: thank God specifically, and then do the thing you promised in the third question. If you said you would act, act. The most common failure of petitionary prayer is not that the prayer is unanswered; it is that the answer arrives and the person does nothing.

If the thing was refused: do not conclude that you prayed badly. Take the refusal to prayer and say the thing you actually feel — anger, grief, confusion. The psalms give you permission; half of them are complaints. Then take it to a director or a confessor, and let it be examined over months rather than resolved in an hour.

If nothing happened at all: keep the record. Some of the most important prayers in a life are answered in the third or thirtieth year, and the ledger is how you will know.

· · ·

A note on what this rite is not

It is not a technique, and it must not become one. The moment it is taught as “nine days and you will get the thing,” it has become a novena-as-mechanism, which is a real and common abuse, and which the Catechism warns against directly (CCC 2111).

Three safeguards:

  1. Never promise an outcome. Not to yourself, and never to another person.
  2. Never sell it. It costs nothing, and it must cost nothing.
  3. Always leave the result to God. The relinquishment is not a rhetorical flourish; it is the difference between a prayer and a spell.

There is a fourth safeguard, and it is the most important one: do it with others. A novena said alone is a practice; a novena said by a household, a parish group, or a family is a liturgy. The manifest space cannot produce a household practice, because its unit is the individual. The Church can, and this is one of the places where the difference is most visible.

· · ·

Why this rite, and not another

There are a hundred Catholic practices that could be offered to a person formed by the manifest space: the Rosary, the Divine Mercy chaplet, the Stations, lectio divina, Adoration. All of them are better than anything the manifest space has, and any of them can be given.

The reason for constructing this particular rite is diagnostic. The Novena of Desire is designed to do, in nine days, what the manifest space cannot do in a lifetime: it makes the person ask a person, name the desire, consider the neighbour, face the possibility of refusal, act on what is hers, and record the truth.

If it works — if people do it, and are more free, and the fruit is real — then it should be tested by the Church, corrected, and given away. If it does not work, it should be discarded, and something better built in its place.

That is what a practice is for. And the test is not whether it is beautiful. It is whether it makes people holy.

The point

The nine days move from asking to thanksgiving, and day five is the pivot: what if the answer is no? A prayer that can survive that question is a prayer; a technique cannot survive it at all.

Do this

Begin the nine days tonight, with one intention and one sentence you will say even when it is hard.

What this sets up

But most people will meet this book in a conversation, not in a novena.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 32

Pastoral Triage

The one-page answer for the person who has to say something on Monday. Green, amber, red; two questions; and the rule about the bedside.

This chapter is written for the person in the car park.

It assumes no expertise, no library, and no time. It assumes a real person in front of you who has asked a real question, and about four minutes in which to answer it without doing harm.

· · ·

The first rule: do not begin with the metaphysics

The temptation, for anyone who has read a book like this one, is to begin with the doctrine. Do not. The person in front of you has not asked a doctrinal question. She has asked whether she is allowed to keep doing the thing that is keeping her sane.

Begin with the practice, and with her. Ask what she does, when, and what it does for her. Listen for two minutes without correcting anything. You will learn more in those two minutes than in an hour of explanation, and — this matters more than the information — she will learn that she has been heard, which is the first thing the manifest space gave her and the first thing the Church usually fails to give.

· · ·

The two questions

Almost all the diagnostic work is done by two questions. Ask them gently, and in this order.

1. “What do you think this practice is doing?”

The answer tells you the metaphysics. If she says “it helps me focus and keeps me hoping,” she has a practice with a thin theory, and the work is catechesis and a better practice. If she says “it makes things happen,” she has the system, and the work is longer. If she says “it’s just a bit of fun,” and then cannot stop, you have learned something else again.

2. “If it stopped working tomorrow, what would you do?”

The answer tells you the god. If she says “I’d be devastated, but I’d still have Mass and my family,” the practice is not ultimate. If she says “I don’t know — I’d have nothing,” you are not dealing with a hobby. You are dealing with the thing she is actually trusting, and it is not God. That is a conversation about faith, not about superstition, and it should be had with great gentleness and over months.

· · ·

The three colours

Green — ordinary and good. Goal-setting; journalling; gratitude lists; positive self-talk about one’s own capacities; habit and sleep routines borrowed from the self-help world; “manifesting” used as a colloquial word for hoping. Response: affirm it, and quietly supply the theological frame. Do not pathologize. A young person who writes down her goals is doing something the tradition calls studiositas, and she should be encouraged.

Amber — ambiguous; needs catechesis and a substitute. Visualization of a desired good; affirmations; vision boards; “manifesting” a job or a relationship in a strong sense; crystals as aesthetics; astrology as entertainment; “energy” language used loosely. Response: distinguish the practice from the metaphysics; give the transposition (chapter 27–30); supply a concrete Catholic practice, with instructions; check in after a month. The key sentence: “Almost everything you’re doing is fine. The reason you were given for why it works is not, and here is a better one.”

Red — renounce, and replace. Channeling or “higher self” guidance; consulting mediums; attempts to control another person’s will; “reality shifting”; curses and hexes; the claim that illness is self-caused used on a sick person; any practice that requires secrecy from the Church, from a spouse, or from a director; anything involving a fee for spiritual power. Response: name it, briefly and without disgust; sacramental confession; and then — this is the part that is usually forgotten — put something in the space. A person who is told to stop and given nothing will return to the practice within a fortnight.

· · ·

The six cases

The teenager. She is manifesting her exams, a boy, and her mother’s health. Do not take the practice away; take it up. Teach her the Novena of Desire, or the examen, or the Jesus Prayer, and let her keep the notebook — the notebook is not the problem, the addressee is. Give her something to do at 11:11.

The scrupulous person. She is terrified that her intrusive thoughts are attracting disasters, and she has begun to confess the thoughts themselves. This is one of the most urgent cases, because the manifest space’s metaphysics manufactures scrupulosity. The doctrinal correction is precise and liberating: thoughts are not creative; temptation is not sin; the first movement is not consent. Say it plainly, repeat it, and if the scrupulosity is severe, involve a clinician — this is not a failure of faith, and treating it is not a lack of trust.

The grieving person. Someone has told her that she attracted the death, or that she did not manifest hard enough. Do not argue with the person who told her; argue with the sentence, gently, and then bury it. The medicine is John 9, Job, and the Cross, and the manner is silence. Say: “That is not true, and it is not what the Church teaches, and I am sorry that you were told it.” Then sit down.

The person in an abusive situation. If the manifest teaching is being used to keep her in the situation — “you attracted this,” “change your vibration and he will change” — the pastoral priority is her safety, not her metaphysics. The Church’s teaching on the dignity of the person and the reality of sin is the doctrinal ground for leaving; it is not a failure of forgiveness to be safe. Refer to the appropriate services. This is a case where getting the doctrine right has immediate, physical consequences.

The person refusing treatment. She has stopped taking the medication, or has decided against the surgery, because “affirming the illness” would only manifest more of it, or because she is waiting for the healing she has been visualizing. This is not a metaphysical disagreement; it is a medical situation with a doctrinal component, and the doctrinal component has a short answer: the ordinary means of preserving life are to be used, and using them is not a failure of faith but the acceptance of a created good. The sacrament of the sick is given alongside the doctor — James says to call for the elders, not to dismiss the physician. Say the doctrinal sentence once, and then say the practical one: “Take the medicine, and keep praying.” If she is a minor, or confused, or frightened in a way that is preventing her from thinking clearly, involve her family and her doctor the same day. Do not let a conversation about metaphysics delay the phone call.

The person who has had an experience. She prayed, or she visualized, and something happened — a healing, a coincidence, a word. Do not dismiss it, and do not endorse it as supernatural without examination. The Church’s norms exist for exactly this: test the fruit, look for doctrine, ask about the guidance, and be slow. Nihil obstat — “for now, nothing stands in the way” — is a real and useful verdict, and it is not the same as approval.

· · ·

The rule about the bedside

There is one situation in which all of this should be set aside, and it is the one that matters most.

Do not teach, correct, or catechize a person who is dying, or a person in acute grief, or a person in the first days of a catastrophic diagnosis.

At the bedside, the only doctrine is presence. Sit down. Ask what would help. Bring food. Pray if you are asked, and if you are not, be quiet. Say, if it is true and if it is the right moment, that God is not punishing her, that she did not cause this, that she is loved. Say it once. Do not argue.

Everything in this book is for the weeks and months afterwards, in the ordinary time, with a person who is not drowning. Used at the bedside, the best doctrine in the world becomes another weight.

· · ·

What to hand over

Leave the person with three things, if you can.

One practice. Small, specific, repeatable, and written down. “Say this, at this time, for this many days.” Not a reading list.

One name. A person she can talk to — a director, a confessor, a religious sister, a lay chaplain. The manifest space’s strength is that it is always available. The Church’s weakness is that the person who could help her is available on Thursdays. If you can give her a name, you have done more than a chapter of this book.

One sentence. The thing she will remember at 2 a.m. Choose it carefully. Mine, if I had to choose one for every case in this chapter, would be: You did not do this, and you are not being punished, and God is not disgusted by you.

· · ·

Pastoral care is not the application of a system to a case. It is the art of being with a particular person at a particular moment in a way that makes it possible for her to receive what God is giving. Everything in this part of the book — the transpositions, the rite, the triage — is scaffolding for that, and the scaffolding should be taken down when the building is up.

The last word belongs to the tradition, and it is the oldest rule of all: accompany, do not control. The manifest space’s great sin is that it offers control. The Church’s great gift is that she offers company. And company, unlike control, can be given by anyone in a car park with four minutes to spare.

The point

Two questions, three colours, one rule: at the bedside, presence only.

Do this

Learn the two questions by heart. They do most of the work and they cost nothing.

What this sets up

Which brings us from the person to the institution.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Part Five

The Programme

What you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.

2 Timothy 2:2

An argument is not a programme. The first four parts of this book have tried to establish what is true; this part asks what would have to be built if the truth were taken seriously at the scale at which it is needed.

The precedent is instructive here for a reason that is easy to miss. Thomas did not win the thirteenth century by writing better arguments than the Averroists. He won it by founding a school, persuading an order, attaching a curriculum to a university, and outlasting his own condemnation by half a century. The instruments were institutional: translations, chairs, disputations, quodlibetal questions, sums, and the slow machinery of canonization. Ideas do not survive on their merits. They survive in buildings, in syllabi, in the habits of people who have been taught them by someone whose face they can see.

So this part is deliberately practical, and it is addressed to the people who can actually do these things: campus ministers, diocesan offices, religious orders, publishers, teachers, and the pastor with four minutes in a car park. Five chapters, in the order the work has to happen — listen, publish the questions, build, measure, and wait.

Chapter 33

Listening

The first institutional act is not a refutation but a description. Here is how to do the Moerbeke work in 2026 — who to talk to, what to ask, and the disciplines that keep it honest.

Thomas’s first move was to commission translations. He did not begin with a verdict; he began with the text. The modern equivalent is not a translation of Greek into Latin but an act of attention: sitting with the people who practise manifestation until you can describe what they do in terms they would accept.

This chapter is a plan for that. It is deliberately concrete, because the difference between a description and a polemic is usually a matter of method, and method can be written down.

· · ·

Why this is not optional

Three reasons, in ascending order of importance.

Because you will get the facts wrong otherwise. The manifest space is not one thing. It has at least four live variants (theistic, mentalist, energetic, psychologized), a dozen media formats, and a vocabulary that shifts every eighteen months. A person who has read The Secret knows one variant, from 2006, and will be speaking to people who have never heard of it.

Because contempt is epistemically fatal. The moment you decide the person in front of you is a fool, you stop being able to learn from her, and she stops telling you the truth. This is not a counsel of niceness; it is a condition of accurate knowledge.

Because the description is itself a form of respect, and respect is the first thing the Church owes. The person who has been manifesting for six years has been trying to make her life bearable. She has been doing something wrong. She has not been doing nothing. A description that can hold both of those facts is the only kind that can be used.

· · ·

Who to talk to

Not a random sample; a strategic one. Six groups, roughly ten to fifteen people each.

  1. Practitioners who are thriving. Not the ones in crisis. The ones for whom it is working, who have a practice and a community and a vocabulary. They will tell you what the system looks like from the inside when it is at its best, which is the version you have to answer.
  2. Practitioners who are frightened. The ones who have begun to suspect that it is harming them, or who are scrupulous about their thoughts, or who have been told that their illness is their fault. They will tell you the cost.
  3. Defectors. People who left. They will tell you what broke, and — this is the valuable part — what they miss.
  4. Catholic hybridizers. People who do both. They are the largest group and the least studied, and they are the actual pastoral situation. They are not confused; they have a working arrangement, and the arrangement is what you have to understand.
  5. Clergy and catechists. What they are asked, what they answer, what they avoid.
  6. The young. Under twenty-five, because the vocabulary is theirs and it is already mutating away from the books.
· · ·

What to ask

Six questions, in this order. Do not ask about beliefs first; ask about practice. Beliefs are reconstructed after the fact, and people are unreliable about them.

  1. “Walk me through what you did yesterday.” Concrete. Time, place, object, words.
  2. “When did you start, and what was happening in your life?” The origin is usually a crisis.
  3. “What has it done for you?” Let them tell you the good, at length, without qualifying it.
  4. “What has it cost you?” Ask this later, not earlier, and only after the first three.
  5. “What would you do if it stopped working?” The diagnostic from chapter 32, applied in research.
  6. “Who knows about it?” The diagnostic from chapter 21.

And one question for the Catholics: “How do you hold the two together?” The answer will be some version of compartmentalization, and the shape of the compartment is the real theological problem.

· · ·

The disciplines

Four rules for the listener, and each of them is a guard against a specific failure.

State the position in its strongest form before criticizing it. Write the steel man down. Read it to a practitioner and ask: “Is that fair?” If she says no, rewrite it. Do not proceed to the critique until she says yes.

Do not correct during the interview. Not once. Note the error, and keep listening. The correction can come in the book, in the sermon, in the conversation six months later. If you correct in the interview, you will get compliance and lose the data.

Record the good. The temptation is to collect harms, because harms make the case. But a description that contains only harms is not a description; it is an indictment, and it will be recognized as one by the people it is about.

Say what you do not know. In writing. The manifest space is full of confident claims; the answer to a confident claim is not another confident claim. It is a description with its limits marked, which is what the best scholarship does and what most polemic does not.

· · ·

The six-month plan

Months 1–2: reading. The primary texts, not the secondary. The Secret; Neville’s Feeling Is the Secret and The Power of Awareness; a Hicks book, for the metaphysics; one contemporary popularizer (Nafousi or equivalent) for the current idiom; two or three of the Catholic-adjacent titles, because they are the actual competition. Plus the 2003 Pontifical Council document, which is the best official description available in any language.

Months 2–4: interviews. Sixty to eighty conversations, in the six groups above. A written protocol, so the data are comparable. An ethics of consent: no names, no identifying details, no recording without permission, and an agreement to show each person the paragraph in which she appears.

Months 3–5: the content audit. A coded sample of the top few hundred items of manifestation media by reach: what claims are made, in what order, with what proof, with what call to action. Code by the seven-point grammar from chapter 2, and note where the grammar has mutated.

Month 6: the description. A hundred pages, written in ordinary prose, with the practitioner’s own words in it, and a final chapter on what the Church has that the manifest space lacks. Circulate it to critics on both sides before publication. Publish it even if it is unflattering to your own position.

· · ·

What the description will probably find

Three predictions, offered so that they can be falsified.

First, that the manifest space is much less metaphysical than its critics think. Most practitioners do not hold a cosmology. They hold a practice, a hope, and a phrase. The cosmology lives in the books and the coaches, and it is absorbed by a minority.

Second, that the harms are concentrated in two places: the sick and the scrupulous. The healthy practitioner with a journal and a job is, in most cases, doing something harmless that could be baptized in an afternoon. The person who has been told that her cancer is her fault is in a different situation entirely, and the difference is not one of degree.

Third, that the Catholic hybridizers are the largest and most neglected group, and that they are not confused. They have made a working peace between two systems, and the peace is unstable, and they know it. They are waiting for someone to explain the difference, and the explanation they have received so far has been either a prohibition or a shrug.

If those three predictions hold, the strategy of this book holds with them: describe, distinguish, refuse, replace, and institutionalize. If they fail — if, say, the cosmology turns out to be widely and explicitly held — then the audit needs to move earlier in the process and the catechesis needs to be more basic than this book assumes.

Which is why the listening comes first. A plan that cannot be corrected by the data is not a plan; it is a position.

The point

The first institutional act is description: the Moerbeke work of reading the thing closely enough to state it in terms its practitioners accept.

Do this

Interview one practitioner this month, and do not correct anything during the interview.

What this sets up

Which produces a body of work, if the genre is right.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 34

The Disputed Questions

The quaestio is the most portable intellectual technology the Church ever invented: a form that forces charity on the author and gives the reader a verdict they can test. It is also perfect for short-form video.

If this book were to leave behind a single artefact, I would want it to be this one: not a treatise, but a body of quaestiones disputatae — disputed questions — on the manifest space.

The form is medieval and it is almost absurdly well-suited to the present moment. A question is posed. The strongest objections are stated, in the objector’s own voice, and answered on their merits. A contrary authority is cited. Then the master gives his determination, and replies to each objection in turn.

It is a machine for intellectual honesty. It makes the author state the opposing case well enough that the opponent could recognize it. It makes the reader able to check the reasoning at every step. And it produces a short, self-contained unit with a clear question and a clear answer — which is, incidentally, exactly the shape of a good three-minute video.

· · ·

The anatomy

Every question has seven parts, and each part has a job.

1. The question. Stated as a yes/no proposition: Whether the imagination creates reality. Not “thoughts on manifestation.” A determinate question forces a determinate answer.

2. The objections. Three or four, in the strongest form, each with an authority or an argument attached. They begin videtur quod — “it seems that…” This is the part that most contemporary writing omits, and its omission is the reason so much of it is useless.

3. The contrary authority. Sed contra. A scriptural verse, a conciliar text, a line from a doctor of the Church. Not a proof; a signpost that the tradition has something to say.

4. The determination. Respondeo dicendum quod. The master’s answer, with the distinctions that make it work. This is where the real work happens, and it is where the reader finds out whether the author has anything to say.

5. The replies. One for each objection. Each reply either denies a premise, distinguishes a term, or concedes the point and limits it. A reply that merely restates the determination is not a reply.

6. The practice. Not medieval, but necessary for this audience: a short paragraph on what to do differently.

7. The further questions. Two or three links to related questions, so that the body of work becomes a network rather than a list.

· · ·

Why the form works now

It is honest by construction. You cannot write a good quaestio and cheat, because the objections are printed above your answer in the objector’s own words, and the reader sees whether you have answered them or merely survived them.

It is short. Fifteen hundred words, or three minutes of video. It fits the medium without being deformed by it.

It is catechetical without being a lecture. Each question teaches a doctrine by using it. A person who reads forty of them will have learned the whole shape of the faith — creation, grace, providence, sacrament, eschatology — without ever being handed a syllabus.

It is disputable. The determination can be argued with. The replies can be contested. This is the opposite of the manifest space’s sealed epistemology, and the contrast is itself an argument.

It is cumulative. Forty questions, cross-referenced, make a Summa in fragments — and fragments are how people actually read now.

· · ·

The forty questions

A proposed body of work. Each would be developed at length; several are foreshortened in this book.

On God and the universe

  1. Whether the universe can hear.
  2. Whether the universe is God.
  3. Whether God is an energy.
  4. Whether God can be manipulated by technique.
  5. Whether God wants you to be rich.
  6. Whether God’s will can be known from signs.

On creation and the person

  1. Whether the world is a projection of consciousness.
  2. Whether you create your reality.
  3. Whether you are God.
  4. Whether the self is an illusion.
  5. Whether everyone is you pushed out.
  6. Whether human beings have a “higher self.”
  7. Whether the body is a message from the mind.

On desire

  1. Whether desire is a reliable guide.
  2. Whether it is wrong to want things.
  3. Whether detachment is a technique.
  4. Whether you can want something too much.
  5. Whether God gives us the desires of our hearts.

On thought and speech

  1. Whether the imagination creates reality.
  2. Whether thoughts are things.
  3. Whether words have power over events.
  4. Whether affirmations work.
  5. Whether it is wrong to speak of a desired outcome as though it had happened.
  6. Whether the name of Jesus can be used as a technique.

On suffering

  1. Whether illness is attracted by the sufferer.
  2. Whether suffering is a lesson.
  3. Whether we choose our trials before birth.
  4. Whether it is wrong to want to be healed.
  5. Whether grief can be manifested away.

On time and memory

  1. Whether the past can be revised.
  2. Whether the future can be known.
  3. Whether the dead can be consulted.
  4. Whether 11:11 means anything.

On the Church

  1. Whether a Catholic may practise manifestation.
  2. Whether manifestation is a form of divination.
  3. Whether a priest should refuse absolution to a manifesting penitent.
  4. Whether a Catholic may sell manifestation coaching.
  5. Whether the saints can be “manifested.”
  6. Whether the Church has its own manifestation practices.
  7. Whether this whole project is a mistake.

Question 40 is not a joke. Any body of disputed questions that does not include the strongest argument against itself is not a disputation; it is propaganda with footnotes.

· · ·

How to build it

Write the objections first. Not the answer. The answer will be better if it has been forced to reckon with a well-stated objection, and the objection is the harder half.

Use the objector’s vocabulary. Not “the New Age teaches that…” but a quotation, with a citation, from a text that a practitioner would recognize as her own.

Keep the determination short. Three paragraphs. If it needs ten, the question is really three questions and should be split.

Publish in public, one at a time, over three years. One a month. Each one is a video, a page, a podcast segment, a bulletin insert. Each one can be argued with in the comments, which is where the next revision comes from.

Let others write them. The body of questions should not be the work of one person; a Summa with one author is a system, and a system is exactly what the manifest space is. The form should be open to anyone who will state the objections fairly, and the best answers should be selected by argument, not by platform.

· · ·

The reason this matters more than the book

Books are read once, by a few thousand people, and then they sit. A body of disputed questions is a toolkit: it can be excerpted, translated, adapted, argued with, taught from, made into video, put in a bulletin, handed to a catechist, and used by someone who has never heard of this book.

And it has a property that no treatise has: it can be added to. Forty questions can become a hundred. A hundred can become the ordinary reference work for a generation of pastors. The manifest space will mutate; the questions can mutate with it, because the form is a method and not a monument.

That is what Thomas actually left behind, and it is the thing worth imitating: not the conclusions, but the machine for arriving at them in public.

The point

The disputed question is honest by construction: the objections are printed above the answer, so the reader can see whether the answer survives them.

Do this

Write the strongest objection to your own position, in the objector’s voice, and read it to someone who agrees with her.

What this sets up

Ideas do not survive on their merits; they survive in institutions.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 35

Institutions, or Why a Sermon Needs a Building

Ideas do not survive on their merits. They survive in institutions — and the manifest space has better ones than we do. Seven institutions the Church would need to build, and the governance that keeps them honest.

Thomas’s Summa survived because of the Dominican order, the University of Paris, and a century of teachers who used it. The idea was excellent; the institution is what made it last.

This is the least romantic chapter in the book and possibly the most important. Everything in Parts One to Four can be true and still evaporate, because truth does not reproduce itself. It is transmitted by people, in institutions, over generations, and the manifest space understands this better than the Church currently does. It has publishers, platforms, coaching certifications, conferences, apps, and — above all — a delivery system that puts a thirty-second practice in front of a lonely person at eleven at night.

The Church has parishes. They are, potentially, the most powerful delivery system in the world. At present, in most places, they are not being used for this.

· · ·

1. A centre

Not a bureaucracy: a small research centre, attached to a university or a diocese, with three or four people and a library. Its job is to do the listening (chapter 33), maintain the description, and answer enquiries from bishops, seminary rectors, and journalists.

The model is the small institute rather than the large faculty: a place where two or three people who know the material can be found by the people who need it. The cost is the cost of three salaries and a room. The alternative is that every diocese improvises, badly, and that the same questions are answered from scratch two hundred times a year.

2. A journal, or a standing section

The scholarly infrastructure matters less for scholars than for legitimacy. A body of work with peer review, footnotes, and a place to publish corrections is a body of work that can be argued with. A body of work that exists only in podcasts cannot be corrected, and will drift.

If a new journal is not feasible, a standing section in an existing one — Nova et Vetera, Communio, The Thomist, a diocesan theological review — would do. The point is not the masthead. The point is a place where a claim can be tested in public and where a correction is possible.

3. A formation module

Two audiences, two products.

For seminarians and clergy: a single-semester module, taught from the disputed questions, covering the phenomenon, the four tests, the triage, and the practice. The outcome is not expertise; it is the capacity to answer the question in the car park without doing harm. Every seminary could have this within two years if someone wrote the syllabus.

For laypeople: a short course — six sessions — for parishes, campus ministries, and parents. The outcome is the same, at a lower level, plus the practices from Part Four. This is the product that scales, and it should be free.

4. A publisher, and a free library

The manifest space is free at the point of use, and the response must be too. This is not a funding strategy; it is a credibility strategy. A person who has been paying a coach will not trust a free pamphlet less for being free; she will trust it more.

The model: a small imprint for books, and a digital library — the disputed questions, the lexicon, the practices, the triage card, the homilies — under an open licence, translated, printable, and usable offline. The whole of this book is a proof of concept: it can be built in a repository and given away.

5. A community

This is the hardest and the most necessary. Institutions outlast programmes; charisms outlast institutions. If this work is to survive fifty years, it needs people whose vocation it is — a religious community, a secular institute, or an ecclesial movement with this charism at its heart.

The precedent is the Divine Mercy devotion, which survived a nineteen-year suppression because the Marians kept it alive, and the liturgical movement, which was carried by abbeys. A body of writing without a body of people is a library with no readers.

It is also the hardest to plan. One does not found a charism; one can only make room for one, and wait. But a bishop or a superior can do the making-room, and that is the institutional act.

6. A network of directors

The single most effective pastoral intervention described in this book is a person with a spiritual director, and the single greatest bottleneck is that there are not enough directors.

What is needed is not a certification industry — which would replicate the manifest space’s coaching market — but a network: formation for lay directors, a register that a diocese can publish, a rule of free service, and a supervision structure. The model is the Church’s own tradition of anamchara and of the lay retreat director, not the therapeutic marketplace.

7. A diocesan desk

Every diocese has a marriage tribunal, a liturgical office, and a catechetical office. Almost none has anyone whose job is to answer questions about the New Age, the occult, and popular spirituality — which are, by volume, among the most common questions the faithful actually ask.

A single person, half-time, with a phone number and a page on the diocesan website, would do more than a conference. Their tools are the triage card, the norms of 1978 and 2024, a list of exorcists and clinicians to refer to, and the humility to say “I don’t know; let me find out.”

· · ·

The governance that keeps it honest

Five rules, derived from the failures catalogued in chapter 7 and the norms of the Church.

Submit to a bishop, from the beginning. Not at the end, when the work is complete and the ask is a blessing. From the beginning, when the work can still be shaped. The norms put the local Ordinary first for a reason: the process is not a formality, and a project that cannot be supervised cannot be trusted.

Appoint a censor of books before you need one. Have every text read by someone with the authority and the independence to stop it. Publish the fact that you do.

Never sell spiritual power. Courses may be free or at cost; books may be sold; nothing that promises a spiritual effect may be priced. The negative criterion in the Church’s own norms — “evidence of a search for profit or gain” — is not a suggestion.

Publish your failures. Every pilot that did not work, every practice that did not land, every prediction from chapter 33 that turned out false. The manifest space’s epistemology is unfalsifiable; the response must be conspicuously falsifiable, and the only way to demonstrate that is to be seen being corrected.

Do not build a personality. The single greatest risk to a project like this is that it becomes a platform. The form should be designed so that the work can continue without any particular person — which means multiple authors, open materials, and a refusal to put a face on the front of it.

· · ·

What it would cost

A centre, a journal, a course, a library, a network, and a desk: in the first five years, the cost of perhaps a dozen people and a modest budget for translation and printing. That is less than a single mid-sized parish plant.

The return, if it works, is not measurable in the ordinary way. It is the difference between a generation that has a practice of prayer and a generation that has a practice.

· · ·

The manifest space did not win because it was true. It won because it was available: on the phone, at night, for free, in a form a lonely person could follow. The Church’s answer will not be a better argument. It will be a better availability — a place to go, a person to ask, a practice to do, a book that is free, and a community that will not charge for hope.

That is an institutional problem, and it has institutional solutions. The good news is that the institution already exists. The bad news is that it is not, at present, pointed at this.

Pointing it is the work of a generation. The next chapter is about how we would know whether it was working.

The point

A centre, a journal, a formation module, a free library, a community, a network of directors, and a diocesan desk — with five rules of governance.

Do this

Name the one institution you could actually influence in the next two years, and write down how.

What this sets up

And how would we know whether any of it was working?

Chapter 36

Measuring Fruit

The Church has criteria for judging a spiritual movement, and they are better than the metrics of the market. This chapter turns them into an instrument.

A movement that cannot be evaluated will be evaluated by its marketing. The manifest space evaluates itself by testimonials; the response must do better, or it will be indistinguishable in kind.

The good news is that the Church already has criteria. They are in the 1978 norms for the discernment of presumed revelations, retained in the 2024 revision, and they are remarkably well designed for the purpose.

· · ·

The Church’s criteria

The norms list, among the positive criteria:

  • Moral certitude about the facts — did this actually happen as described?
  • The qualities of the recipient — psychological balance, honesty, moral rectitude, docility to authority.
  • The soundness of the doctrine — is what is being taught true?
  • “Healthy devotion and abundant and constant spiritual fruit (for example, spirit of prayer, conversion, testimonies of charity).”

And among the negative:

  • Manifest error about the facts.
  • Doctrinal error.
  • Evidence of a search for profit or gain.
  • Grave immorality in the principals.
  • Psychological disorder.

Note the shape. Two of the criteria are about truth, one is about the person, one is about money, and one — the most important for our purposes — is about fruit: prayer, conversion, charity. The Church’s test of a spiritual movement is not whether it produces experiences. It is whether it produces holiness.

· · ·

What to measure

Translate the criteria into instruments that can be used in a parish pilot. Four primary measures and three safety measures.

Primary

  1. Spirit of prayer. Not “does she pray more” in the abstract, but: does she have a daily practice, does she keep it, and does she describe it as a relationship rather than a technique? A three-question instrument, self-reported, plus a one-month follow-up.
  2. Conversion. Has anything changed in her moral life? Specifically: has she been to confession, reconciled with anyone, changed a behaviour she had not been able to change? Behavioural indicators, not feelings.
  3. Charity. What has she done for someone else in the last month, concretely? Hours, acts, money. The Catechism’s “testimonies of charity” is not a metaphor; it can be counted.
  4. Freedom. This is the one that matters most and is hardest to measure. Does she feel able to stop the practice? Does she describe her relationship to God as trust or as performance? Does she report less fear, or more?

Safety

  1. Scrupulosity. A validated scale, or a simple set of questions about intrusive thoughts and confession frequency. The manifest space manufactures this; a Catholic practice should reduce it.
  2. Blame of the sick. Questions about how the person would explain an illness in someone she loves. A practice that increases this has failed regardless of its other results.
  3. Dependence on a guide. Does she need the programme, the director, or the author to keep praying? The test of a good formation is that it makes itself unnecessary.
· · ·

How to measure without scientism

Two errors to avoid, and they are symmetrical.

The first is the substitution of metrics for judgement. A pilot can show that attendance rose and scrupulosity fell and still be a spiritual failure, because the thing that matters — holiness — is not a number. The numbers are diagnostic, not definitive. They tell you where to look; they do not tell you what you are looking at.

The second is the refusal to measure at all. “The fruit will show itself” is true and is often an excuse. The manifest space says the same thing about its own results. A tradition confident enough to be tested should be willing to be tested.

The resolution is the one the Church has always used in the discernment of spirits: the mixed method. Numbers, plus the judgement of wise people, plus time, plus the test of the cross. A practice that produces measurable growth in prayer and charity, is judged sound by directors who are not invested in it, survives a decade, and helps people suffer well, is a practice that can be recommended. A practice that produces excitement and dependence, is judged sound only by its promoters, and collapses when the results do not arrive, is not.

· · ·

The pilot design

A single parish, thirty participants, twelve weeks.

Week 0. Baseline: the four primary measures, the three safety measures, and one open question — “describe your current practice of prayer.”

Weeks 1–4. The Novena of Desire (chapter 31), with a weekly group meeting of forty-five minutes.

Weeks 5–8. The transpositions, one per week: word and image, time and body, memory and desire, signs and guidance. Each with a written instruction sheet.

Weeks 9–12. A rule of life: each participant writes a personal rule of three practices, and lives it.

Week 12. Repeat the measures, plus a qualitative interview with each participant, plus a follow-up at six months.

The comparison group. A second parish that receives the same amount of attention — a weekly meeting, a course on prayer — without the manifest-space content. This is the control that most parish programmes omit, and without it you cannot tell whether the effect was the content, the community, or the attention.

The null result. Publish it. If the course makes no difference, that is data, and it is the kind of data that the manifest space never produces.

· · ·

The instrument

A one-page questionnaire, ten items, scored simply. Draft:

  1. In the last week, how many days did you pray in a set form (a psalm, the Rosary, the Jesus Prayer, the Hours)?
  2. In the last month, have you been to confession? (Y/N, and whether you would have gone otherwise)
  3. In the last month, have you done something concrete for someone else that cost you time or money? (describe)
  4. Do you feel able to stop your practice for a week without anxiety? (always / sometimes / never)
  5. Do intrusive thoughts frighten you because they might “cause” something? (never / sometimes / often)
  6. If someone you loved became seriously ill, would you wonder what they had done to attract it? (never / sometimes / often)
  7. Do you pray because you want to, or because you are afraid of what happens if you don’t? (want / both / afraid)
  8. Has your picture of God changed in the last twelve weeks? (describe in one sentence)
  9. Do you have someone you can talk to about your prayer? (Y/N, who)
  10. What would you say to a friend who asked you whether to manifest? (two sentences)

Items 5, 6, and 7 are the safety measures. Items 1, 3, 4, and 9 are the fruit measures. Item 10 is the test of whether the formation has become portable — the only reliable sign that a person has actually learned something.

· · ·

The theological criterion

There is one measure that cannot go on the instrument and must not be omitted from the judgement: holiness.

Holiness is not measurable, and it is discernible. It shows up as a person who is more free, more loving, more patient, more truthful, less impressed by herself, and less afraid of death. It is recognized by the people who live with her, and it is recognized slowly, over years.

The Church’s entire method of canonization is built on this: not on a single miracle, but on a life, a reputation, a body of testimony, and a long examination. That is the model for evaluating this work. Not a launch, not a conference, not a bestseller — a life, over time, examined by people with the authority and the independence to say no.

The manifest space will be judged by its testimonials. The response will be judged by its saints. That is not a fair fight either, but it is the one that matters.

The point

The Church’s criteria — prayer, conversion, charity, freedom — are better than the market’s, and they can be measured without turning holiness into a number.

Do this

Run the ten-item instrument on yourself, honestly, and keep the score somewhere you will find it in a year.

What this sets up

Which leaves the timescale, and the expectation of failure.
