Chapter 37

The Fifty-Year Horizon

Five phases, five scenarios, and the discipline of expecting to be condemned. What success would actually look like in 2076 — and why it will not look like a movement.

Every plan in the Church is either short-term or dishonest. The pastoral problem is immediate; the formation that would solve it takes a generation; and the institution that would carry the formation takes two.

So this chapter is written on a fifty-year horizon, and it is written with the expectation that the reader will not live to see the end of it. That is not pessimism. It is the ordinary timescale of the things that last.

· · ·

The phases

Years 0–2: listening and description. The audit of chapter 33. Sixty to eighty conversations, a content survey, a hundred-page description, published and circulated for criticism. No proposals, no campaigns. The output is a map.

Years 2–5: the disputed questions. Forty questions, written by several hands, published one a month, argued with in public. The output is a body of work that can be corrected.

Years 5–10: the first institutions. A centre, a formation module in three or four seminaries, a free digital library, a pilot in ten parishes with a control group, and the first published results — including the null ones.

Years 10–25: formation. The slow penetration of the material into seminary curricula, lay formation, campus ministry, and the ordinary preaching of a few hundred priests. This is the phase in which the work either becomes part of the furniture or dies, and its success is measured in the number of people who can answer the car-park question without having read this book.

Years 25–50: reception. A generation of Catholics for whom providence, petition, discernment, and the manifestation of conscience are ordinary. A body of practice that is simply there, the way the Rosary is there. And, at some point in this phase, a magisterial document that treats the whole question as settled — which will be the signal that the work is finished and can be forgotten.

· · ·

The five scenarios

1. Ignored. The most likely outcome for any given book, and the least harmful. The material sits in libraries; a few people use it; the phenomenon mutates and outlives it. The cost is that the pastoral problem is met by improvisation for another generation.

2. Condemned. The 1277 scenario, and the 1959 scenario, and the ordinary fate of anything that uses the enemy’s vocabulary before the guardians can see the difference between use and surrender. What will be condemned is not the theology but the permission: some sentence will be read as saying that a Catholic may practise the law of attraction, and it will be on a list within a year. This is survivable, and it was survived before. The rules are in chapter 7: stay inside, publish the method, do not monetize, do not build a personality.

3. Co-opted by the market. The most likely outcome in a culture like ours, and the most damaging. “Catholic manifestation” becomes a genre: journals, courses, retreats, certifications, a subscription. The theology is thinned to a mood, the metaphysics survives under the aesthetics, and the whole thing becomes the thing it was supposed to answer. The tell will be a price list and a promise.

4. Partially received. The most likely good outcome. Some of it enters the ordinary life of the Church — the examen, the novena, the discernment of spirits, the triage — and some of it is forgotten. The manifest space fades, not because it was refuted but because its practices were replaced. This is what usually happens, and it is enough.

5. Absorbed. A synod, a dicastery, a vademecum: the material becomes the Church’s own, is corrected in the process, and is taught to people who have never heard of this book. This is the best outcome, and it takes the longest, and it requires that the work be given away rather than owned.

· · ·

Expecting the condemnation

If this work is ever noticed, it will be opposed, and the opposition will come from three places.

From the guardians of orthodoxy, who will be right about some of the borrowings and wrong about the method, and who will not be able to tell the difference in the first decade. The response is not to argue in public; it is to submit in private, answer questions in writing, and wait.

From the market, which will find the whole thing unprofitable, and will say so in the language of realism: nobody wants doctrine, people want results. The response is to keep the results modest and the doctrine free.

From the academy, which will find the work insufficiently rigorous and the phenomenon insufficiently serious. The response is to publish the footnotes and to be corrected.

What is not on the list is persecution, and it is worth saying so. Nobody in this scenario is going to be martyred. The worst that happens to the author of a book like this in a wealthy country is that he is ignored, or mildly censured, or invited onto a panel to be condescended to. That is not suffering; it is admin. The people who will actually suffer in this story are the ones the manifest space is already hurting, and they are the reason the work is worth doing.

· · ·

What success looks like in 2076

Not a movement. A movement would be a failure, because a movement is a thing that can be joined, marketed, and dissolved.

Success looks like this: a young woman in a parish in 2076 has a question about her life, and the first thing she does is pray, and the second thing she does is ask someone, and the third thing she does is write it down. She has never heard of the law of attraction, or if she has, it is like hearing about phrenology — a curiosity from her grandmother’s time. She knows the psalms. She has a director. She goes to confession. When her mother is dying, she does not wonder what her mother did to cause it. When her own prayer is unanswered, she is angry, and she says so, and she keeps praying.

That is not a triumph. It is the ordinary life of the Church, which is the only thing this book has ever been trying to restore.

· · ·

The eschatological reserve

There is a reason to end this part with a limit rather than a plan.

“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Cor 3:6). The work of the Church is not a project with a deliverable; it is a planting, and the growth is not ours, and the harvest is not in our lifetime. This is not an excuse for idleness; Paul planted with great energy. It is a correction of the fantasy that the outcome depends on us — the same fantasy, in its ecclesiastical form, that the manifest space holds in its personal form.

Which means the honest posture for anyone who takes this up is the one Thomas had at the end: to do the work as well as possible, to submit it, to hand it on, and to be prepared to discover that it was straw.

The book you are holding will be obsolete within twenty years. The phenomenon will have mutated; the vocabulary will have moved; the practices will need to be rebuilt. That is not a failure. It is what it means for a work to be alive: it is corrigible. The alternative is a monument, and monuments are what happened to Thomas after six hundred years, and it took a pope to rescue him.

So: plant. Water. Publish the failures. Submit to the bishop. Give it away. And leave the growth to the one whose it is.

The point

Expect to be ignored, condemned, co-opted, partially received, or absorbed — in that order of likelihood — and plan for fifty years.

Do this

Decide what you will do in the first two years, and what you will refuse to do at any point.

What this sets up

And now the objections, beginning with the ones from our own side.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Part Six

Contested Questions

The one who states his case first seems right, until the other comes and examines him.

Proverbs 18:17

A book that has argued this hard owes its reader the strongest case against itself.

The objections come from two directions, and they are not symmetric. From the tradition comes the charge that the whole project is a concession dressed as a critique — that to speak of baptizing the manifest space is to admit that the Church has lost the argument and is now negotiating terms. From the manifest space comes the charge that the critique is a category error — that it judges a practice by the standards of a metaphysics the practice never claimed, and that the people who practice it have already made their peace with the fact that it is a technique and not a religion.

Both charges are serious. Neither can be answered by a paragraph. The next two chapters take them one at a time, in the voice of the people who make them, and answer as well as the case allows. Where an objection cannot be fully answered, the book says so, because a reader who is told that every question has been settled has been told something false about the subject and something false about books.

Chapter 38

Objections from the Tradition

Seven objections from within the Church, each of which has real force, and none of which survives the distinction between use and surrender.

The most serious objections to a project like this do not come from the manifest space. They come from the tradition, and they come from people who have reason to be suspicious, and they deserve to be answered carefully.

· · ·

1. “This is syncretism.”

The objection. You are proposing to baptize a system whose metaphysics denies creation. That is exactly what syncretism is: the retention of a foreign framework under a Christian name.

The answer. It would be, if the proposal were to retain the framework. The whole audit in Part Two is designed to do the opposite: seven of the fourteen claims are rejected outright, and the three “correct” verdicts are corrections of causality, not adjustments of vocabulary. What is being received is a set of observations about attention, habit, imagination, and speech that the tradition already holds — and holding them is not syncretism, it is recovery. The test of whether syncretism has occurred is not whether the vocabulary overlaps. It is whether, when the two conflict, the faith yields. In every transposition proposed in Part Four, the faith governs and the practice is reconceived.

That said, the objection names a real danger, and the danger is not theoretical: the “Catholic manifestation” genre already exists, and much of it is syncretistic. This book’s disagreement with that genre is the subject of chapter 39’s fifth objection.

2. “Why not simply preach the Gospel?”

The objection. The Church does not need a theory about manifestation. She needs to preach Christ crucified. Everything else is a distraction dressed as relevance.

The answer. Agreed, and the book is an attempt to do exactly that — the whole of Part Three is an exposition of Scripture, and the practices in Part Four are the Church’s own. But “preach the Gospel” is not a strategy; it is a description of the goal. The question is what the preaching is about when the person in front of you believes that her thoughts create reality. A sermon on the Incarnation that does not address the fact that the hearer believes she is a small god will be heard as one more option in a market of options.

The Gospel is preached to these people, in this culture, with these misconceptions. That is what the entire missionary tradition has always done — Paul at the Areopagus, the Fathers against the Gnostics, the Jesuits in China. Preaching the Gospel has never meant preaching it in the abstract.

3. “You are giving occultism a hearing.”

The objection. By treating these practices as serious and describing them sympathetically, you legitimize them.

The answer. The opposite is more likely. The practices are already legitimate in the eyes of the people who use them, and they will remain so as long as the only Catholic response is a prohibition issued by someone who has not read them. A serious description, with clear verdicts, is more damaging to the system than a denunciation, because it takes the system’s own claims and tests them. Denunciation produces sympathy for the denounced; analysis produces doubt.

Where the objection does have force is in the tone: a description that is too admiring, or that lingers on the beauty of the thing, can function as an advertisement. That is a real risk in this book, and it is why the audit precedes the reclamation, and why the verdicts are stated so bluntly.

4. “The desire for relevance is the disease.”

The objection. The Church is dying of the attempt to be interesting to the world. Every generation of accommodation has produced a weaker Church. Stop trying to speak the language of the age and speak the language of the saints.

The answer. There is a real and well-documented pattern here, and it is a warning that any project of this kind should take seriously. But it is a warning against accommodation, not against translation, and the difference is the same as the difference between the two thirteenth-century options: the Averroists accommodated, and Aquinas translated. Accommodation changes the doctrine to fit the audience. Translation changes the vocabulary to carry the doctrine.

The test is simple and severe: does the work make the faith easier to believe or easier to practice? If the former, it is accommodation and should be stopped. If the latter, it may be the ordinary work of catechesis.

5. “The Fathers would have condemned this.”

The objection. The patristic tradition is ferocious about magic, divination, and theurgy. Read the penitentials, read Tertullian, read Augustine on the astrologers. There is no room for a “Catholic law of attraction.”

The answer. The Fathers condemned magic, and they were right, and this book condemns it in the same terms (CCC 2111–2117; the fourteen verdicts). What the Fathers also did, and what is less often noticed, is substitute: they replaced the pagan practice with a Christian one, at the same time and often in the same place. The feast replaced the festival; the relic replaced the charm; the blessing replaced the incantation; the saint replaced the local spirit. The penitentials are full of substitutions, and the substitution is the operative pastoral strategy.

So the patristic precedent supports the method of this book, not the objection to it. What the Fathers would have condemned is a technique that promises a result and charges a fee. What they would have recognized is the replacement of one practice by a better one, in the same hungry place.

6. “You have no mandate.”

The objection. You are not a bishop, not a theologian with a chair, not a canonized saint. Why should anyone listen?

The answer. No reason at all, except that the argument can be tested. This is why the book publishes its method, its sources, its verdicts, and its failures; why it repeatedly tells the reader to submit it to an authority; and why its most ambitious proposal is that the work be taken out of the author’s hands. A layman writing about the faith is not a novelty in the Church; it is the normal condition of most of her intellectual life. What would be illegitimate is a claim to authority, and none is made.

7. “The Church has its own problems. Fix those first.”

The objection. You are devoting a book to a popular spirituality while the Church is in crisis — abuse, division, collapsing practice, credibility in ruins. This is a distraction from the real work.

The answer. The objection is right about the priority, and wrong about the exclusivity.

It is right that no program of this kind will be credible while the Church’s own house is disordered, and that the reform of the Church is the first work. A people who have been betrayed by their shepherds will not be persuaded by a treatise on providence. That is not a reason to write the treatise; it is a reason to be honest about its limits.

It is wrong that the two are alternatives. The person who has been hurt by the Church and the person who has been hurt by the manifest space are often the same person, and what she needs is not a choice between two systems but a community that is actually what it claims to be. The best argument against the law of attraction is a parish that prays and tells the truth. Everything in this book is a description of what that parish would teach.

· · ·

There is a pattern in these seven objections, and it is worth naming, because it applies far beyond this book.

Each of them is true in its warning and false in its conclusion. Syncretism is a real danger; therefore do not attempt the work. Relevance-seeking is a real disease; therefore do not translate. The Fathers condemned magic; therefore do not distinguish. The Church is in crisis; therefore do not think about anything else.

That structure — a true premise, a non-sequitur, and a counsel of inaction — is the ordinary form of the argument that keeps an institution from doing the thing it most needs to do. The answer to it is not to deny the premise. It is to accept the warning, build the safeguards, and do the work anyway, in the open, where it can be corrected.

The point

Each objection from the tradition is true in its warning and false in its conclusion: a real danger, a non sequitur, and a counsel of inaction.

Do this

Pick the objection that stings most, and answer it in writing, in private, before you answer it in public.

What this sets up

The objections from the other side are sharper.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 39

Objections from the Manifest Space

Seven objections from the other side — including the two that are genuinely hard: that prayer is just manifestation with extra steps, and that the mystics said the same thing.

A book that only answers its friends is a pamphlet. The objections from the manifest space are, in several cases, sharper than the objections from the Church, and two of them require real work.

· · ·

1. “You’re limiting God.”

The objection. You say that we cannot compel outcomes. But Jesus said, “Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours” (Mark 11:24). You are putting a hedge around a promise that God did not hedge.

The answer. The verse is real, and the Church has never explained it away. She has, however, read it in the context of everything else Jesus says about prayer, and that context includes three things that the manifest space omits.

First, the same Jesus prays “not as I will, but as you will” (Matt 26:39) — and he is the only person in history whose prayer was perfectly aligned. Second, James explains why some prayers are not answered: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions” (James 4:3). Third, the Church’s whole doctrine of impetration assumes that the promise is made to prayer in the name of Jesus, which means prayer according to his will and his character, not a formula attached to a desire.

So the hedge is not mine. It is in the text, and it is there because the alternative is a God who is not free, which is to say, not God. A promise without a condition would make prayer into a mechanism and God into a function of the petitioner. The Church limits God in exactly one respect: she refuses to make him limited by us.

2. “The Church is a controlling institution.”

The objection. You are asking people to hand their interior lives to a hierarchy that has abused children, silenced victims, and told the sick that their suffering is God’s will. Why would anyone trade a practice that belongs to them for an institution that has proved it cannot be trusted?

The answer. There is no clever reply to this, and the attempt to give one would be obscene. The abuse is real, the cover-up is real, and the loss of credibility is a just consequence.

What can be said is this: the alternative on offer is not freedom. The manifest space has its own authorities — coaches, influencers, platforms, and an algorithm that decides what a lonely person sees at 2 a.m. — and they are unaccountable in a way that the Church, at its worst, has never quite managed, because the Church at least has a law, a court, a public record, and a long tradition of being criticized from within. The choice is not between an institution and no institution. It is between an institution that can be held to account and a market that cannot.

And the deepest point: the Church’s authority is not her own. She claims to forgive sins in Christ’s name, not her own; to teach what she has received, not what she has invented. When she acts as though the authority were hers, she becomes exactly what her critics say she is. The remedy is not to abandon the authority but to purify its exercise — which is what reform is, and which is why the reform of the Church and the answer to the manifest space are the same work.

3. “Prayer is just manifestation with extra steps.”

The objection. This is the hard one. Strip away the theology and you have two practices: an interior act of desire, repeated, with an expectation of an external effect. You say the difference is the addressee. But an addressee you cannot see, hear, or verify is functionally indistinguishable from a law with a personality.

The answer. The objection is strongest when it is made against bad Catholic preaching, and there is a great deal of bad Catholic preaching that is functionally a law of attraction with a beard: name the promise, claim the verse, expect the result, and if the result does not come, you did not believe enough. The Word of Faith movement is not a Protestant eccentricity; it is the same structure, and it exists in Catholic devotional practice too.

But the difference between prayer and manifestation is not the addressee. It is the shape of the act.

A manifestation is an act that treats the outcome as the point. Its success condition is the result, and its failure condition is the absence of the result. A prayer is an act whose point is the relationship, and whose success condition is fidelity — which is why the Church can say that a prayer was heard and refused, and mean both.

You can test which one a person is doing by asking what happens when the result does not come. The technique has no resources; it can only re-describe the failure. The prayer has resources, because the relationship survives the refusal — indeed, the refusal is where the relationship is most itself. That difference is not visible from outside, which is why the objection has force. It is entirely visible from inside, which is why people who have prayed through a refusal do not make this objection.

4. “You’ve never tried it.”

The objection. You write about manifestation as a critic who has read the books. Anyone who has actually practised it knows that something happens that your categories cannot explain.

The answer. Partly true, and it is the reason chapter 4 exists. I have taken the practice seriously enough to say that it works in a limited and real sense: attention, expectation, rehearsal, and gratitude all change a person, and a changed person changes her circumstances. What I deny is the mechanism, and I deny it on the grounds that a better mechanism — habit, action, relationship, providence — explains the same data without the cost.

The cost, moreover, is not hypothetical, and it is not paid by the critic. It is paid by the woman who believes she caused her mother’s cancer. If the practice’s only defence is that it works for the healthy, it has already lost the argument.

5. “The mystics said the same thing.”

The objection. This is the second hard one. Meister Eckhart, the author of the Cloud of Unknowing, the Sufi poets, the Upanishads — they all speak of the identity of the self with the divine, of creation by consciousness, of the world as appearance. Your “orthodox” position is a Latin administrative narrowing of a much wilder tradition.

The answer. There are real and striking parallels, and any honest account has to grant them. The tradition of apophatic mysticism does speak of the ground of the soul, of union, of the dissolution of the separate self, of a world that is not what it seems. The manifest space drew on Neoplatonism, and Neoplatonism is in the Church’s bloodstream.

Three distinctions, however, do the work.

First, direction. The mystic’s dissolution of the self is kenotic: the self is emptied, and the emptying is a death, and it is accomplished by grace and not by technique. The manifest space’s expansion of the self is imperial: the self is enlarged until it is coextensive with reality, and the enlargement is accomplished by a method. “I am God” said by a man who has been annihilated by love is a different sentence from “I am God” said by a woman with a journal, even when the words are the same.

Second, Christology. The Christian mystics are, without exception, Christological. Eckhart’s ground of the soul is not a generic cosmic self; it is the place where the Word is born. The Cloud is a treatise on love of God in Christ, not on the divinity of the practitioner. When the manifest space quotes the mystics, it quotes the sentences about union and omits the sentences about the Cross, and the omission is the whole difference.

Third, verification. The Church tested her mystics. Eckhart was investigated; some of his propositions were censured. John of the Cross was imprisoned by his own order. The discernment was not a formality: it was the mechanism by which the tradition distinguished genuine union from spiritual inflation. The manifest space has no such mechanism, which is why it cannot tell the difference between a saint and a salesperson — and neither can the person reading at 2 a.m.

6. “It works for me.”

The objection. I am not interested in your metaphysics. I started doing this at the worst time of my life, and my life is better now. Who are you to tell me it is false?

The answer. Nobody. And I am not telling you that your life is not better. I am telling you that the thing that made it better may not be the thing you think, and that the difference matters — because the belief that your interior state causes events is the same belief that will tell you, on the day something terrible happens, that you caused it.

Keep the practice. Change the explanation. That is not a demand for conversion; it is an invitation to keep the good thing you have found and lose the thing that will hurt you.

7. “You are afraid of your own power.”

The objection. The whole book is a long argument for a smaller self. You are frightened of the possibility that human beings are more than the Church has told them.

The answer. The Church’s claim about the human person is not small. She says that a human being is made in the image of God, redeemed by the blood of God, indwelt by the Spirit, destined for divinization, and raised in a body that will be like Christ’s. She says that the saints will judge angels. It is difficult to imagine a higher account of the human person, and it is the manifest space’s account that is finally small: a being whose only power is to rearrange its own projections, in a universe with no one else in it.

The difference is not the size of the self. It is whether the self is a creature. And the creature’s power is greater than the creator’s, because the creature can receive, and the creator can only invent.

· · ·

Two of these objections — that prayer is manifestation with extra steps, and that the mystics said the same thing — cannot be answered by assertion. They can only be answered by a life.

A person who prays through a refusal, and stays; a person whose union with God has made her more ordinary and less impressive; a person who has been emptied and not enlarged — that person answers both objections, and she does it without an argument, and the answer is more convincing than this chapter.

Which is, in the end, the argument of the whole book. The Church does not win this by being right. She wins it by being holy, and holiness is the one thing the manifest space cannot manufacture, because it is the one thing that is given.

The point

Two objections have real force — that prayer is manifestation with extra steps, and that the mystics said the same thing — and both are answered by a life rather than by an argument.

Do this

Answer “it works for me” with compassion the next time you hear it: keep the practice, change the explanation.

What this sets up

Which brings us back to the girl at eleven-eleven.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Chapter 40

Conclusion: The Manifestation of the Children of God

Return to the girl at eleven-eleven. What to say to her, in four sentences — and why the whole world is waiting for the thing she is actually looking for.

We began in a bedroom at 11:11 with a notebook and a girl who had been told that her thoughts could move the world, and who had begun, somewhere in the year her mother was ill, to be afraid of her own mind.

Everything in this book has been an attempt to answer her.

Not to refute her — she has not made an argument. Not to correct her — she has not made a mistake, exactly, or rather she has made the mistake that her whole culture made and handed to her in a beautiful package. But to answer the question she was actually asking when she opened the notebook, which was not how do I get what I want but is anything listening, and am I to blame.

· · ·

Here is what I would say to her, if I had an hour and she would let me. Four sentences, and then a practice.

First: you are not creating reality, and that is good news. You are cooperating in a reality you did not make, which means that the disaster is not your fault and the good thing is not your achievement and the world is not a mirror of your worst thought. The weight you have been carrying is not yours, and you can put it down.

Second: your desire is real, and it is not an instruction from the universe. It is a signpost, and signposts can be read wrongly, and the reading is what a life of prayer is for. What you want matters. It matters enough that it needs to be purified, which is a different thing from being suppressed, and much better.

Third: there is someone listening, and he can say no. That sounds like bad news and it is the best news in the world, because a someone who can say no is a someone who can love you, and a law that always says yes is a machine, and a machine cannot love you and cannot be loved and cannot forgive you, and you need to be forgiven much more than you need to be obeyed.

Fourth: what you are actually waiting for is not the thing in the notebook. It is the manifestation of the children of God — the revealing of what you are, in glory, with the wounds still in you and the body restored. The whole creation is on tiptoe for it. It is not available by technique. It has been promised by someone who keeps his promises.

And then a practice: five minutes, tonight, before you sleep. Say the name of Jesus, slowly, and then say the thing you actually want, and then say not my will but yours, and then go to sleep. Do it tomorrow. Do it badly. Do it for a month, and then come and tell someone what happened.

· · ·

Now, having said that to her, it is worth saying what the book has been saying to us.

The manifest space is not a heresy in the ordinary sense. It is a parody, and a parody is the most instructive thing there is, because it shows you the shape of the original by distorting it. Look at what it has reproduced, in a distorted form:

  • It has a doctrine of providence — the universe responds — with the person removed.
  • It has a doctrine of creation — you make your world — with the givenness removed.
  • It has a doctrine of grace — alignment, abundance, flow — with the giver removed.
  • It has a doctrine of revelation — the universe is always speaking — with the word removed.
  • It has a doctrine of sacrament — the method, the ritual, the object — with Christ removed.
  • It has a doctrine of communion — energy, connection, oneness — with the other removed.
  • It has a doctrine of glory — manifestation, abundance, the wish fulfilled — with the Cross removed.

Every one of those is a Christian doctrine with its centre cut out. That is why the system feels, to the people inside it, so familiar and so right, and why it is so hard to argue with: it is not a foreign religion. It is our religion, in a version that has had the person of God removed from it.

Which means the answer is not to build a new thing. It is to restore the centre — the person — to a structure that is already there, and to trust that when the centre is restored, the whole thing will come right, because a parody is healed by the original and not by a refutation.

· · ·

There is a temptation at the end of a book like this to make a large claim for it. I will make a small one.

If a reader puts this book down and does three things, it will have done its work. If she learns one short prayer and says it at a fixed time every day. If she finds one person to whom she can manifest her conscience — a confessor, a director, a friend who is wise. If she keeps one honest record of her petitions and God’s answers, including the refusals.

Three things: a practice, a witness, a record. They are not impressive. They are what the Church has always given to a person who asks how to begin, and they are enough, over a lifetime, to produce the only result that matters.

· · ·

The book ends where the faith ends, which is not at a conclusion but at a promise.

“For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the children of God” (Rom 8:19). The word is apokalypsis: an unveiling, a manifestation. It is the thing the manifest space has been reaching for with the wrong tools, and the thing the Church has been carrying in a tabernacle, and the thing that the world is actually groaning for, whether it knows it or not.

It has not happened yet. Your life, if you are a Christian, is hidden with Christ in God, and it will be manifested, and the manifestation will not be a technique but a resurrection, and it will not be your achievement but your adoption, and it will be given to you in a body, in a communion, in a world made new, with the wounds still in it and the glory coming through them.

Until then: pray. Ask for what you want. Say not my will. Go to confession. Keep the record. Sit with the sick and do not explain their suffering to them. Refuse the systems that tell them it is their fault. Give away whatever you learn.

And when you are tempted to think that nothing is happening, remember the girl at 11:11, and the woman who wrote nine times a day for a year and did not get what she asked for, and the fact that she is still there, in a bedroom, hoping — because hope is the one thing the manifest space could never manufacture and could never destroy, and it is the one thing that the Church has always known how to keep.

The point

You are not creating reality, your desire is not an oracle, there is someone listening who can say no, and what you are waiting for is the manifestation of the children of God.

Do this

Five minutes tonight: the name of Jesus, the thing you actually want, and “not my will but yours.” Then sleep.

What this sets up

Nothing. The book is finished; the appendices are the apparatus — a triage card, a pilot protocol, forty questions still open, and an index for the reader who wants to argue.

Appendix

The Forty Disputed Questions, I

Questions 1–20, in the scholastic form but compressed — each with the objection that gives it force, the distinction that answers it, and what follows in practice. They are offered as a skeleton for a larger work, and for argument.

The question is stated; the strongest objection is given in italics; the determination follows; and each ends with the practice that follows from the answer. Where a question is treated at length elsewhere in the book, the chapter is given.

· · ·

1. Whether the universe can hear?

It seems that it can, since prayers are answered and coincidences cluster around intention. The universe is a creature, and a creature is not a person. What “hears” is the one who made it. The experience of being heard is real; the addressee has been misidentified. Hearing requires a knower, and a knower requires a person or an angel, not a totality that includes the one praying. Practice: address the maker, not the made.

2. Whether the universe is God?

It seems so, since God is everywhere and all is one. Pantheism confuses the Creator with the creature and makes God subject to change, composition, and death. The world is in God “by essence, presence, and power,” not as a part of him. Practice: when you are moved by a landscape, thank the painter; do not drink the paint.

3. Whether God is an energy?

It seems so, since the scriptures speak of power going out from him. “Energy” in the modern sense is a measured quantity of a physical system. God is not a quantity, is not measured, and is not part of any system. The tradition’s energeia means operation or act, and the divine energies are God himself, not a force he emits. Practice: stop trying to feel the current; start trying to keep the commandments. (Ch. 9.)

4. Whether God can be manipulated by technique?

It seems so, since the Church has sacraments, which work ex opere operato. The sacraments are promises, not levers; their efficacy is God’s fidelity, and they are ordered to the covenant. A technique controls its object; a promise binds the one who makes it. To treat a sacrament as a technique is the sin of superstition (CCC 2111). Practice: receive, do not operate. (Ch. 20.)

5. Whether God wants you to be rich?

It seems so, since he promises abundance. He promises himself, and he promises enough. Wealth is a good when it serves and a curse when it rules; the Gospel’s warnings about riches are not rhetorical. The prosperity gospel mistakes a promise of the kingdom for a promise of the market. Practice: ask for what you need, give away what you do not. (Ch. 17.)

6. Whether God’s will can be known from signs?

It seems so, since Gideon asked for a fleece and got one. Signs are ambiguous and infinitely interpretable, and the desire to read them is a desire for control over the future (CCC 2116). God’s will is known through his commands, through the discernment of movements, through counsel, and through the ordinary use of reason. Practice: ask for counsel, not for codes. (Ch. 30.)

7. Whether the world is a projection of consciousness?

It seems so, since “the world is yourself pushed out” and since perception is constructed. Perception is indeed constructed; reality is not. The world is a creature with its own givenness, which is why it can resist you, surprise you, and outlive you. A projection cannot be loved, and the world can. Practice: go outside and let something be other than you. (Ch. 18.)

8. Whether you create your reality?

It seems so, since attention shapes action and action shapes circumstance. You cooperate in a reality you did not create; you are a real cause inside an order you did not establish (CCC 306–307). The difference is responsibility: a creator is responsible for the whole, a cooperator for her part. Practice: distinguish what is yours to do. (Ch. 13, claim 7.)

9. Whether you are God?

It seems so, since the scriptures say “you are gods” (Ps 82:6) and the Church speaks of divinization. By nature, no; by grace, yes — and the two are not close. Divinization is a gift received, which makes the creature more itself; the claim to be God by nature is the oldest lie, and it makes the creature a rival rather than a son. Practice: say “I am not God, and I am not nothing” once a day. (Ch. 13, claim 10.)

10. Whether the self is an illusion?

It seems so, since the mystics speak of the dissolution of the self and neuroscience finds no fixed centre. The self is not an illusion; it is a relation. It exists as constituted by God, as a body, as a member of a people, as one who is known. What is dissolved in contemplation is the false self — the self constructed by grasping — not the person God made. Practice: let yourself be known by someone; that is where the self is. (Ch. 12.)

11. Whether everyone is you pushed out?

It seems so, since our assumptions shape how others appear to us and respond to us. Our assumptions shape our perception and our conduct, and therefore some of our experience. They do not constitute other people, who are creatures with their own freedom and their own standing before God. The doctrine destroys love by destroying the other. Practice: ask a question and listen to the answer. (Ch. 12.)

12. Whether human beings have a “higher self”?

It seems so, since we experience a self that judges the self, and the tradition speaks of the ground of the soul. What the tradition names is conscience, the imago Dei, and the indwelling Spirit — none of which is a part of the self, and all of which are other. The “higher self” is a way of domesticating the voice of God so that it cannot command. Practice: obey what accuses you, and do not identify it with yourself. (Ch. 14.)

13. Whether the body is a message from the mind?

It seems so, since stress causes illness and the psychosomatic is real. Some illness is behaviourally and psychologically mediated, and medicine studies it. The claim that the body is a message, and that illness is therefore unexpressed emotion, converts a partial truth into a total explanation and makes the sick the author of their sickness. Practice: treat the body as a creature to be cared for, not a text to be decoded. (Ch. 11.)

14. Whether desire is a reliable guide?

It seems so, since desire is natural and the Psalms ask God for what they want. Desire is revelatory and unreliable: it tells you what you love, and what you love may be false. It requires interpretation and purification, which is what the spiritual life is for. Practice: ask the three questions — the object beneath, the neighbour, and the open hand. (Ch. 23.)

15. Whether it is wrong to want things?

It seems so, since the saints speak of detachment and the world passes away. It is not wrong to want; it is wrong to be possessed by wanting. The will is made for the good, and the good includes created goods; what must be purified is the inordinateness, not the desire. A Christianity that forbids desire produces either despair or hypocrisy. Practice: want boldly, and hold openly. (Ch. 23.)

16. Whether detachment is a technique?

It seems so, since the manifest space teaches “let go and it will come.” Detachment as a technique for obtaining the thing is the precise opposite of detachment: it is attachment wearing a disguise. Ignatian indifference is freedom from the outcome, not a method for securing it. Practice: test your detachment by what happens when the thing is refused.

17. Whether you can want something too much?

It seems so, since the saints speak of disordered affections. Yes — and the sign is not the intensity of the desire but its position: what you are willing to do, and to sacrifice, and to believe, in order to have it. An inordinate desire is one that has become a god. Practice: name what you would not do to get it, and check whether you would still do it.

18. Whether God gives us the desires of our hearts?

It seems so, since Psalm 37:4 says exactly that. The promise is attached to delight in God: delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give… The desires of a heart that delights in God are different desires from those of a heart that does not, because the delight reforms the desire. Practice: pray for the delight before the desire. (Ch. 23.)

19. Whether the imagination creates reality?

It seems so, since Neville Goddard and the whole tradition of imaginative prayer. The imagination is a real power and a real medium of presence; it is not a cause of being. It mediates what is given; it does not give what is not. Practice: imagine the Gospel, where the object is real. (Appendix A, q. 19 in the longer form; ch. 27.)

20. Whether thoughts are things?

It seems so, since we speak of “the power of thought.” Thoughts are acts of a spiritual power; they are real and they have effects — on the thinker, on her character, on her conduct. They are not substances and they do not act at a distance. The confusion of “real” with “physical” and of “efficacious” with “creative” is the whole error. Practice: take your thoughts to confession, not to the universe.

← PreviousContentsNext →
Appendix

The Forty Disputed Questions, II

Questions 21–40, including the strongest objections to this book — 40 being whether the whole project is a mistake.

21. Whether words have power over events?

It seems so, since Proverbs says life and death are in the tongue. Words have power over speakers, hearers, and communities, and over events through the actions they cause. They do not act on events directly. The “name it and claim it” teaching is a category error with a proof text. Practice: bless rather than curse, and mean it. (Ch. 13, claim 3.)

22. Whether affirmations work?

It seems so, since repetition forms the mind. Repetition does form the mind, which is why the tradition has aspirations. What works is not the formula but the attention, and attention to a false sentence forms a false self. Choose a true sentence and address it. Practice: one verse, three times a day, out loud. (Ch. 27.)

23. Whether it is wrong to speak of a desired outcome as though it had happened?

It seems so, since faith is “the assurance of things hoped for.” Faith’s assurance is about God’s promise, not about the outcome of my wish. Speaking a false present tense as true trains the speaker in a small dishonesty, and the fruit of that training is visible. Practice: speak in the tense of petition and trust. (Ch. 27.)

24. Whether the name of Jesus can be used as a technique?

It seems so, since the apostles used it and the demons fled. The name is a person. It is powerful because he is, not because the syllables are. Used as a formula, it becomes an incantation, and the Church’s own tradition warns against exactly that. Practice: say it to him, not at the problem. (Ch. 27.)

25. Whether illness is attracted by the sufferer?

It seems so, since the mind affects the body and some illness is stress-related. Some illness is mediated by behaviour and stress; none is caused by a “frequency,” and the claim that it is has made the sick the authors of their suffering. It is refuted by John 9, by Job, and by the Cross. Practice: never explain someone’s suffering to them. (Ch. 11.)

26. Whether suffering is a lesson?

It seems so, since “all things work together for good” and we do learn from pain. God can and does bring good out of evil, and sometimes the good is a lesson. But “suffering is a lesson” as a general explanation assigns a purpose to the evil and a fault to the sufferer. The promise is about God’s capacity, not about suffering’s meaning. Practice: say “God can bring good from this,” never “God did this to teach you.”

27. Whether we choose our trials before birth?

It seems so, since “soul contracts” explain seemingly meaningless suffering. The doctrine has no scriptural warrant, and it makes the sufferer the author of her suffering with a longer timeline. It is also unfalsifiable by construction, since the contract is not remembered. Practice: learn to say “I do not know why.” (Ch. 29.)

28. Whether it is wrong to want to be healed?

It seems so, since the saints accepted illness and “thy will be done” seems to forbid asking. It is not wrong; it is commanded. We are to ask for our daily bread and for healing, and to add the clause that makes the asking Christian. The error is not in the asking but in the demand. Practice: ask for healing, and mean the clause. (Ch. 23.)

29. Whether grief can be manifested away?

It seems so, since “low vibration” is to be avoided. Grief is not a failure of alignment; it is the price of love, and the Lord wept at a tomb he was about to open. To suppress grief in the name of frequency is to refuse to be human, and it delays the healing it claims to produce. Practice: grieve in the company of the Church, which has a liturgy for it. (Ch. 11.)

30. Whether the past can be revised?

It seems so, since memory changes and people report release. Memory changes, and release is real — but not by denial. The past is forgiven in confession and healed in prayer, and in neither case is it deleted. A past that can be rewritten cannot be forgiven. Practice: confess, and keep the record. (Ch. 29.)

31. Whether the future can be known?

It seems so, since the prophets foretold and the saints have had foreknowledge. God can reveal what he wills, to whom he wills, and the Church tests such claims severely. The disciplined desire to know the future is divination; the disciplined desire to do God’s will is discernment. Practice: seek counsel, not prediction. (Ch. 30.)

32. Whether the dead can be consulted?

It seems so, since Saul consulted Samuel and the saints are invoked. The saints are asked to pray, which is an act of the communion of the living; mediums attempt to summon the dead for information, which is forbidden (CCC 2116) and is a traffic in power rather than an act of love. Practice: ask the saints to pray for you; do not interrogate the dead.

33. Whether 11:11 means anything?

It seems so, since it keeps happening when I need it. God can use anything, and gratitude for a coincidence is harmless. But the practice of decoding trains a person to relate to reality as a code and to live in low-grade anxiety, and the Church names it among the omens she rejects. Practice: thank God for the moment, and go on with your day. (Ch. 30.)

34. Whether a Catholic may practise manifestation?

It seems so, since much of what it recommends is harmless and some is good. A Catholic may journall, set goals, imagine, be grateful, and ask God for what she wants. She may not attribute the results to resemblance-causation or treat a technique as efficacious. The verdict is therefore not on the practices but on the framework, and it is a qualified no. (Ch. 13.)

35. Whether manifestation is a form of divination?

It seems so, since it seeks to obtain outcomes by a hidden means. Divination seeks knowledge or power over the future through hidden powers; manifestation seeks outcomes through a claimed law of the mind. In its “law” form it is superstition rather than divination (CCC 2111); in its “channeling” and “reality-shifting” forms it moves into divination. The distinction matters for the pastoral response. (Ch. 32.)

36. Whether a priest should refuse absolution to a manifesting penitent?

It seems so, since superstition is a sin against religion. Absolution is refused for lack of disposition, not for confusion. A penitent who is confused, or who uses the language without the metaphysics, should be taught, not refused. Refusal is for the person who persists in a gravely sinful practice with full knowledge and full consent. Practice: teach in the confessional, and be slow to refuse.

37. Whether a Catholic may sell manifestation coaching?

It seems so, since the culture sells everything and the market is there. Selling spiritual power — a technique with a promised effect — is the sin of simony’s cousin and fails the Church’s own criterion about profit (1978 norms, I.B.c). A Catholic may sell books, courses, and labour; she may not sell the promise of a spiritual result as though it were a product. Practice: give it away. (Ch. 35.)

38. Whether the saints can be “manifested”?

It seems so, since people report a saint “coming to them” after a novena. The saints can intercede and can be experienced as present, and the Church’s tradition is full of such accounts, which she tests. They cannot be summoned, managed, or attracted by technique; they are persons, and persons are not mechanisms. Practice: ask, and accept that the answer may be no.

39. Whether the Church has its own manifestation practices?

It seems so, since the novena, the Rosary, and the sacramentals look very like them. She has them in abundance, and this is the book’s central practical claim: the manifest space is a parody of a set of practices that the Church possesses and has largely stopped teaching. The answer is not invention but retrieval. (Ch. 26–31.)

40. Whether this whole project is a mistake?

It seems so: because it lends a Christian vocabulary to a system that denies creation; because it invites the Church to spend a generation on a passing fashion; because the author has no mandate; because the resources would be better spent on the poor; and because a parody is best left to die.

The objection is the strongest in the book, and it is answered only by the criterion that governs every other question here: does it make people holy? If the practices of Part Four produce prayer, conversion, charity, and freedom, then the project is justified by its fruit, whatever becomes of its author. If they do not, then the objector is right, and this book should be put down — firmly, and without ceremony — and the work done again by someone else.

That is the risk of any work of this kind, and it is not removed by writing a chapter about it. It is only made honest.

Appendix

The Triage Card

One page. Photocopy it. It is not a substitute for a trained director, a confessor, or a clinician.

Two questions, always first

  1. “What do you think this practice is doing?” — reveals the metaphysics.
  2. “If it stopped working tomorrow, what would you do?” — reveals the god.

Green — affirm and add the frame. Goal-setting · journalling · gratitude lists · positive self-talk about one’s own capacities · habit, sleep and exercise routines from self-help · “manifesting” used loosely for hoping.

Amber — catechesis and a substitute. Visualization of a desired good · affirmations · vision boards · strong-sense “manifesting” of a job or partner · crystals as aesthetics · astrology as entertainment · loose “energy” talk.

Say: “Almost everything you’re doing is fine. The reason you were given for why it works is not, and here is a better one.” Give: one practice from Part Four, written down, with a time.

Red — renounce, and replace. Channeling or “higher self” guidance · mediums · attempts to control another’s will · “reality shifting” · curses and hexes · telling a sick person she caused her illness · anything requiring secrecy from the Church, a spouse, or a director · any fee for spiritual power.

Say it briefly, without disgust. Then put something in the space.

Six cases in one line each

  • The teenager: do not take the notebook; change the addressee. Give her a novena.
  • The scrupulous: thoughts are not creative; temptation is not sin; the first movement is not consent. Repeat. Refer if severe.
  • The grieving: “That is not true, and it is not what the Church teaches, and I am sorry you were told it.” Then sit down.
  • The person in danger: safety before metaphysics. Refer.
  • The person refusing treatment: using medicine is not a lack of faith. “Take the medicine, and keep praying.” Involve family and doctor the same day.
  • The person with an experience: test the fruit; be slow; nihil obstat is not approval.

The rule about the bedside

No teaching, correction, or catechesis with the dying, the acutely grieving, or the newly diagnosed. Presence only. Say once, if it is true and the moment is right: you did not do this, and you are not being punished, and God is not disgusted by you.

What to hand over

  • One practice — small, timed, written down.
  • One name — a director, confessor, or chaplain, with a phone number.
  • One sentence she will remember at 2 a.m.

When to refer

Persistent scrupulosity · intrusive thoughts causing distress · any suggestion of self-harm · suspected abuse · symptoms of psychosis · involvement with a group that demands secrecy or money. Refer to a clinician, a safeguarding officer, or both. This is not a failure of faith.

Appendix

The Thirty-Day Pilot

A design for a parish or campus test: four weeks, thirty participants, a comparison group, and a commitment to publish the result whether or not it flatters the proposal.

Purpose. To test whether the transpositions of Part Four produce the fruit the Church’s criteria name — prayer, conversion, charity, freedom — in ordinary people, over a month, with a comparison group.

Participants. Thirty, recruited openly, with no selection for or against the manifest space. A comparison group of thirty in a second parish receiving equal attention (a weekly meeting and a course on prayer) without the manifest-space content.

Structure. Four weeks. One group meeting weekly, forty-five minutes. One daily practice, ten to twenty minutes.

WeekPracticeInstructionGroup session
1The Novena of Desire begins (days 1–7)one page; a fixed time; the four movementsintroductions; the two questions; the relinquishment
2Novena concludes (days 8–9), then word and imagewritten petition; one aspiration; fifteen minutes of compositio loci twicewhat happened when you asked; the possibility of refusal
3Time and bodya fixed morning and night prayer; one bodily practice (kneel, fast, walk)the body at prayer; what was difficult
4Memory, desire, and signsconfession or a conversation with a director; the movements logwriting a personal rule of three practices

Measures. At day 0 and day 30, and again at six months: the ten-item instrument of chapter 36, plus one qualitative interview and one behavioural indicator (acts of charity performed, confessions made, reconciliations).

What counts as success. Not enthusiasm. Four movements, in this order of importance:

  1. Safety: no increase in scrupulosity, self-blame, or blame of the sick; a decrease if possible.
  2. Practice: a majority praying daily in a set form at day 30, and half still doing so at six months.
  3. Freedom: participants able to stop for a week without anxiety, and describing God in terms of trust rather than performance.
  4. Charity: measurable acts of service, and at least one reconciliation per participant where one was needed.

What counts as failure. Any of the following: participants become dependent on the group leader; the practice is described as a technique; scrupulosity rises; the six-month follow-up shows collapse; the qualitative interviews describe a God who must be managed. If the pilot fails, publish it and redesign.

Ethics. Written consent; anonymity in publication; a named safeguarding contact; referral pathways; no recording without permission; no fee; no promise of any spiritual or physical outcome at any point.

Cost. Approximately the cost of printing, refreshments, and one facilitator’s time. The pilot is designed to be run by a parish without a budget and without a theologian on staff.

Appendix

A Reader’s Guide and Bibliography

What to read, in what order, and why. Asterisks mark the ten works that would let a reader reconstruct this book’s argument from the sources.

The tradition

Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae. The indispensable text, and more accessible than its reputation. For this book: I, qq. 1, 22, 44–46, 103–105; I-II, qq. 1–5, 49–67; II-II, qq. 83, 95–97. *

Leo XIII, Aeterni Patris (1879). The document that made Thomas the Church’s default, and the source of the motto vetera novis augere et perferre — to strengthen and complete the old by aid of the new. Read it for the method, and read it critically for what it cost.

John Paul II, Fides et Ratio (1998). Especially §§49–51 on the Church’s non-ownership of any philosophy, and §§71–72 on inculturation. The corrective to a Thomism that has become a monument. *

Benedict XVI, Spe Salvi (2007). §§32–34 on prayer as the school of hope and the purification of desire are the theological heart of this book’s anthropology. *

Francis, Gaudete et Exsultate (2018). §§47–59 on contemporary Pelagianism; the diagnosis that applies, with the polarity reversed, to the manifest space.

Catechism of the Catholic Church. 302–314 (providence), 460 (divinization), 946–962 (communion of saints), 1996–2005 (grace), 2111–2117 (superstition and divination), 2735–2741 (prayer and its apparent failure). *

Pontifical Council for Culture and Pontifical Council for Interreligious Dialogue, Jesus Christ, Bearer of the Water of Life (2003). The most precise official description of the phenomenon in any language, and the most neglected. *

Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Norms… on presumed apparitions or revelations (1978), and the Dicastery’s Norms for proceeding in the discernment of alleged supernatural phenomena (2024). The governance template, and a usable taxonomy. *

The sources of the method

M.-D. Chenu, Nature, Man, and Society in the Twelfth Century. The best short account of the crisis that produced the synthesis.

Étienne Gilson, The Christian Philosophy of St. Thomas Aquinas. Still the clearest map.

Josef Pieper, The Four Cardinal Virtues. The best modern introduction to habitus for a non-specialist. *

Erich Przywara, Analogia Entis. Difficult, and the source of the argument in chapter 9. *

Bernard Lonergan, Method in Theology. On conversion and the levels of operation; useful for Part Five.

John Henry Newman, An Essay in Aid of a Grammar of Assent. Real and notional assent; the reason chapter 15 exists.

The movement’s own sources

Phineas P. Quimby. The Quimby Manuscripts, edited by Horatio W. Dresser (1921). The origin, as his students transcribed it: disease as belief, and the cure as argument. Read it beside the chapter 2 genealogy, and notice how much metaphysics he never supplied.

Warren Felt Evans, The Mental Cure (1869) and Mental Medicine (1875). The first books of the movement, and the moment a clinic became a system.

Mary Baker Eddy, Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures (1875). The rival branch of mind cure — not the same thing, and not on good terms with it. Read with Satter on why the quarrel mattered.

Emma Curtis Hopkins (1849\u20131925), Class Lessons of 1888 and High Mysticism. The movement’s teacher of teachers: almost every founder of its institutions studied with her or with one of her students. Read her for the mysticism, which the business wing quietly dropped.

Wallace D. Wattles, The Science of Getting Rich (1910); Charles F. Haanel, The Master Key System (1912); Napoleon Hill, Think and Grow Rich (1937). The business wing, which supplied the promise and the course.

Ernest Holmes, The Science of Mind (1926). Religious Science: the movement’s most systematic attempt at a theology, and the reason some of its teachers can sound almost orthodox.

Norman Vincent Peale, The Power of Positive Thinking (1952); Joseph Murphy, The Power of Your Subconscious Mind (1963). The passage into mainline respectability, and the paperback that carried the method into the places a parish priest is likely to meet it.

The manifest space, described seriously

Neville Goddard, Feeling Is the Secret (1944) and The Power of Awareness (1952). The most metaphysically explicit version. *

Rhonda Byrne, The Secret (2006). The popular synthesis, and the version most critics are actually answering.

Esther and Jerry Hicks, Ask and It Is Given (2004). The energetic variant, and the clearest statement of the “Abraham” material.

Kate Bowler, Blessed: A History of the American Prosperity Gospel (2013). Indispensable on the Christian genealogy.

Beryl Satter, Each Mind a Kingdom (1999). The social history of New Thought.

Tara Isabella Burton, Strange Rites (2020) and Self-Made (2023). The contemporary landscape, written with sympathy and without credulity.

Eva Illouz, Saving the Modern Soul (2008). The therapeutic register, and why it is so compelling.

Practice

Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises. §§23 (indifference), 47 (composition of place), 121–126 (application of the senses), 169–189 (election), 313–336 (discernment). *

John of the Cross, Ascent of Mount Carmel. I.13 (the nada maxims) and II.11–12 (on not clinging to apprehensions).

Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul. The little way, which is the whole answer to the manifest space’s scale.

Jean-Pierre de Caussade, Abandonment to Divine Providence. The doctrine of the present moment, and a cure for the fantasy of control.

Romano Guardini, The Spirit of the Liturgy. On sacred time; read with chapter 28.

Alexander Schmemann, For the Life of the World. The sacramental worldview, from the East.

A note on what is missing

There is no adequate scholarly literature on the current, post-2020, algorithmic form of the manifest space. The ethnography has not been done; the content audits have not been published; the pastoral data do not exist. That is the largest gap this book points at, and it is the reason chapter 33 is a research plan rather than a summary.

Appendix

Glossary

The technical terms used in this book, in plain language, for the reader who is not a theologian — and for the theologian who wants to know which sense is meant.

Analogy of being (analogia entis). The doctrine that words said of God and of creatures are neither univocal (the same meaning) nor equivocal (no relation), but analogous: the same order of meaning, different mode. The instrument that dissolves “energy,” “alignment,” and “frequency.” (Ch. 9)

Aspiration. A short prayer, often scriptural, repeated through the day. The Catholic counterpart of the affirmation. (Ch. 27)

Charism. A grace-gift given by the Spirit for the common good (1 Cor 12:7), not an achievement and not under the recipient’s control. (Ch. 17)

Consolation / desolation. In Ignatian discernment, an interior movement that increases faith, hope, and love and brings peace, or its opposite: darkness, disquiet, and a pull away from God. Not the same as feeling good or bad. (Ch. 30)

Divinization (theosis). The doctrine that the Christian becomes God by grace, by adoption and participation — not by nature. The true doctrine that the manifest space’s “you are God” parodies. (Ch. 13, claim 10)

Ex opere operato. “By the work worked”: the sacraments confer grace by Christ’s action and promise, not by the minister’s worthiness. The opposite of a technique, and easily confused with one. (Ch. 20)

Habitus. A stable disposition, formed by acts, by which a power is disposed well or ill; the technical term behind “virtue,” and the true version of the “law of assumption.” (Ch. 24)

Impetration. The asking by which we obtain from God what he has ordained to give through asking (ST II-II, q. 83, a. 2). Real causality, not manipulation. (Ch. 22)

Indifference (indiferencia). Ignatian freedom from inordinate attachment to any outcome, such that one is ready to receive health or sickness, riches or poverty, provided it serves God. Not apathy, and not a technique. (Ch. 23)

Manifestation (phanerōsis, apokalypsis). In Scripture, the making-visible of God in Christ, of the Spirit in the Church, of the children of God at the end. Never a technique of the self. (Ch. 16)

Manifestation of conscience (manifestatio conscientiae). The disclosure of one’s interior to a director or confessor in order to be judged, healed, and directed. The reverse of projection. (Ch. 21)

Nihil obstat. In the 2024 norms, the judgment that “nothing stands in the way” of a devotion — without any claim about its supernatural origin. The most useful verdict in the Church’s vocabulary, and the one most often forgotten. (Ch. 7, 32)

Pelagianism. The teaching that human beings can fulfil God’s commands by their own powers without grace. The manifest space is its most complete modern form. (Ch. 10)

Providence. The order of all things to their end in the divine mind, executed through real secondary causes, including free creatures. Not fatalism; not deism. (Ch. 22)

Secondary cause. A creature acting as a real cause within God’s governance. The doctrine that makes human action serious without making it divine. (Ch. 22)

Superstition. In the Catechism, attributing a magical importance to practices otherwise lawful, or attributing the efficacy of prayer or sacrament to the external performance alone (CCC 2111). The error of the Catholic as well as the manifester. (Ch. 20)

Tempting God (tentare Deum). Requiring a specified result as the price of faith; putting God to the test. The theological name for the technique that guarantees an outcome. (Ch. 13, claim 14)

Theodicy of participation. The claim that the answer to suffering is not an explanation but a presence, a promise, and a transformation. Contrasted with every theodicy that consoles by assigning blame. (Ch. 11)

Appendix

Note on the Text

How this book was made, how to correct it, and what it is not.

Status. This is a first edition, not an approved publication, and it is a theological research project rather than a settled statement of doctrine. It has no imprimatur, no nihil obstat, and no ecclesiastical mandate of any kind: it is not authoritative, and it does not ask to be treated as though it were. It was written with the help of the Holy Spirit — which is a claim about help received and not about authority conferred, and the two are worth keeping apart, because the second is a bishop’s to make and the first is not. It is submitted to the judgment of the Church, and any reader who finds an error should assume that the error is the author’s and not the faith’s.

Provenance. The manuscript is written in plain text, one file per chapter, and built by a small script into four editions: a single-file reading edition; a print edition set for 5.5 × 8.5 inch pages; an EPUB 3 file with a navigation document and cover; and a typeset PDF with running heads, page numbers, and a contents page whose numbers are generated from the finished book. The word count and the page estimate printed at the end of the reading edition are generated by the build, not asserted by the author, and they change every time a chapter is added. The PDF is the only edition in which the pages are fixed, and therefore the only one in which “one page” means what it says.

Citations. References are given in the text rather than in footnotes, in a short form: Aquinas by part, question, and article (ST I-II, q. 49, a. 1); magisterial documents by paragraph; the Exercises by paragraph number (SpEx 23); the Catechism by paragraph (CCC 2111). Appendix D gives the editions relied on.

Composite portraits. The named persons in the early chapters are composites; their details have been combined and altered, and no composite corresponds to a single identifiable individual. Direct quotations from published authors are real and are cited. Where a number appears, it is drawn from a published source; where the author is reasoning from impressions, the text says so.

What this book is not. It is not a diagnosis of any individual. It is not a substitute for spiritual direction, confession, or clinical care. It is not an argument that a Christian may practise the law of attraction — the verdicts in chapter 13 are mostly reject. And it is not the last word: it is a first attempt at a method, offered in the hope that others will do it better.

How to correct it. The most useful corrections are of four kinds: a factual error about a source; a misdescription of a practice by someone who does it; a doctrinal error identified with a citation; and a report of a pilot — including a failed one. A book of this kind is worth exactly as much as it is corrigible, and the corrigibility has to be real, which means that the corrections have to be able to change the text.

Acknowledgements. To the priests and catechists who answered questions they were not trained for; to the people who described their practices without requiring that they be admired; to the tradition that has been doing this work for two thousand years, and to the saints who did it without writing anything down.
